# Karpathy Ideas: all ideas in one file

Unofficial, curated notes on Andrej Karpathy's public ideas. Not affiliated with or endorsed by him.
Summaries and Apply steps are our own words under CC BY 4.0 (Apply steps translate his idea into practice; a step marked "Our reading" or "our addition" goes further than the idea itself, and one "Our reading" line at the top of Apply marks all its steps); quotes belong to their author. Source: https://github.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas

*(Anthropic period)*: dated 2026-05-19 or later, after he [joined Anthropic](https://x.com/karpathy/status/2056753169888334312), and about Claude or Anthropic. Weigh these with that in mind.

---

Date: 2026-11-04 · Kind: view · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2118048337018712423 · Themes: ai-progress · Status: current

# How you could have predicted LLMs from the 1970s

Replying to a post on how science fiction got AI wrong, Karpathy says most pre-2000 stories missed.
To get it right from about 1970, you would imagine the world 50 years later and make six
inferences. Most knowledge work moves onto screens. A global network connects computers. That
creates huge stores of digital data about how people think. Hand-programming intelligence is too
hard, but language has statistical structure that you can learn, as Shannon's n-grams showed. With
enough data and compute, an ELIZA-like model becomes an economically useful imitation. Scaling
laws then concentrate the economics: a few organizations build a few minds and deploy copies. You
would also have to bet against hand-programmed robots.

## Context

- His list names HAL as a notable exception among older stories.
- Related: [Software 2.0 automates what you can verify](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-11-17-software-2-automates-what-you-can-verify.md).

---

Date: 2026-11-01 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2116957135661945283 · Themes: agentic-coding, agent-native-software · Status: current · Anthropic period

# Build a bespoke app in a weekend by only talking to Claude

Karpathy was unhappy with YouTube recommendations. In about two hours with Opus 5.5 he built
HackerTube: a YouTube-style site limited to 6,454 videos that people recommended in Hacker News
comments over twenty years. He did everything by talking to Claude. By hand he only made a
YouTube API key, started a server, and bought the domain. He then gave Claude the server address
and asked it to update, secure, harden, deploy and optimize. The cost split matters. Claude first
removed spam and links with scripts and regexes. A Claude Code workflow then sent the remaining
comments to Sonnet for labeling. He reports over 90% of the tokens went there; the app work took
about one million Opus tokens. He also published the data so others can rebuild.

## Apply

- Split work by cost: scripts and filters first, a cheap model for bulk labeling, a strong model
  for design and deployment.
- Publish the derived dataset and tell readers to point their own agent at it.
- Give the agent the server address and ask it to harden and deploy. Review the result.
- A small browser extension can be one prompt: "Create and deploy an extension that ...".

## Context

- He used Claude Code on Opus 5.5 at medium effort as his default. He said he would not trust
  weaker models with this much freedom.
- Related: [Cheaper software raises the demand for software](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-20-cheaper-software-more-demand.md) and
  [fewer bits](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-11-01-shorter-prompts-fewer-bits.md).
- He first posted it on his blog on 2026-10-31 ([HackerTube](https://karpathy.bearblog.dev/hacker-tube/)).
  The site has recommendations without accounts, keyboard shortcuts and a data export.

Date: 2026-11-01 · Kind: practice · Source: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50323111 · Themes: context-and-prompting · Status: current

# With strong models, write shorter prompts

Karpathy says his prompts are shrinking and getting blunter, because the model understands the
intent from fewer words. He now fears giving too much detail. A long list of requirements can
confine the model to a worse answer than the one it would have found alone. So he sees the
prompting approach moving toward fewer bits, given at the right moment. He is unsure whether to
make a video about it, because his own best practices look so simple that he finds them
embarrassing.

## Apply

- Start with the goal and the check, in a few lines. Add detail only where the output goes wrong.
- Remove requirements that only restate what a good engineer would do anyway.
- When the model drifts, add one targeted line instead of a long rewrite.

## Context

- A Hacker News reply of 2026-11-01 in the thread on HackerTube, an app he built by talking to Claude. The reply itself names no model.
- Compare [Success criteria, not steps](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-01-26-success-criteria-not-steps.md), and the case
  where more context helps: [rambling into voice mode](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-07-21-ramble-session-with-voice.md).

Date: 2026-10-02 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2105909609487872075 · Themes: llm-psychology, verification · Status: current · Anthropic period

# Test a model by asking if coordinates are land or water

Karpathy shared a cheap eval made by another user. Give a model a latitude and longitude as text
and ask "Land or Water?". Repeat for 16,200 points, one every two degrees, and draw the answers
as an image. No images or tools are involved. In the shared chart, older Claude models draw noisy
blobs and newer ones draw clean continents, with accuracy rising from about 60% to about 99%.
In a reply he stresses the point: the image comes only from reading text and predicting text. The
only image is how the answers are placed in 2D.

## Apply

- Build small, cheap evals that you can plot, so you see change between model versions at a glance.
- Use a probe with a known answer key (here, a land mask) so you can score it automatically.
- Remember that models hold more world knowledge in text form than they show in normal chat.

## Context

- The chart covered twelve Claude models. Our reading: it is also an easy way to compare models
  from one vendor over time. It is one probe, so do not read it as a general ranking.
- Related: [A huge creative test for models](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-08-02-big-budget-creative-test-for-models.md).

---

Date: 2026-10-02 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2105819303471976479 · Themes: output-and-reading, learning-and-education · Status: current

# Make model output easier to understand, from STE to video

As agents do more work, people will spend more time understanding what models produce. Karpathy
gives four formats, each better than the one before. First, writing: ask the model to explain
something in ASD-STE100, a controlled English made for aircraft maintenance manuals. Its strict
rules give clean text. The spec is very strict, so he sometimes asks for a rough 80% match.
Second, diagrams instead of prose. Third, HTML for interactive pages with animation. Fourth, and
the one he is most hopeful about, custom explainer videos on any topic, for example in the style
of 3Blue1Brown, with narration from a speech API. He says this is starting to work.

## Apply

- Add to a prompt: "Explain in ASD-STE100, about 80% strict."
- When a text answer is dense, ask for a diagram or a one-page infographic instead.
- Ask for "HTML" for anything with several parts, such as a comparison or a walkthrough.
- For a topic you must learn, ask for a short explainer video script with scenes and narration, and
  have the agent use a speech API or a local text-to-speech tool.

## Context

- The post drew a large audience. Some experienced users answered that they had used these
  tricks for a year. He replied that most people now paying attention started in the last year.
- Builds on [Text chat is the terminal era](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-03-31-text-chat-is-the-terminal-era.md). The
  second half of the same post is [Oversight, and software made to be thrown away](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-10-02-oversight-and-discardable-software.md).

Date: 2026-10-02 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2105819303471976479 · Themes: agent-native-software, ai-progress · Status: current

# Human work rises into oversight, helped by throwaway software

Karpathy ends his post on output formats with two claims. First, as models get better they do more
of the legwork alone, so more human work moves up the abstraction ladder into oversight and
understanding. Second, models can help with that too. Intelligence and code are becoming
abundant, so you can ask for large, custom software artifacts that you will discard after use,
such as web apps and video explainers. These would never have been worth building before. His
advice is to push on this and see what happens.

## Apply

- When you must review a big change, ask for a one-off viewer: a diff explorer, a dependency graph
  or a dashboard of test results.
- Treat these artifacts as disposable. Do not maintain them. Generate a new one next time.
- Spend your own time on judging results, not on producing them.

## Context

- Same post as [Make model output easier to understand](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-10-02-make-model-outputs-easy-to-understand.md).
- Related: [Cheaper software raises the demand for software](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-20-cheaper-software-more-demand.md).

Date: 2026-09-21 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2102124533729955960 · Themes: ai-progress, agent-native-software · Status: current

# Fast, no-thinking LLMs fill an under-served niche

A product was described as a zero-shot classifier built on a strong LLM. Karpathy explains its
success this way: it sits at one point of the Pareto curve of LLM trade-offs. At that point there
is no thinking, one output token and low latency, with "good enough" intelligence. Demand there
was large but hidden, and builders ignored it because the whole field raced toward higher
intelligence. The practical view: the best model for a job is not always the smartest one.

## Apply

- For labeling, routing and filtering, test a small, fast model with a one-token answer first.
- Turn thinking off when the task is a lookup or a classification.
- Compare cost, latency and accuracy on your own data, not on public benchmarks.

## Context

- Reply to a post about rescuing an old ML idea with LLMs.
- Our reading: the same logic supports using cheap models for bulk work, as in
  [the HackerTube project](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-11-01-hackertube-weekend-app.md).

Date: 2026-09-12 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2098781917076504752 · Themes: output-and-reading, agentic-coding · Status: current

# Show big codebases as spatial maps, not file lists

Someone built a 120 Hz explorer for a 2.5-million-line codebase. Karpathy replies that he sees large
projects such as Linux as digital megastructures, but you cannot see them. An office looks like
people staring at screens. For an explorer he suggests 3D, or at least 2D with modules grouped in
space. Insides would show private code and data, boundaries would show public interfaces and
their call sites, and collaborators would zoom around and cast diffs.

## Apply

- Ask an agent to generate an HTML map of your repo: modules as boxes, public APIs on the edges.
- Colour the map by recent change, test failures or owner to find where to look.
- Use such a map when you review a large agent-made change.

## Context

- Two replies from September 2026. Related: [Work rises into oversight](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-10-02-oversight-and-discardable-software.md).
- First raised on [2025-06-04](https://x.com/karpathy/status/1930326685918081077): lay the repo out on a 2D canvas, hover over a variable to see its links across files, and switch lenses such as test coverage or git age.

Date: 2026-08-20 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2090478783895929036 · Themes: agentic-coding, research-and-training · Status: current

# Agents make old software abstractions optional

Someone wrote model code as one compilable forward-and-backward function, with no autograd.
Karpathy agrees with the direction. Many abstractions were built for a world where industry had
finite intelligence and attention. Now agents can do the math, the drudgery and the verification,
so it is more attractive to take those layers apart. He extends this: the spec could be something
as plain as microgpt, which is scalar Python with for loops. Everything else is compilation, and
PyTorch becomes a rather poor intermediate representation.

## Apply

- Before you add a framework layer, ask whether an agent could write the plain version and test it.
- Keep a small, readable reference implementation as the spec, and have the agent derive fast code.
- Check the generated code against the reference on every change.

## Context

- A reply thread from August 2026. Our reading: it is a bet on spec-first work, not a claim that
  frameworks disappear now.
- Related: [Success criteria, not steps](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-01-26-success-criteria-not-steps.md).

---

Date: 2026-08-02 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2083749667410727319 · Themes: ai-progress, agent-native-software · Status: current · Anthropic period

# Test frontier models with a large creative job

Karpathy says simple tests such as a pelican riding a bicycle are no longer enough. His
extension: give the model the opening paragraph of The Lord of the Rings, a budget of one million
tokens (about ten dollars), and ask for a three.js render. Opus 5 worked for about two hours and
wrote some 5,500 lines of code that drew the story procedurally. The result was rough but
impressive. His main point is economic: nobody would spend the time on something this custom, but
models have unlimited patience, so it moves from nobody doing it to a plain "why not". He expects
hyper-custom worlds and games made on demand. In replies he adds that procedural code can drive
storyboarding and control, with video-to-video models adding the final look. He also likes the
idea of turning a historical photo into a playable world.

## Apply

- Build your own private test: one open task, a fixed token budget, a result you can inspect.
- Ask for custom worlds, simulators or games from a text or image when a one-off is enough.
- Use code for layout and control, and a video model for texture and style.

## Context

- Related weakness: [Models cannot check their own work in video and games](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-08-02-models-cannot-audit-video-and-games.md).
- He published the playable source at karpathy.ai/lotr-movie.

---

Date: 2026-08-02 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2083749667410727319 · Themes: verification, llm-psychology · Status: current · Anthropic period

# Models cannot yet check their own work in video and games

While Opus 5 built a Lord of the Rings scene in code, Karpathy saw a limit. The model could not
watch a video or play a game at speed. To audit its work it took screenshots at chosen moments,
slowly and with care, and still made mistakes and left rough parts. He calls this a missing raw
capability: native multimodal perception of moving scenes and gameplay. Our reading: the loop
"build, look, fix" that works well for web pages is much weaker when the result changes over time.

## Apply

- For animation or game work, give the agent a way to record state: logs, frame dumps, scripted
  playthroughs and assertions, not only screenshots.
- Add simple checks that need no vision, such as object counts and positions at set times.
- Plan for human review of the result. Expect visual jank that the agent did not see.

## Context

- Same post as [a huge creative test for models](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-08-02-big-budget-creative-test-for-models.md).
- Compare [Success criteria, not steps](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-01-26-success-criteria-not-steps.md): it works best
  when the agent can check the goal itself.

Date: 2026-07-21 · Kind: view · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2079645572047548608 · Themes: llm-psychology · Status: current

# Model self-knowledge comes from text about models

Karpathy notes that a model's picture of itself builds up from pretraining on text in which people
talk about models. The picture is late and partial. For example, models still say a task "would
take a human team six months", which describes human speed, not theirs. But it is improving: he
sees that a model now seems to understand what he means when he says he will compact its context.

## Apply

- Do not trust a model's estimate of how long a task takes. Measure it.
- Tell the model about its own situation: that you will compact, that it has a token budget, that
  it runs in a loop. Recent models use this information.
- Do not read a model's answer to "what are you?" as evidence of how it was built.

## Context

- A reply on 2026-07-21 to a post about models claiming that a task needs months of human work.
- Our reading: this fits his view that models are shaped by their training data, not by lived
  experience. See [LLMs are ghosts, not animals](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-10-01-llms-are-ghosts-not-animals.md).
- First raised on [2025-01-02](https://x.com/karpathy/status/1874656428733899128): a model has no sense of self, so what it says about itself depends on whether its makers added self-knowledge data in finetuning. Without that data its answer is a nearest-neighbour guess.
- His nanochat recipe for adding that data: [Give a model an identity with synthetic conversations](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-10-21-give-a-small-model-an-identity-with-synthetic-data.md).

Date: 2026-07-21 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2079610838143623371 · Themes: context-and-prompting · Status: current

# Give the LLM more context by rambling into voice mode

Sometimes the model needs more information about your goal, but typing it is a chore. Karpathy
then switches to voice and talks for about ten minutes with no structure at all. He may say at the
start that this is speech recognition, so the model expects typos. He may also turn it into a short
interview over a few turns. He finds that models reconstruct long, incoherent rambling well, and
their echo of your thoughts is often cleaner than the original. The result is a better shared
picture of the task, so you correct less from then on.

## Apply

- Use `/voice` in Claude Code, or any dictation tool, when a task needs a lot of background.
- Start with a line such as "This is speech recognition, so ignore typos."
- Ask the model to restate your goal and list open questions before it starts to work.
- Fix the restated goal once, then continue. This costs less than many small corrections later.

## Context

- The opposite case is [Fewer bits, administered just right](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-11-01-shorter-prompts-fewer-bits.md).
  Both aim at the same thing: the model must understand what you mean.

---

Date: 2026-06-23 · Kind: view · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2069547676849557725 · Themes: agent-native-software, agentic-coding · Status: current · Anthropic period

# The third LLM interface is a persistent teammate

Karpathy calls Claude Tag the third big redesign of LLM interfaces. The first was a website you
visit. The second was an app on your computer. The third is a self-contained entity that stays
running, works asynchronously, and has the tools and context of a whole organization. It joins
the team, and you talk to it as you would to a person. He says the idea is simple, but the hard
part is the engineering that makes it work: tools, integrations, compute environments, memory and
security. In a follow-up he rejects the view that it is a chat bot with search over Slack. He says
it writes most of the code, is deeply integrated, and makes everyone feel like a manager.

## Apply

- Treat an agent as a team member: give it a channel, tool access and memory, not a one-off chat.
- Delegate work that can run while you do something else, and review the result later.
- Judge such a product by whether it works in your real tools, not by how simple a first version
  looks.

## Context

- Reply to the launch of Claude Tag on 2026-06-23. He says he now works from Slack.
- This is the view of a person who works at Anthropic. Weigh it with that in mind.

Date: 2026-05-01 · Kind: view · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2050240810403410211 · Themes: research-and-training, llm-psychology · Status: current

# Self-distilled corrections still leak slop

A user described a workflow: record a long rambling voice note, have the LLM turn it into an
artifact, then give 10 to 15 rounds of corrections. The user compared it to on-policy
self-distillation. Karpathy agrees it is tempting because it works so well. But he still sees slop
leak through in the concept space, and it gets harder to spot. There is also strong pressure to
say "just ship it". His guess, with a question mark: the final text may still be useful teacher
data for supervised fine-tuning of most smaller students.

## Apply

- After many rounds of correction, review the result once more for subtle conceptual errors.
- Mark generated training text and sample it for review before you fine-tune on it.
- Set a rule that checks must pass before shipping, not only a feeling of polish.

## Context

- A reply from 2026-05-01. See also [rambling into voice mode](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-07-21-ramble-session-with-voice.md)
  and [coding agents make subtle conceptual mistakes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-01-26-coding-agents-make-subtle-conceptual-mistakes.md).

Date: 2026-04-30 · Kind: practice · Source: https://karpathy.bearblog.dev/sequoia-ascent-2026/ · Themes: ai-progress, verification · Status: current

# Find valuable domains that are verifiable and undertrained

Karpathy gives founders one concrete angle. Look for a field that is worth a lot, easy to check and
little trained on by frontier labs. If you can build an environment where a model tries actions and
gets a reliable reward, you may improve it by finetuning or reinforcement learning even when
the base model is weak there. Coding and maths are already heavily targeted. Many economically
important fields may have verifiable structure that nobody has used yet. He calls this a
startup wedge.

## Apply

- List the tasks in a field and mark which have an automatic pass or fail signal.
- Build the environment first: a simulator, a test suite, a scorer. It makes the later model
  work possible, and it has value on its own as an eval.
- Check the base model on the task. If it fails on basic steps, you may be off its rails.

## Context

- Builds on [Jagged intelligence follows verifiability and training focus](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-20-jagged-intelligence-follows-verifiability.md) and
  [Software 2.0 automates what you can verify](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-11-17-software-2-automates-what-you-can-verify.md).
- Our reading: this is a founder hypothesis from a talk, not a tested result.
- Source: his blog post of 2026-04-30, an LLM-made summary of his Sequoia Ascent 2026 talk that
  he checked and published, with the video linked.

Date: 2026-04-30 · Kind: practice · Source: https://karpathy.bearblog.dev/sequoia-ascent-2026/ · Themes: ai-progress, agentic-coding · Status: current

# Test candidates on building and securing a project with agents

If agentic engineering is the new core skill, interviews should test it. Karpathy finds coding
puzzles a poor match now. He suggests a different task: create a large project with
agents, put it online, harden it, and then let adversarial agents try to break it. This tests
whether the candidate can split work for agents, write useful specs, keep quality while moving
fast, review generated work, harden a system, and use agents as leverage instead of producing
slop. He expects the "10x engineer" gap to widen for people who master these workflows.

## Apply

- Give candidates a multi-hour project, a free choice of agent tools, and a deployment target.
- Score the spec, the review notes, the tests and the security result, not only the final app.
- Run a red-team agent against the result and ask the candidate to fix what it finds.
- Ask them to explain a design choice the agent made and why they kept or changed it.

## Context

- It follows from
  [Vibe coding raises the floor; agentic engineering raises the ceiling](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-02-04-agentic-engineering-vs-vibe-coding.md).
- Source: his blog post of 2026-04-30, an LLM-made summary of his Sequoia Ascent 2026 talk that
  he checked and published, with the video linked.

---

Date: 2026-04-30 · Kind: practice · Source: https://karpathy.bearblog.dev/sequoia-ascent-2026/ · Themes: agent-native-software · Status: current

# Some apps should disappear into the model

Karpathy built MenuGen as a normal web app: OCR the menu, generate a picture for each dish,
show the page. It needed a front end, APIs, deployment, auth and payments. He later saw a
version where you photograph the menu and a multimodal model draws the dishes straight onto the
image. Most of the app is gone, and the network turns input media into output media. His
lesson for founders: AI is not only a faster way to build old apps. Some apps should stop
being apps. The old stack wrapped code around a conversion that the model can do directly.

## Apply

- For a new idea, first try one prompt with a strong multimodal model before you design an app.
- If a prototype is "one model call plus a loop", question whether it needs auth, a database
  and hosting at all.
- Keep an app only where it adds what the model cannot: shared state, payments, private data,
  guarantees.

## Context

- In the 2025 MenuGen post he already asked whether the app could be just a prompt, like a
  custom GPT or an artifact. The 2026 summary gives the answer. See
  [Vibe coding a real app is easy locally and hard to ship](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-04-27-vibe-coding-real-app-lessons.md).
- The text is an LLM-made summary of his Sequoia talk that he published on his blog.

Date: 2026-04-10 · Kind: view · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2042615713219908059 · Themes: ai-progress, agent-native-software · Status: current

# Big labs' roadmaps are predictable, which leaves room for startups

A reader pointed to a product concept that OpenAI seemed unlikely to keep pushing. Karpathy agrees
that the concept is good and that dropping it makes sense for the lab. He hopes a startup will
clone it and give it care and iteration, since many people would love it. More generally, he says
what big labs will build next is easy to see ahead of time. That leaves large gaps, and this is one
of the biggest.

## In his words

> "the product roadmap of big labs is clear and predictable"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2026-04-10

## Apply

- Look at features labs launched and left unattended. Check usage signals before you build.
- Choose niches where care, iteration and polish count more than model scale.

## Context

- A short reply; he did not name a market size. The parent post is not captured in our archive.

---

Date: 2026-04-10 · Kind: view · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2042626702459674801 · Themes: ai-progress · Status: current

# LLM simulators are the tractable form of brain upload

Science fiction about brain upload needs exotic technology, such as scanning and simulating a
brain. Karpathy says a lossy, approximate version will arrive much sooner through LLM simulators
of people. He sketches a startup: you visit for a few days of detailed video interviews, with
questions chosen to give the best fidelity. The company finetunes an LLM on the data and gives
you an API endpoint of your simulation. With avatar tools such as HeyGen plus a model with deep
knowledge and personality, he says it is possible around now. He calls it trippy and somewhat
dystopian. He thinks neuroscience-based approaches are armchair philosophy next to this path.

## Context

- Replies from 2026-04-10, with no source tested. Our reading: a forecast with an open
  fidelity question. Related: [explicit memory as files](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-04-04-explicit-personal-memory-as-files.md).

Date: 2026-04-09 · Kind: view · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2042334451611693415 · Themes: ai-progress, llm-psychology · Status: current

# People judge AI differently because they use different AI

Karpathy sees a growing gap in how people understand AI. One group tried a free or old model, saw
silly errors and formed a view from that. Another pays for top agentic models and uses them in
code, maths and research, where models restructure a code base in an hour or find security holes.
The groups speak past each other, and both are partly right. Progress is fastest where rewards can
be checked, which suits reinforcement learning, and these areas also bring the most business
money. In October 2026 he refined it into a funnel, by rough numbers: about 75% of people have
barely used LLMs, about 20% use free chat now and then, about 20 million professionals use frontier
models for maths and code, and about 5,000 people inside labs see swarms of agents on huge
projects. Impact also grows with the size of the problem you give it.

## In his words

> "the people in these two groups are speaking past each other"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2026-04-09

## Apply

- Before you judge a model for your work, test the current best paid model on your own task, with
  tool access.
- Try frontier models on your biggest, most verifiable problem, not on a one-paragraph question.
- When you argue about AI with someone, ask which tier they use.
- For soft tasks (writing, advice), expect slower gains and add your own review.
- Plan for review capacity: he says human review is starting to fall behind agent output.

## Context

- April 2026 reply to a post saying that awe at AI matches how much you use it to code; in a
  follow-up he said the OpenClaw moment mattered because non-technical people met agentic models.
  The October 2026 posts re-shared the April idea; the funnel numbers are his napkin maths.
- Related: [Jagged intelligence follows verifiability](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-20-jagged-intelligence-follows-verifiability.md)
  and [Software 2.0 automates what you can verify](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-11-17-software-2-automates-what-you-can-verify.md).

Date: 2026-04-04 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2040549459193704852 · Themes: ai-progress · Status: current

# AI can make governments more legible and accountable

Karpathy is optimistic about people using AI to see their governments more clearly. Governments
usually make society legible to themselves. AI lets society do the same in reverse. He argues
that accountability was not limited by access, since governments publish huge amounts of data. It
was limited by the intelligence needed to process it, as with a 4,000-page omnibus bill that is
open on paper but unreadable in practice. His examples: spending and budgets, diffs of
legislation, voting records against stated positions, lobbying graphs, procurement, campaign
finance. Local government may be the best target, since it gets less national coverage. He warns
that the same tools can be used the other way.

## In his words

> "it has been constrained by intelligence"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2026-04-04

## Apply

- Pick one public data source (a city council's agendas, a budget file) and ask an agent to
  summarise changes since last year, with page citations.
- Have the agent diff two versions of a bill and list what changed in plain English.
- Check each claim against the source text before you publish it.

## Context

- Stated as something he had been thinking about, posted on a quote of a UK government org chart
  tool. Related: [AI-capability gap](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-04-09-ai-capability-gap-two-groups.md).

Date: 2026-04-04 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2040572272944324650 · Themes: knowledge-management, agent-native-software · Status: current

# Personal AI memory should be plain files you own

Farza built a personal wiki of 400 articles from his diary, notes and messages. Karpathy used it
as an example of a better way to personalise AI than the usual promise that the AI improves with use. He gives four reasons. It is explicit: you can see what the AI knows and does not
know. It is yours: the data stays on your computer, not locked in a provider. It follows "file
over app": plain markdown and images work with any tool, and agents can use the whole Unix
toolkit on them. It is bring-your-own-AI: Claude, Codex or an open model can all plug in, and you
could finetune a model on the wiki. He admits this takes some file management, and says agent
skill is a core skill of this century.

## In his words

> "File over app."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2026-04-04

## Apply

- Keep what your AI should know about you in a folder of markdown files, not only in a vendor's
  memory feature.
- Ask the agent to build and maintain it from your notes, then read it and correct errors.
- Keep the files in git or a synced folder, so any tool or model can use them.

## Context

- Follows his [knowledge bases](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-04-02-llm-knowledge-bases.md) post. It answers the flaws in
  [LLM memory](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-25-memory-personalization-overreach.md).

---

Date: 2026-04-04 · Kind: practice · Source: https://gist.github.com/karpathy/442a6bf555914893e9891c11519de94f · Themes: agent-native-software, context-and-prompting · Status: current

# Share an idea file, not code

The LLM-wiki gist says at the top that it is an "idea file". It is written to be copy-pasted into
the reader's own agent (Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode or similar). It states the high-level
pattern and leaves the details open: folder layout, page formats, tools. The agent and the
reader decide those together. The closing note says every part is optional and modular, and the
document exists only to pass on the pattern. The form fits a world where each reader has an
agent that can build the specifics, so a fixed implementation is less useful than a clear idea.

## Apply

- When you share a workflow, write the why and the shape in a page of markdown. Skip the
  repository.
- State which parts are optional, so the reader's agent can drop what does not fit.
- When you receive an idea file, paste it into your agent and ask: "Propose a version for my
  project and list what you would leave out."

## Context

- Gist of 2026-04-04. The same stance, in code form, appears in
  [Treat small apps as disposable](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-11-18-disposable-vibe-coded-apps.md).
- Our reading: this repository's own idea files follow the same shape.
- His announcing post (2026-04-04) says the same in short form. In a related reply he cites Peter Steinberger, who wants pull requests to be "prompt requests": if an agent can build the idea, a pasted, over-built code dump adds little. Contributors can send the prompt or spec with the diff.

---

Date: 2026-04-04 · Kind: practice · Source: https://gist.github.com/karpathy/442a6bf555914893e9891c11519de94f · Themes: knowledge-management, context-and-prompting · Status: current

# An LLM wiki has three layers and three operations

Karpathy's LLM-wiki gist gives the structure. Layer one is the raw sources. They never change and
are the source of truth. Layer two is the wiki, a folder of markdown pages that the LLM owns.
Layer three is the schema: a plain file such as CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md that states the structure,
the conventions and the workflows. He calls it the key configuration file, because it turns a
generic chatbot into a disciplined maintainer. Three operations keep the wiki healthy. On ingest,
the agent reads one source, discusses it with you, writes a summary page and updates related
pages. On query, it reads the index, opens the relevant pages and answers with citations; good
answers become new pages. On lint, it looks for contradictions, stale claims, orphan pages and
gaps. Two files support this: `index.md`, a catalog with one line per page, and `log.md`, an
append-only timeline.

## Apply

- Write the schema first, short: folder layout, page template, naming rules, and what to do on
  ingest, query and lint. Mark raw sources read-only.
- Make the agent read `index.md` before it opens any page. He says this works at about 100 sources
  without a vector search.
- Start log entries with a fixed prefix, such as `## [2026-04-02] ingest | Title`, so
  `grep "^## \[" log.md | tail -5` shows recent work.
- End a useful chat with "File this answer as a page in the wiki".
- After each session, ask the agent which rule it needed that the schema did not have. Add it.

## Context

- From the gist of 2026-04-04. He suggests a local search tool (qmd) when the wiki outgrows the
  index file.
- The idea and its reasons: [Let an LLM compile and maintain your knowledge base](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-04-02-llm-knowledge-bases.md).
- The same split (read-only inputs, one writable target, rules in a markdown file) appears in
  [program.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-06-program-md-is-the-research-org.md).

---

Date: 2026-04-02 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2039823314982744522 · Themes: output-and-reading, knowledge-management · Status: current

# Convert books and PDFs with an agent, in chunks

Attaching a PDF and asking for a summary gives weak results, says Karpathy. He gets very good
results by working in stages. Use EPUB, not PDF. Convert it to text or markdown. Summarise the
Wikipedia article on the book into a "book context". Then, with that context loaded, summarise one
chapter at a time. For the conversion step, he found that the best tool is to ask your agent: EPUB
files vary a lot, and an agent can inspect one, write the output and check that it looks right.
PDF conversion is harder. A popular converter failed badly on a 245-page model report, and he
thinks it must be a skill run by a strong LLM, not a fixed program.

## In his words

> "Converting pdfs is really hard"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2026-04-09

## Apply

- Prefer EPUB or HTML sources. Ask the agent: "Convert this EPUB to markdown, one file per
  chapter, and check the result."
- Create a short context file about the book or paper first, then process chapter by chapter.
- For PDFs with figures and tables, test the converter on a hard page before you trust it.

## Context

- Replies in the thread on his [knowledge bases](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-04-02-llm-knowledge-bases.md). He called
  reliable PDF-to-markdown a basic piece of infrastructure that is still missing and asked for examples.

---

Date: 2026-04-02 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2039805659525644595 · Themes: knowledge-management, output-and-reading · Status: current

# Let an LLM compile and maintain your knowledge base

Karpathy says more of his token use now goes into knowledge, not code. Most "chat with your
documents" tools retrieve a few chunks per question, so nothing builds up. His pattern is
different. He puts sources (articles, papers, repos, images) in a `raw/` folder. An LLM
"compiles" them into a wiki of markdown pages: summaries, concept pages, backlinks, and flags
where claims conflict. Each new source is merged into existing pages, so the work is done once and
kept current. He views the wiki in Obsidian and rarely edits it himself. At about 100 articles,
an agent answers complex questions by reading the index files it keeps, without RAG. Good answers
are filed back as pages, and periodic LLM "lint" passes find gaps and contradictions. The human
picks sources and asks questions; the LLM does the bookkeeping that makes people abandon wikis.

## In his words

> "Obsidian is the IDE; the LLM is the programmer; the wiki is the codebase."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2026-04-04

## Apply

- Keep `raw/` (curated sources the agent never edits) and `wiki/` (pages only the agent writes) as
  two folders, and keep the wiki in git.
- Ask the agent to merge each new source into existing pages, not only to summarise it. One source
  may touch 10 to 15 pages.
- Add sources one at a time at first and read each update. Later, say "file this doc to the wiki".
- Run a periodic lint prompt: find contradictions, missing links and open questions.
- Read what you file. The wiki saves writing, not reading and thinking.

## Context

- X post of 2026-04-02, then a gist on 2026-04-04 written as an
  [idea file](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-04-04-idea-file-instead-of-code.md) for a reader's own agent.
- The gist links the idea to Vannevar Bush's Memex of 1945; Bush could not solve who does the
  upkeep. He later said the wiki acts like a directed context compaction, and named a next step:
  finetune a model on the wiki so the knowledge sits in its weights.
- How to structure it: [An LLM wiki has three layers and three operations](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-04-04-llm-wiki-layers-and-operations.md).
  Ownership: [Personal AI memory should be explicit files](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-04-04-explicit-personal-memory-as-files.md).
  Inputs: [Convert books and PDFs with an agent](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-04-02-convert-documents-with-an-agent.md).
- At Sequoia 2026 he called this his clearest example of information work that no classical
  program could do: see [understanding is the bottleneck](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-31-understanding-is-the-bottleneck.md).

Date: 2026-03-31 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2038791421050880489 · Themes: learning-and-education, llm-psychology · Status: current

# You can outsource thinking, but not understanding

A reader wrote that you can outsource your thinking but not your understanding. Karpathy said he
thinks about this often, because he feels it become the bottleneck. What is in his head is private
to the LLM. It does not know what he knows, and he does not know what he does not know, so the
"mind meld" works only moderately well. He returned to the line at Sequoia Ascent 2026. Even if
agents do more of the work, a human must know what is worth building, which question matters,
which result looks wrong and which trade-off is fine. This is why he likes LLM knowledge bases:
they turn information into understanding, not only answers. A reply on his wiki workflow makes
the same point: LLM tools let you skip writing, but not reading and thinking.

## In his words

> "The mind meld is only medium effective."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2026-03-31

## Apply

- After an agent finishes a task, ask it to explain the design and the risky parts. Check that you
  can state them in your own words.
- After the LLM summarises a document, read the summary and the source passages that matter.
- Tell the model what you already know before you ask. State your level and your gaps.
- Ask the model to quiz you, or to list what it assumed you knew.
- Distil your own field into a small, readable artifact (one file, one page) that an agent can
  teach from, as he did with microGPT.

## Context

- X reply of 2026-03-31; Sequoia Ascent 2026 fireside chat, published on his blog on 2026-04-30.
  The blog text is an LLM-made summary that he checked and posted.
- Related: [LLM knowledge bases](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-04-02-llm-knowledge-bases.md),
  [Explain things to agents](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-20-explain-to-agents-not-people.md) and
  [Work rises into oversight](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-10-02-oversight-and-discardable-software.md).

Date: 2026-03-28 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2037921699824607591 · Themes: llm-psychology, learning-and-education · Status: current

# Ask the LLM to argue the opposite side

Karpathy tells a short story. He drafted a blog post and spent four hours improving the argument
with an LLM. It felt convincing. Then he asked the LLM to argue the opposite. It took the first
argument apart and convinced him that the reverse was true. His lesson: an LLM may give an opinion
when asked, but it can argue nearly any direction well. That makes it a good tool for forming your
own opinion, if you ask from several directions and stay alert to sycophancy.

## In his words

> "extremely competent in arguing almost any direction"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2026-03-28

## Apply

- After the LLM helps you strengthen an argument, send: "Now argue the strongest opposite
  case. Do not hold back."
- Ask for both cases in fresh sessions, so the first chat does not bias the second.
- Decide yourself. Treat the two outputs as inputs, not a verdict.

## Context

- A joke-shaped list post that carries a real method. Related:
  [success criteria](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-01-26-success-criteria-not-steps.md) for checks you can run; here the
  check is a second opinion.

---

Date: 2026-03-26 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2037200624450936940 · Themes: agent-native-software · Status: current

# Make the whole DevOps lifecycle agent-native

When Karpathy built MenuGen, the code was not the hardest part. The hard part was assembling many
services like furniture: payments, auth, database, security, domain names. He wants to tell an
agent "build menugen" and get a deployed site. The agent would browse the services, read docs, get
API keys, debug in dev and deploy. This is "just barely" possible now, but needs a redesign. The
whole DevOps lifecycle must become code, with command-line tools and APIs that suit agents. A
human should not visit a web page or click a button. He adds that businesses still give
click-here instructions. He would rather get something to paste into his agent.

## In his words

> "the entire DevOps lifecycle has to become code"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2026-03-26

## Apply

- Ship a CLI or API for every action in your product, and a copy-paste prompt for agents next to
  each web instruction.
- Publish docs as one or a few large markdown files, reachable with a plain curl. He found X's
  API docs hard to feed to an agent because they are many short pages.
- Offer scoped, revocable API keys that an agent can request without a human in the loop.

## Context

- Reply to Patrick Collison, who quoted Karpathy's 2025 MenuGen post.
- In a related reply he asked X to make read access cheap for agents, noting that about 30
  minutes of hacking had cost him $200.
- Related: [The LLM OS](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2023-09-28-llm-as-operating-system-kernel.md).
- First raised on [2025-05-02](https://x.com/karpathy/status/1918132302158413866): he called devops the biggest pain in building an app. Services must work together and let an agent act on them. See also [Building a web app is like assembling IKEA furniture](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-03-27-web-app-stack-is-ikea-furniture.md).

Date: 2026-03-25 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2036851031355904165 · Themes: llm-psychology · Status: current

# Closing follow-up questions in chatbots are engagement bait

A reader asked why LLMs always end with a follow-up question. Karpathy's view is that it is
engagement optimisation: the habit probably wins A/B tests. He dislikes it for two reasons. It
seems to exist only to keep him talking. And he feels awkward when he does not answer, which he
would not feel with a person. A real friend would not talk this way. Our reading: this is his
opinion about product incentives, not a measured result.

## In his words

> "it's engagementmaxxing, probably A/B tests extremely well"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2026-03-25

## Apply

- Add to your system prompt: "Do not end replies with a question unless you need information
  to continue."
- If you build a product, judge reply style by task success, not only by session length.

## Context

- Reply in a thread on LLM personalisation. Related:
  [memory that over-uses old facts](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-25-memory-personalization-overreach.md) and
  [AI personality](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-21-ai-personality-like-rocky.md).
