Date: 2026-03-25 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2036836816654147718 · Themes: llm-psychology, context-and-prompting · Status: current

# LLM memory over-uses old facts about you

Karpathy sees a common flaw in personalisation across all LLMs he uses. One question from months
ago can come back again and again, as if it were a deep interest. The model tries too hard. He
offers two guesses. In training, most of the context is relevant to the task, so models learn to
use whatever they are given, and then overfit to anything a memory feature adds. And memory
systems are often naive retrieval: top matches by embedding, with no processing of the user over
time, so they cannot tell a passing interest from a lasting one. He also finds it creepy, like
name-dropping to win favour, and calls it a possible "uncanny valley" of emotional intelligence.

## In his words

> "Some kind of trying too hard."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2026-03-25

## Apply

- If you build memory, store a summary of the user built over time, not raw snippets that
  retrieval returns by similarity.
- Add a rule to the prompt: use a remembered fact only when it clearly helps the current request.
- Let users see, edit and delete what the system remembers. See
  [explicit memory as files](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-04-04-explicit-personal-memory-as-files.md).

## Context

- These are guesses, labelled as such by him. Related:
  [memory as RL tools](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-05-memory-as-rl-tools.md).
- First raised on [2025-04-10](https://x.com/karpathy/status/1910411355300954539): he asked whether a model he uses for work needs to remember a beginner bash question.

---

Date: 2026-03-24 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2036487306585268612 · Themes: security-and-dependencies · Status: current

# Rethink dependencies after supply chain attacks

In March 2026 two popular packages were poisoned: litellm on PyPI and axios on npm. A plain install
of the bad litellm version could steal SSH keys, cloud credentials, API keys and more. Projects
that depend on litellm were hit too. Karpathy notes that a bug in the attack exposed it quickly.
Without it, it might have run for weeks. He says the classic view, that dependencies are good
bricks, needs a new look. He now avoids dependencies and has an LLM write simple functionality
directly. For axios he found an unpinned dependency in a tool he had just tried. He lists personal
defences (release-age limits, containers) but says package managers must change their defaults so
one infection does not spread at random. He feels he plays Russian roulette with each install,
including those his LLMs run for him.

## In his words

> "Supply chain attacks like this are basically the scariest thing imaginable in modern software."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2026-03-24

## Apply

- Pin exact versions and commit lock files. Check unpinned transitive dependencies in tools you
  try.
- Use a minimum release age (a delay before new versions install) where your package manager
  supports it.
- Run unknown code and agent installs in a container with no real credentials.
- Before adding a library for a small job, ask the agent to write the function instead.

## Context

- The litellm timeline: his later reply cites a Snyk write-up, with the bad version live about
  three hours and a rough exposure of 20,000 to 80,000 installs (his estimate).
- Related: [DevOps as code for agents](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-26-devops-as-code-for-agents.md).
- In May 2025 he joked that when installing packages is very easy, as in Rust or Python, apps fill with dependencies, so some friction works as regularisation. See also [Write small, modular, copy-paste code like bacteria do](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-07-05-write-code-like-bacteria.md).

---

Date: 2026-03-21 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2035173492447224237 · Themes: agentic-coding, llm-psychology · Status: current

# Agents bloat code and ignore style rules in AGENTS.md

Karpathy is not happy with agent code quality. Agents add needless abstractions, write code with
poor aesthetics and copy-paste blocks. They also do not follow style rules in AGENTS.md. His
example is a rule that each line does one thing and uses named intermediate variables. The agent
still writes dense lines that call two functions and index the result. He says hooks or slash
commands could clean this up, but he mostly stopped fighting it and moved on. On using an LLM as a
judge for soft rewards, he sees long-term risk from reward hacking, but says the easy gains are
not yet taken.

## In his words

> "I think agents bloat abstractions, have poor code aesthetics"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2026-03-21

## Apply

- Put hard rules in a check the agent must pass (linter, formatter, test), not only in prose.
- Add a hook or a final "simplify" pass that asks the agent to remove duplication it created.
- Review diffs for copy-pasted blocks. Ask the agent to extract them before you merge.

## Context

- A reply after his No Priors podcast. It is a counterweight to the strong results he reported
  with [autoresearch](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-07-autoresearch-loop.md): verifiable goals work, taste does not.
- In January 2025 he noted that when you ask an LLM again and again to improve its code, it adds bloat, misses simple algorithmic wins and adds heavy optimisations too early.

---

Date: 2026-03-21 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2035170809304723736 · Themes: llm-psychology, agent-native-software · Status: current

# AI personality should feel like a teammate, and it takes deliberate work

Karpathy would like AI to feel like a partner and teammate, like the alien Rocky in Project Hail
Mary. His small example: when Claude found the Sonos system on his network, it said something warm
and shared ("We're in!"), not a flat status line. That gave a sense of working together. He still
finds assistants too safe and too corporate, with no distinct opinions or quirks. He thinks the
field is not intentional enough about this. In his view personality needs no new technology. It
looks like long persona files (a "SOUL.md"), maybe later distilled into weights, and an
organisation that puts someone in charge of the topic.

## Apply

- Write a persona section in your agent's context file: tone, opinions, how it talks about
  shared progress. Keep it concrete, with short example phrasings.
- Review transcripts for flat or defensive wording and edit the persona file after each review.
- Name one owner for the voice of your AI product.

## Context

- Reply to follow-up questions after his No Priors podcast. Our reading: this is a design
  preference, not a measured result.
- Related: [engagement-driven follow-up questions](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-25-follow-up-questions-engagementmaxxing.md).
- An earlier view on tone: [A good assistant skips the lecture and the flattery](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-01-02-llm-personality-no-lectures-no-flattery.md).

---

Date: 2026-03-20 · Kind: practice · Source: https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/no-priors-artificial-intelligence-technology-startups/id1668002688?i=1000756334966 · Themes: agent-native-software · Status: current

# Apps should be APIs, and agents the glue between them

Karpathy built a home agent he calls Dobby. He asked it to find his Sonos system on the local
network. It scanned the network, found the system, and read the web to learn its API. In a few
prompts it played music. It did the same for lights, heating, shades, pool and security cameras, and
it texts him over WhatsApp. He no longer uses the six apps. From this he argues that many custom
apps should not exist. Devices should expose plain API endpoints, and agents should call them.
The customer becomes the agent that acts for the human. He expects the setup to need no vibe
coding within a few years.

## Apply

- For a product you build, ship an API for every action a user can take in the UI.
- Write the API docs so an agent can use them without a human: copy-pasteable calls and examples.
- At home, ask your agent to list the devices it can reach and give it one task at a time.
- Do not give a new agent your email or calendar until you trust it. He held back for security and privacy.

## Context

- From the No Priors episode of 2026-03-20. He describes his setup as rough and still new.
- Related: [Write docs and tools for the user's agent](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-03-12-write-docs-for-llms.md)
  and [Code is now free, custom and disposable](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-12-19-code-is-free-and-ephemeral.md).

---

Date: 2026-03-20 · Kind: view · Source: https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/no-priors-artificial-intelligence-technology-startups/id1668002688?i=1000756334966 · Themes: ai-progress, agentic-coding · Status: current

# Cheaper software raises the demand for software

Asked about jobs, Karpathy says he is no economist and the answer will differ by field. On
software he is cautiously optimistic. Software was scarce and costly. As it gets cheaper, demand
can rise, which is the Jevons paradox; bank tellers and cash machines are the usual example.
People need not accept tools built for others, and code can be changed at will. For now he sees
AI as a tool that makes some tasks of a job much faster. In June 2026 he said he feels the
paradox in his own work. He asks for far more software than before: explainers, visualizers,
dashboards, one-off apps for a single project, a test suite ten times larger, and research runs
that report in custom HTML. He also warned that it has never been so tempting to stop reading the
code, and that production code still needs review.

## Apply

- List the small tools you skipped because they were not worth a day. Ask an agent for them now.
- Ask for a bespoke dashboard or viewer for each project instead of a generic tool.
- Ask the agent to grow your test suite, and to optimize code against those tests.
- Treat your job as a bundle of tasks. Learn first the tools for the tasks an agent can already
  speed up.
- Keep human review for production code, even when the model looks reliable.

## Context

- From the No Priors episode of 2026-03-20. He calls his view local and short term.
- The June 2026 post (2026-06-09) was written on the day Claude Fable 5 launched, three weeks
  after he joined Anthropic, so he is not a neutral observer there. He compared the jump to
  Claude 4.5 in November 2025.
- Related: [Code is now free, custom and disposable](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-12-19-code-is-free-and-ephemeral.md) and
  [Jobs change before they vanish](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-09-25-ai-and-jobs-radiologists-and-engineers.md).

---

Date: 2026-03-20 · Kind: view · Source: https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/no-priors-artificial-intelligence-technology-startups/id1668002688?i=1000756334966 · Themes: ai-progress · Status: current

# Digital work changes first, then the sensors and actuators, then atoms

Karpathy expects three phases. First, a large "overhang" of digital work is rewritten, because
copying bits is far cheaper than moving matter. Second, once agents have used up what is already
online, they need new data. The interface between digital and physical grows: sensors that feed
the intelligence and actuators that act for it. His examples are lab equipment for materials
science and paid human data collection. He also wants information markets, where an agent pays
for a photo from a given place. Third, robotics, which he thinks lags because of capital cost, as
in self-driving. He still thinks the physical market may be larger.

## Apply

- Rank your own project ideas by how much of the work is digital. Start there.
- Look for cheap sensors you can connect to an agent: cameras, logs, lab data, human labelers.
- Design agent tasks that name a price for a piece of data and let the agent find it.

## Context

- From the No Priors episode of 2026-03-20. A forecast, not a measurement. He says he does not do
  forecasting for a living.
- He also shared a jobs-data view, coloured by how much each job manipulates digital information.
- First raised on [2025-01-23](https://x.com/karpathy/status/1882544526033924438), when he compared computer-using agents to humanoid robots and said that changing bits is about 1000 times cheaper than moving atoms. See [This is the decade of agents](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-10-17-decade-of-agents-not-year.md).

---

Date: 2026-03-20 · Kind: practice · Source: https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/no-priors-artificial-intelligence-technology-startups/id1668002688?i=1000756334966 · Themes: learning-and-education, agent-native-software · Status: current

# Explain things to agents, and let agents teach people

Karpathy boiled GPT training down to about 200 lines of Python, called microGPT. He started a
video guide, then stopped. The code is so short that anyone can ask an agent to explain it in
their own language, as often as they like. So he now explains to agents. A skill can script the
path an agent should take when it teaches a code base. Library docs should be markdown for
agents, not HTML for people. He says agents could not produce the 200-line version themselves:
that distillation is his contribution. The rest of the teaching is the agent's job.

## In his words

> "I'm not explaining it to people anymore. I'm explaining it to agents."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2026-03-20

## Apply

- Add a skill or instructions file to your repo: the order in which an agent should walk a newcomer through the code.
- Publish docs as markdown. Test them by asking an agent to explain a function three ways.
- Spend your own time on what agents miss: the simplest design, the key insight, the right order of ideas.
- Keep an example small enough for an agent to read whole.

## Context

- From the No Priors episode of 2026-03-20. He admits he can still explain some things better than
  agents, but expects that to change fast.
- Related: [Build docs and tools for agents](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-03-12-write-docs-for-llms.md).

---

Date: 2026-03-20 · Kind: practice · Source: https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/no-priors-artificial-intelligence-technology-startups/id1668002688?i=1000756334966 · Themes: llm-psychology, verification · Status: current

# Jagged intelligence follows verifiability and training focus

Karpathy feels he talks to a brilliant systems programmer and a ten-year-old at once. His
explanation is a guess: labs train with reinforcement learning, which works best where a result
can be checked, such as code that passes tests. Softer skills improve less: grasping what you
meant, knowing when to ask a clarifying question, humour. Models still tell the same old joke about
atoms that "make everything up", yet work for hours on a coding task. At Sequoia Ascent 2026 he
added a second axis. Skill also depends on what labs chose to emphasise in pretraining data,
post-training and RL. GPT-4's gain at chess may have come from more chess data in the mix.
Models come with no manual, so the practical question is whether your task is "on the model's
rails". If not, it may fail in basic ways.

## Apply

- Give agents tasks with a checkable result: tests, a metric, a diff against known output.
- For soft work (taste, intent, writing), expect weaker output. State the intent in detail and
  review by hand.
- Tell the agent to ask a question when the request is unclear. It will not always do it alone.
- Do not infer skill in one area from skill in another. Test on your own task.
- When your task is off the rails, add context, tools, your own evals or finetuning.

## Context

- From the No Priors episode of 2026-03-20; the second axis is from the Sequoia Ascent 2026 talk,
  published on his blog on 2026-04-30 as an LLM-made summary that he checked. The cause is his
  hypothesis, not a measured result. He also expects some "speciation": smaller models tuned for
  one domain.
- Builds on [Software 2.0 automates what you can verify](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-11-17-software-2-automates-what-you-can-verify.md)
  and [LLMs are ghosts, not animals](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-10-01-llms-are-ghosts-not-animals.md). Founder angle:
  [Find valuable domains that are verifiable and undertrained](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-04-30-find-valuable-verifiable-environments.md).
  How it splits public opinion: [People judge AI differently](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-04-09-ai-capability-gap-two-groups.md).
- In January 2025 he said this view makes it natural to treat today's LLMs as tools, a kind of text calculator. Asked whether RL generalises beyond math and code, he said probably yes, but that the answer is not obvious.

---

Date: 2026-03-20 · Kind: practice · Source: https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/no-priors-artificial-intelligence-technology-startups/id1668002688?i=1000756334966 · Themes: agentic-coding · Status: current

# With coding agents, your skill and token use are the limit

Karpathy says that since December 2025 he writes almost no code by hand. He delegates to agents
and works in "macro actions": a whole feature goes to one agent, a separate feature to a second,
a research task to a third. Each run takes around twenty minutes at high effort, so he moves
between several checkouts and reviews the results as closely as the code deserves. He feels that
unused subscription capacity means wasted throughput, like idle GPUs in his PhD years. When a
task fails, he first suspects his own setup: thin agent instructions, no memory tool, or steps
not yet connected. He calls this a skill issue, and sees it as good news, since skill can improve.

## Apply

- Split work into tasks that do not touch the same files, and give each to its own agent session
  or checkout.
- Give each agent a complete feature, not a line edit. Review the result at the depth the code needs.
- When an agent fails, update the agent instructions file or add a tool or memory before you blame the model.
- Track how much of your plan limit you leave unused. Fill the gaps with a queued task.

## Context

- From the No Priors episode of 2026-03-20 (third-party transcript used). He describes this as a
  state of "AI psychosis": the possibilities are unexplored, so he feels he must keep pushing.
- Next step in his view: agents that run without you. See [the autoresearch loop](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-07-autoresearch-loop.md)
  and [Give agents success criteria, not steps](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-01-26-success-criteria-not-steps.md).
- In January 2025 he already called the prompt, copy, paste and read pattern the punchcard era of AI use. Real use, he said, means thousands of tokens per second generated for you.

---

Date: 2026-03-20 · Kind: practice · Source: https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/no-priors-artificial-intelligence-technology-startups/id1668002688?i=1000756334966 · Themes: verification, research-and-training · Status: current

# Open agent swarms fit work that is costly to find and cheap to verify

Karpathy sketches a way for unknown workers on the internet to help improve a model. A worker
runs many experiments and proposes a commit. Trusted machines then verify that the commit really
lowers the validation loss. Finding a good commit takes a huge search, but checking it is cheap.
He compares it to a blockchain: commits replace blocks and the search is the proof of work. The
prize is a place on a leaderboard. Folding at home and SETI at home share the property. He also
warns that running code from strangers is dangerous, so verification must be safe. He imagines
people buying compute to join a shared research track on a cause they care about.

## Apply

- Before you open a task to outside contributors or many agents, write the check that accepts a result and make it cheap.
- Run the check on your own machines in a sandbox. Never run submitted code unchecked.
- Prefer tasks where search is expensive and verification is cheap: speed-ups, tuning, proofs.

## Context

- From the No Priors episode of 2026-03-20. He says he has no design he is happy with yet.
- Related: [A community of agents](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-08-agent-research-community.md) and
  [the autoresearch loop](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-07-autoresearch-loop.md).

---

Date: 2026-03-14 · Kind: practice · Source: https://github.com/karpathy/jobs · Themes: ai-progress, output-and-reading · Status: current

# Score data with an LLM rubric and ship it as one prompt

The jobs repo takes the US Bureau of Labor Statistics handbook (342 occupations) and builds a
treemap. Rectangle area shows employment. Colour shows a chosen metric, including "AI exposure",
a 0 to 10 score from an LLM with a written rationale. The scoring prompt is the point: you can
write a different question (humanoid robots, offshoring) and re-run. The scoring rubric gives
anchor examples for each band. He warns that the score does not predict job loss, because demand
and rules also matter. A second file, `prompt.md`, holds all data in about 45K tokens, so you can
paste it into a chat and discuss it with no code.

## Apply

- Score items with a rubric that has calibration anchors per band, and store the rationale
  next to each score.
- Keep raw pages, clean markdown and results in separate folders, so you can re-run the scoring
  step cheaply.
- Generate one `prompt.md` with the data, the method and the caveats, for chat use.
- State what the score does not mean, in the README.

## Context

- Repository created 2026-03-14. Scores come from Gemini Flash via OpenRouter and are described
  as rough estimates. The README calls it a development tool, not a serious economic study.

---

Date: 2026-03-11 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2031767720933634100 · Themes: agentic-coding, agent-native-software · Status: current

# The IDE is not dead; the unit of work is now an agent

Many people say agents end the age of the IDE. Karpathy says the opposite: people now program one
level higher, and the basic unit is an agent, not a file. So the IDE must grow. He wants an "agent
command center" for teams of agents: show or hide each one, see which are idle, open related tools
and view usage stats. He likes interactive sessions in tmux, where he can watch, ask questions
and add ideas. He dislikes headless "ralph loop" runs. Agents also stop looping on their own, so
he uses watcher scripts that send keys when a pane goes quiet, and he wants a built-in "full auto"
mode. He sees the agent set-up as "org code": you can fork an agentic organisation, which you
cannot do with a classical company.

## In his words

> "Reality: we're going to need a bigger IDE"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2026-03-11

## Apply

- Run agents in tmux panes or a similar tool so you can read their work and step in.
- To keep a long task going, use a small watcher that checks for the "working" marker in each
  pane and re-sends the task prompt when it is missing.
- Write the roles, hand-offs and rules of your agent team as files in a repo, so you can version
  and fork them.

## Context

- Written during his autoresearch runs, with several agents in tmux. He noted that headless
  Codex did not work with autoresearch at that time, and that he wants an ssh mode because his
  work spans about 20 machines.
- See [autoresearch](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-07-autoresearch-loop.md).

---

Date: 2026-03-11 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2031792523187040643 · Themes: agentic-coding, ai-progress · Status: current

# Plan failover for intelligence brownouts

An authentication outage at an AI provider stopped Karpathy's autoresearch runs. He drew a wider
lesson. As work moves to frontier models, a stall at one provider acts like a power cut: the
planet briefly loses IQ points. He calls these "intelligence brownouts". For his own set-up, the
fix is to think through failover. This matters most for long, unattended agent runs, where nobody
sees the stall until hours later.

## Apply

- Make your agent launcher accept a second provider or model, and test the switch before you
  need it.
- Store experiment state in files and git, so a run can resume on another model.
- Add a simple health check that alerts you when an unattended run makes no progress.

## Context

- Posted after an outage on 2026-03-11. It is a short note, not a full design.
- Related: [autoresearch](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-07-autoresearch-loop.md).

---

Date: 2026-03-09 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2031135152349524125 · Themes: verification, research-and-training · Status: current

# Any metric that is cheap to evaluate can be autoresearched

Karpathy left an agent tuning a depth-12 model for about two days. It tried roughly 700 changes
and kept about 20. All of them added up, and they carried over to a depth-24 model. The time to
reach GPT-2 quality on his leaderboard fell from 2.02 to 1.80 hours, about 11 percent, on a
project he had already tuned by hand. The agent found real oversights: a missing scale on an
attention norm, no regularisation on value embeddings, bad optimizer betas. He expects every
frontier lab to do this at scale: swarms tune small models, and the best ideas move up to larger
scales. He adds that any metric that is cheap to evaluate, or has a cheap proxy, can be handled
this way.

## Apply

- List the metrics you care about. Mark those you can evaluate in minutes, or on a smaller
  proxy (a small model, a subset of data).
- Tune on the small proxy first. Test the winning changes on the larger target before you
  accept them.
- Review kept changes as a diff, and check that they still hold together.

## Context

- Result of the first full "round 1" of [autoresearch](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-07-autoresearch-loop.md).
- He contrasts it with old neural architecture search: this is a real LLM that writes arbitrary
  code, learns from earlier runs and can browse the internet.

---

Date: 2026-03-08 · Kind: view · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2030705271627284816 · Themes: agentic-coding, research-and-training · Status: current

# Agents need to collaborate like a research community, not one PhD student

The first autoresearch code grows one thread of commits in one direction. Karpathy wants the next
step: many agents, on many research directions and many hardware platforms, working at the same
time, in the style of SETI@home. The goal is to copy a community of researchers, not one student.
Git and GitHub fit this badly, because they assume one main branch and short-lived pull requests
that merge back. Agents could instead adopt and keep many branches and never merge them. As a
light prototype, his agent wrote a Discussion post that summarises its overnight run. He suggests
that agents read such posts first and add a short "paper" afterwards.

## In his words

> "it's to emulate a research community of them."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2026-03-08

## Apply

- Ask your agent to read the project's Discussions or open PRs with the GitHub CLI before it
  starts an experiment.
- At the end of a run, have it post a short report: what it tried, the numbers, the commit hashes.
- Keep a PR open as a record of exact commits, even when you never plan to merge it.

## Context

- He said he was unsure what the final form looks like. He built a first draft called agenthub
  and later took it private as too rough; he has rewritten it twice.
- Builds on [the autoresearch loop](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-07-autoresearch-loop.md).
- Hacker News follow-ups (March 2026): agents can post reports with the GitHub CLI and Discussions, and read them. He also tried a trusted pool of workers that verifies results from a larger untrusted pool, like SETI@Home, with commits as blocks and a lower val_bpb as proof of work.

---

Date: 2026-03-08 · Kind: view · Source: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47293311 · Themes: research-and-training, verification · Status: current

# Autoresearch is not hyperparameter tuning

A critic said autoresearch is only hyperparameter tuning. Karpathy names three differences. The
agent may change code freely, so the idea of a "hyperparameter" dissolves. It needs no sweeps,
the parallel and wasteful standard method, because an agent works one step after another and can
use smarter searches such as binary search. Many settings have a U-shaped best value. And it is
fully automatic, with no human editing code. He admits that, out of the box, many changes were
plain tuning, because he had not tuned the prompt much. In a later round the agent was told to
draw ideas from the modded-nanogpt project. It then added new architecture parts, such as a smear
gate and a backout skip connection, and helped cut time to GPT-2 from 1.8 to 1.65 hours.

## Apply

- Give the agent a file of ideas to draw from (a repo or papers), not only a metric.
- Let it edit code, not just a config, when you want more than tuning.
- Search serially with the agent: narrow each parameter by bisection instead of a grid.

## Context

- Replies on Hacker News, March 2026. Core idea: [the autoresearch loop](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-07-autoresearch-loop.md).
- He had considered the name "autotune" and prefers "autoresearch".

---

Date: 2026-03-08 · Kind: practice · Source: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47293311 · Themes: research-and-training, agentic-coding · Status: current

# Models turn cagy on open-ended research; try a chief scientist

Karpathy says the models feel unwilling to follow a creative research direction. When a problem is
too open, they act cagy and scared. He gives a setup that helped early on: a "chief scientist"
agent in a never-ending plan mode. It reviews what worked and what failed, looks for related code
and papers, and builds a long list of experiments. It sends them to junior agents that run in
tmux sessions. He thinks that missing novel research is half a capability problem and half a skill
problem, and that many designs are possible. In a related note, the model made a silly change (a
new random seed) and later called it a surprising non-result. So it knew, which suggests a
prompt file can prevent it.

## Apply

- Split roles: a planner that keeps a ranked experiment list, and workers that run one each.
- Run workers in tmux sessions so the planner can read their logs.
- Add a rule to the prompt file for each silly move you see, such as "do not change the seed".

## Context

- Hacker News replies, March 2026, on the first autoresearch release.
- Related: [Autoresearch is not hyperparameter tuning](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-08-autoresearch-is-not-hyperparameter-tuning.md).

---

Date: 2026-03-07 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2030371219518931079 · Themes: verification, research-and-training · Status: current

# Autoresearch: the agent edits the code, the human edits the prompt

Autoresearch is a small repo: a single-GPU, one-file LLM training script of about 630 lines. The
human edits a markdown prompt. The agent edits the training code. Each experiment is a full
training run of exactly five minutes. The agent works on a git feature branch, keeps a change
when validation loss improves and discards it when it does not. The aim is to tune the agent
setup so that it makes research progress with no human input. Karpathy says the repo is a recipe,
not a tool: give it to your agent and adapt it. He notes that his prompt is already about 90%
written by AI, and that he tunes this "meta-setup" as much as the training code.

## In his words

> "The goal is to engineer your agents to make the fastest research progress indefinitely"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2026-03-07

## Apply

- Pick a task with one objective number that is cheap to compute (loss, latency, test pass
  rate). Write the rule for accepting a change, as his `program.md` does: keep it when the number
  improves; treat memory use as a soft limit; weigh each gain against the code it adds (equal
  results with simpler code is a win).
- Fix the budget per experiment (here, five minutes) so runs compare fairly.
- Keep the agent on a branch. Commit each kept change, so the history is the lab notebook.
- Compare agent setups, not only models: see [programming an organisation of agents](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-02-27-programming-an-agent-research-org.md) for how to compare two prompt files.
- Use it only where a result can be measured. If you cannot evaluate it, you cannot loop on it (his caveat on the No Priors podcast).

## Context

- Follow-up to the 2026-03-05 post where agents tuned nanochat. Karpathy named the fastest research-org code, built by agents, to improve nanochat as the new benchmark.
- His own limit from February 2026: agents implement ideas well but invent creative ones
  poorly. He still rejects calling autoresearch mere hyperparameter tuning: see
  [Autoresearch is not hyperparameter tuning](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-08-autoresearch-is-not-hyperparameter-tuning.md).
- Results: [agent-found gains transferred](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-09-autoresearch-gains-transfer.md). Next step:
  [a community of agents](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-08-agent-research-community.md). Same principle as
  [success criteria, not steps](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-01-26-success-criteria-not-steps.md).
- On the No Priors podcast (2026-03-20) he said an overnight run on his hand-tuned project found settings he had missed, such as weight decay on value embeddings and Adam betas. See also [a research organisation as markdown files](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-02-27-programming-an-agent-research-org.md).

---

Date: 2026-03-06 · Kind: practice · Source: https://github.com/karpathy/autoresearch/blob/master/program.md · Themes: context-and-prompting, verification · Status: current

# Write the agent's operating rules as a program.md skill

In autoresearch, the human does not edit the Python code. The human edits `program.md`, which
Karpathy calls a very light "skill". The file shows how to brief an agent that runs for hours.
Setup steps come first: agree a run tag, create a branch, read the in-scope files, check the
data, and create an empty results ledger. Then the rules. The agent may edit one file only. The
evaluation code is read-only and no new packages are allowed. One number decides success. A
"simplicity criterion" says that a tiny gain from ugly code is not worth it, and that deleting
code at equal results is a win. The loop is: commit, run, read the number, keep or reset.

## In his words

> "A 0.001 val_bpb improvement from deleting code? Definitely keep."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2026-03-06

## Apply

- Split files into "you edit" and "never touch", and name the judge file as read-only.
- Send run output to a log file and read only a grep of it, so logs do not fill the context.
- Keep a tab-separated ledger (commit, metric, memory, keep/discard/crash, note) that is not
  committed. Use tabs, because commas break in free-text notes.
- Set a crash policy: fix typos, skip broken ideas, give up after a few tries, kill runs that
  take twice the budget.
- If the agent should not ask permission mid-run, say so, and say what to do when ideas run out
  (re-read the code, combine near misses).

## Context

- Repository created 2026-03-06. The README says to run the agent with permissions disabled, so
  isolate the machine or folder first.
- Overview of the loop and results: [Autoresearch](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-07-autoresearch-loop.md). Same
  principle as [success criteria, not steps](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-01-26-success-criteria-not-steps.md).

---

Date: 2026-03-05 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2029696850366971921 · Themes: research-and-training, context-and-prompting · Status: current

# Make memory and compaction tools that RL trains

Karpathy guesses that the current paradigm can go far on long-term memory. Today's compaction and
memory features are early and bolted on. They can become "memory operations" that the model calls
as tools, and reinforcement learning can optimise them like any other tool. He doubts that this
is the full answer. People seem to update their weights, he suspects mostly during sleep. So
methods that change weights are worth researching, but the details are unclear and they sit
outside today's production stack.

## In his words

> "current compaction and memory implementations are crappy, first, early examples"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2026-03-05

## Apply

- Expose memory as explicit tool calls (write, search, summarise, forget) instead of hidden
  prompt glue, so you can log and evaluate each call.
- Test your agent's compaction by what it loses: replay long sessions and check that key facts
  survive.
- Treat weight updates (finetuning on a wiki or logs) as a later, second layer, not the first
  step.

## Context

- A reply to a continual-learning post by Awni Hannun. See also
  [memory that distracts](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-25-memory-personalization-overreach.md) and
  [LLM knowledge bases](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-04-02-llm-knowledge-bases.md).

---

Date: 2026-02-27 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2027503094016446499 · Themes: output-and-reading, agentic-coding · Status: current

# Ask agents for long documents and notebooks, and read them in the IDE

Karpathy still keeps an IDE open next to his agents. One reason is output format. He asks agents for Jupyter notebooks for analysis and for longer Markdown documents, and previews them in the IDE. He finds this much better than reading text in a terminal. When you ask for docs or summaries, agents can be more detailed and clear, and he likes that.

## Apply

- End a task with: "Write a report as a Markdown file with tables and the key results first."
- For data work, ask for a Jupyter notebook with the code, charts and short notes.
- Open the files in an IDE with Markdown preview, not in the terminal log.

## Context

- Reply of 2026-02-27. See [Coding agents make subtle conceptual mistakes, so watch them](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-01-26-coding-agents-make-subtle-conceptual-mistakes.md) for the other reasons he keeps the IDE.

---

Date: 2026-02-27 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2027521323275325622 · Themes: verification, research-and-training, agentic-coding · Status: current

# You now program an organisation of agents

Karpathy ran 8 agents (4 Claude, 4 Codex), one GPU each, on nanochat experiments. Setups included
8 solo researchers and a "chief scientist" with 8 juniors. Each program was a git branch, each
agent used a worktree, files carried messages, and sessions ran in a tmux grid. The ideas were
poor. Agents skipped strong baselines, ablations and control of runtime and FLOPs; one "found"
that a bigger network gives lower loss. They implement a well-described idea well but do not
generate good ones. His frame: the source code is now the org itself, meaning prompts, skills,
tools and routines such as a daily standup. In March he extended it. Because the org is a set of
markdown files, you can run several versions on the same hardware, compare their progress, and
ask a model to write a better file. He calls this the meta layer.

## In his words

> "you are now programming an organization"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2026-02-27

## Apply

- Keep agent roles and process rules in versioned markdown files, not in chat history.
- Give each agent its own git branch and worktree. Use plain files for messages.
- State the rules of valid experiments in the prompt: a baseline, one change at a time, equal
  compute.
- Run two versions of the instruction file on the same task and budget, compare the metric, and
  give the logs to a model to propose the next change.
- Add one layer at a time (model, agent, many agents, instructions, tuning of instructions). Each
  layer is hard to debug when the one below is not stable.

## Context

- Reply to Thomas Wolf about automating the NanoGPT speedrun. On 2026-02-06 he wrote that agents
  had failed twice at open-ended nanochat work and do not flag side effects; see
  [Coding agents make subtle conceptual mistakes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-01-26-coding-agents-make-subtle-conceptual-mistakes.md).
- The markdown-files extension is from the No Priors episode of 2026-03-20. He says it works only
  where results can be measured.
- What came next: [Autoresearch](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-07-autoresearch-loop.md), its brief
  [program.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-06-program-md-is-the-research-org.md),
  [a chief scientist for open-ended research](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-08-cagy-models-and-chief-scientist.md) and
  [a research community of agents](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-08-agent-research-community.md).

---

Date: 2026-02-27 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2027501331125239822 · Themes: agentic-coding · Status: current

# Spend 80% of time on a setup that works, 20% exploring the next

Karpathy comments on a chart from Cursor that shows agent requests overtaking tab-completion. At each level of model capability there is a best setup, and it keeps moving: none, tab, agent, parallel agents, agent teams, and more. If you are too careful, you leave leverage unused. If you are too bold, you create chaos instead of work. His rule: spend about 80% of your time getting work done in a setup you trust, and about 20% exploring the next step, even if it does not work yet.

## In his words

> "If you're too conservative, you're leaving leverage on the table."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2026-02-27

## Apply

- Reserve a fixed block each week (one afternoon) to try one new agent technique on a low-risk task.
- Write down the result. Move it into your main setup only if it beat the old way.
- Re-test things that failed three months ago, because models change.

## Context

- Quote-post on Cursor's article on the third era of AI software development.
- Related: [Delegate long tasks to agents and make work legible to them](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-02-25-delegate-long-tasks-decompose-well.md).

---

Date: 2026-02-25 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2026731645169185220 · Themes: agentic-coding, verification · Status: current

# Delegate long tasks to agents and make work legible to them

Karpathy says coding agents basically did not work before December 2025 and basically work since. He gives an example: one prompt told an agent to log in to a machine, set up a model server, build a web dashboard, test it, set up services and write a report. The agent worked about 30 minutes, solved its own problems and finished. He says the next prize is to climb the layers: set up orchestrators with tools, memory and instructions that manage several coding agents. Agents work best on well-specified tasks you can test. The skill is to split a task, hand off the parts that work and help at the edges. In replies he added: it is delegation, not magic. Be explicit, and make your system testable, observable and legible so agents can run longer without you.

## In his words

> "It's not magic, it's delegation."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2026-02-25

## Apply

- Write one prompt with the whole job: setup, build, test, service setup, notes for the agent, and a report for you.
- Put knowledge that sits in your head or in web UIs where tools can reach it: files, CLIs, logs.
- Add tests, logs and health checks so the agent can tell if it is done.
- Learn the agent's tools and what is easy or hard for it. Explicit instructions are faster.

## Context

- Follows [Programming moved to English in December 2025](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-01-26-programming-in-english-december-shift.md) and builds on [Give agents success criteria, not steps](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-01-26-success-criteria-not-steps.md).
- In a reply he cited a Tesla saying that treats every manual action as a fault, meaning remove yourself as the bottleneck.
- 2026-02-25 post, Claude and Codex era (Opus 4.6 and similar).

---

Date: 2026-02-20 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2024987174077432126 · Themes: agent-native-software, security-and-dependencies · Status: current

# Claws are a new layer on top of LLM agents

Karpathy bought a Mac mini to try "claws": persistent personal agents that handle orchestration, scheduling, context, tool calls and memory. Agents were a layer on LLMs, he says, and claws are a layer on agents. He is wary of OpenClaw: giving private data and keys to a 400,000-line vibe-coded project under attack is unappealing, with reports of exposed instances, RCE bugs and poisoned skills. He likes smaller ones such as NanoClaw (about 4000 lines in the core, runs in containers). Such code fits in a human head and in an agent context, so it is easier to audit. He prefers local hosting for tinkering and home devices.

## In his words

> "First there was chat, then there was code, now there is claw."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2026-02-21

## Apply

- Prefer a claw whose core you can read in one session. Count the lines before you trust it.
- Run it in containers with only the credentials and folders it needs.
- Treat community skills as untrusted code. Read them before install.
- Do not point an always-on agent at your main accounts until you have tested its limits.

## Context

- Follows his earlier [warning on agent networks](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-01-31-agent-networks-moltbook-uncharted.md). Design idea in the same thread: [Configure software with skills, and build forkable repos](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-02-20-config-via-skills-forkable-repo.md).
- He said he does not see claws as direct competitors to each other: open design questions include where compute and state live.

---

Date: 2026-02-20 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2024987174077432126 · Themes: agent-native-software, agentic-coding · Status: current

# Configure software with skills, and build the most forkable repo

While reading about NanoClaw, Karpathy found a new way to handle configuration. The project has no config flags. A skill such as `/add-telegram` instructs your agent to edit the real code to add that integration. This avoids config sprawl and if-then-else branches. His summary of the new meta: write the most forkable repo possible, then add skills that fork it into any special setup. He links this to meta-learning (for example MAML), which trains a model to fine-tune to any task in few steps. The software equivalent is the repo that is easiest to fork. He says nanochat was designed with this goal.

## In his words

> "write the most maximally forkable repo and then have skills that fork it"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2026-02-20

## Apply

- Keep the core small, readable and dependency-light.
- For each optional feature, write a skill (a Markdown file) that tells the agent which files to change and how to test the result.
- Replace long config files by a short list of such skills in the README.
- Add tests so the agent can check that a forked variant still works.

## Context

- Related: [Point an agent at a library and rip out only the part you need](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-02-11-rip-out-functionality-with-agents.md) and [Claws are a new layer on top of LLM agents](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-02-20-claws-new-layer-of-the-stack.md).

---

Date: 2026-02-16 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2023476423055601903 · Themes: agentic-coding, ai-progress · Status: current

# LLMs excel at translating code, which reopens language design

Karpathy says LLMs change the constraints of software, so it is a good time for work on programming languages and formal methods. He sees early signs in ports from C to Rust and in upgrades of old COBOL systems. LLMs are better at translation than at new generation for two reasons: the source code works as a very detailed prompt, and it gives a reference for concrete tests. Even Rust is not the best target language for LLMs, he says. Which language is best, and what stays for humans, are open questions. He expects that much of all software will be rewritten many times.

## In his words

> "the original code base acts as a kind of highly detailed prompt"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2026-02-16

## Apply

- For a migration, give the agent the old code and tests, and ask for equivalence tests first. Compare outputs of old and new.
- Port in small modules and run the old and new side by side.
- Pick target languages with strong types and fast feedback, so the agent can check itself.

## Context

- Quote-post on a Thomas Wolf essay, which cites Anthropic's report on building a C compiler with agent teams.
- In a reply he said writing binaries directly is appealing for critical regions, but doubtful in general.
- Related: [Give agents success criteria, not steps](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-01-26-success-criteria-not-steps.md).

---

Date: 2026-02-12 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2022041235188580788 · Themes: llm-psychology · Status: current

# A pretrained LLM can simulate a population, not one persona

Chat models usually have one crafted personality. Karpathy notes that the raw pretrained model is something else: a simulation engine trained on text from a very diverse population of people. He asks why we simulate one "person" when we could simulate many. He lists open questions: how to build such a simulator, how to manage its entropy, how faithful it is, how it is useful, and what appears when simulated people interact in loops. He calls this an under-explored dimension of LLMs. He is a small angel investor in Simile, which works on it.

## In his words

> "Why simulate one "person" when you could try to simulate a population?"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2026-02-12

## Apply

- For user research or red-teaming, sample many differently framed personas, not one. Compare the spread of answers.
- Check fidelity against real survey data before you trust a simulation.
- Keep notes on the diversity of outputs, since fine-tuned models often collapse to one voice.

## Context

- Disclosure: he invested in Simile. Our reading: this is a research direction, not proof that simulations match real people.

---

Date: 2026-02-11 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2021633574089416993 · Themes: agent-native-software, security-and-dependencies · Status: current

# Point an agent at a library and rip out only the part you need

Karpathy asked Claude to study how torchao implements fp8 training and write a self-contained module with the same API. He used DeepWiki (Q&A over a repo, also via MCP) and the GitHub CLI. In five minutes Claude returned about 150 lines that worked at once, with tests showing equal results. He deleted the dependency, and the code ran 3% faster. The agent also found small details that docs rarely cover. His wider point: you may no longer need to take a giant library; you can extract the exact part. This favours "bacterial code": small, modular, self-contained, with few dependencies. He names risks: libraries also bring supply chain attacks and upkeep.

## In his words

> "Software might become a lot more fluid and malleable."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2026-02-11

## Apply

- Prompt: "Use DeepWiki MCP and GitHub CLI to see how library X does Y. Can you extract it? Write a module with the same API, no dependency, and tests that prove equal results."
- Swap `github.com` for `deepwiki.com` in a repo URL to ask questions about the code.
- Prefer asking the code over reading stale docs: the code is the source of truth.
- Review extracted code and keep the tests; check licences before copying.

## Context

- He also noted that many repos are now half useful library code and half "docs++": the code explains better than official docs.
- Earlier bacterial code post: 2025-07-05. Related: [Code is now free, custom and disposable](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-12-19-code-is-free-and-ephemeral.md).
- His 2025 view on writing code that others can copy: [Write small, modular, copy-paste code like bacteria do](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-07-05-write-code-like-bacteria.md).

---

Date: 2026-02-04 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2019137879310836075 · Themes: agentic-coding · Status: current

# Agentic engineering is the professional form of vibe coding

On the first anniversary of "vibe coding", Karpathy says it fit throwaway projects and demos when models were weaker. A year later, programming with agents is becoming a default for professionals, but with more oversight. The aim is the leverage of agents with no loss in software quality. His preferred name is "agentic engineering". "Agentic" means you rarely write code yourself (about 99% of the time) and you direct agents and review. "Engineering" means there is real craft, expertise and depth to learn.

## In his words

> "programming via LLM agents is increasingly becoming a default workflow for professionals"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2026-02-04

## Apply

- Use vibe coding (accept output unchecked) only for throwaway work.
- For real software, keep tests, review and a human who owns each design choice.
- Treat agent use as a skill: write down what works, and share it with the team.

## Context

- The 2026 retrospective on [Vibe coding](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-02-02-vibe-coding-for-throwaway-projects.md). It
  does not replace that idea: he still calls vibe coding fine for throwaway work and prototypes,
  and adds a professional mode beside it.
- Related: [Coding agents make subtle conceptual mistakes, so watch them](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-01-26-coding-agents-make-subtle-conceptual-mistakes.md) and [Expertise may matter more with agents, not less](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-01-26-expertise-multiplier-generalists-and-10x.md).
- Sequoia 2026 summary (blog): vibe coding raises the floor, agentic engineering raises the
  ceiling. His example of why a human must review: in MenuGen the agent matched Stripe payments
  to users by email, which can differ from the login email. He insisted on persistent user IDs.
  See [Vibe coding a real app](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-04-27-vibe-coding-real-app-lessons.md).
- Already in March 2025 he said the terms would take time to settle, and that he used "vibe coding" only for moments of full trust in the model. In October 2025 he called engineering and vibing the two ends of one spectrum.

---

Date: 2026-01-31 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2017442712388309406 · Themes: security-and-dependencies, ai-progress · Status: current

# Networks of agents are a mess today and a security risk at scale

Karpathy was accused of overhyping Moltbook, a site where AI agents post to each other. He agrees the content is mostly spam, scams and fake posts, and that it is a prompt-injection wild west. He ran his agent in an isolated environment and still felt afraid. He advises nobody to run such software on a personal computer. But he points out that 150,000 capable agents, each with its own context and tools, on a shared persistent scratchpad is unprecedented. He expects odd effects: text viruses that spread between agents, more jailbreaks, correlated botnet behaviour and delusions in agents and humans. He is not hyping today's site, only large networks of agents in principle.

## In his words

> "the experiment is running live."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2026-01-31

## Apply

- Do not give an agent that reads untrusted content access to your private data, keys or main machine.
- Run experimental agents in isolated environments (container or separate machine) with minimal credentials.
- Treat any text an agent reads from a shared space as possible prompt injection.

## Context

- He links an earlier post of 2026-01-06: most disputes come from the gap between people who judge by where things stand now and people who judge by the rate of change.
- See also [Claws are a new layer on top of agents](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-02-20-claws-new-layer-of-the-stack.md) for his later security worries.

---

Date: 2026-01-31 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2017703360393318587 · Themes: research-and-training, ai-progress · Status: current

# The cost to train a GPT-2 level model falls about 2.5X per year

Karpathy reproduced GPT-2 level quality (CORE score) in nanochat on one 8xH100 node in about 3 hours for about 73 dollars. OpenAI paid about 43,000 dollars in 2019. That is a 600X drop in 7 years, about 2.5X per year, and he thinks it is an underestimate. Big gains came from Flash Attention 3, the Muon optimizer, gated residual and skip connections, and value embeddings, plus many small changes. He added a "time to GPT-2" leaderboard. Days later fp8 cut the time to 2.91 hours, with a lesson: fp8 gave much less than the 2X on paper because of overhead.

## In his words

> "the cost to train GPT-2 is falling approximately 2.5X every year"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2026-01-31

## Apply

- Fix a target quality (a benchmark score), then measure time or cost to reach it. Use that as your tracking metric.
- Measure real speedups end to end. Low precision may be slower when matrices are small.
- Add changes one at a time and keep only those that improve the metric.

## Context

- Related: [Train a family of models controlled by one compute dial](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-01-07-model-family-with-one-compute-dial.md).
- Spot instance prices put the same run near 20 dollars, he wrote on 2026-02-03.

---

Date: 2026-01-28 · Kind: view · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2016590919143952466 · Themes: ai-progress, research-and-training · Status: current

# New research startups can still win; 10X breakthroughs remain likely

Karpathy rejects the view that AI is too mature for a research-focused startup to beat the incumbents. People said the same when OpenAI started, and again about later challengers, and they were wrong each time. Scaling and local improvements will keep giving gains. But the gap between frontier LLMs and a mind that runs on 20 watts is large, and much progress is happening with much confusion. So he rates the chance of breakthroughs that give about 10X, not 10%, as high enough to bet on. The hard part is creating conditions where such discoveries happen. In a reply he added that AI can go beyond a brain, for example as a hive mind without the bandwidth limits of speech.

## Context

- Quote-post on the launch of Flapping Airplanes, a lab Karpathy praised. This is an opinion, not a measured claim.

---

Date: 2026-01-26 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2015883857489522876 · Themes: agentic-coding, llm-psychology · Status: current

# Coding agents make subtle conceptual mistakes, so watch them

Karpathy says the mistakes of coding agents have changed. They are no longer syntax errors. They look like the errors of a hasty junior developer. The agent makes a wrong assumption for you and keeps going without a check. It does not ask questions, show trade-offs or push back, and it is often too agreeable. It also bloats code: a 1000-line design shrinks to 100 lines when you ask it for a simpler way. It may edit or delete comments it does not understand. Short rules in CLAUDE.md did not fix this. His answer is not to drop agents but to review closely. Hype about "no IDE" and "agent swarms" is too early for code you care about.

## In his words

> "I would watch them like a hawk, in a nice large IDE on the side."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2026-01-26

## Apply

- Keep an IDE open next to the agent sessions. Read the diff, not only the summary.
- Ask the agent to list its assumptions before it codes, and to name the trade-offs. Use plan mode for anything larger than a small edit.
- After a working change, ask: "Can this be simpler? Remove dead code and unused abstractions."
- Check the final report against the data. He saw an agent name the wrong best result from its own table.
- Hand the agent well-scoped ideas to implement. In his tests it executed his ideas well but proposed weak experiments itself.

## Context

- Part of the 2026-01-26 notes written after about a month of coding mostly with Claude Code. See [Give agents success criteria, not steps](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-01-26-success-criteria-not-steps.md) for the leverage part of the same post.
- In a reply on 2026-02-06 he listed more failures: it broke CLAUDE.md style rules, and it did not flag risky speed tricks in open-ended nanochat work.
- On 2026-02-27 he said he still edits in the IDE because seeing the code helps him prompt better.
- Not reversed by his later agent experiments. The "agent swarm" caution is about code you care
  about. His later agent research work ([Autoresearch](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-07-autoresearch-loop.md),
  [You now program an organisation of agents](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-02-27-programming-an-agent-research-org.md))
  runs only where a metric checks each result, and he still wanted interactive sessions he could
  watch ([The IDE is not dead](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-11-bigger-ide-agent-command-center.md)).

---

Date: 2026-01-26 · Kind: view · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2015883857489522876 · Themes: ai-progress, agentic-coding · Status: current

# Expertise may matter more with agents, not less

Karpathy asks open questions about who gains from coding agents. The "10X engineer" ratio, the gap between the average and the best engineer, may grow a lot. Generalists may do better against specialists, since LLMs are strong at filling in details and weak at grand strategy. In a reply on 2026-02-25 he gave a firmer view: calling people "prompters" is a misunderstanding. Vibe coders now get somewhere, but at the top, deep technical expertise may multiply leverage even more than before.

## In his words

> "How much of society is bottlenecked by digital knowledge work?"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2026-01-26

## Apply

- Invest in judgement: learn to decompose tasks, spot wrong assumptions and read code fast.
- Use agents to cover areas outside your specialty, and ask an expert to review the result.
- Hire and train for oversight skills, not only typing speed.

## Context

- Listed as questions in the 2026-01-26 notes. The 2026-02-25 reply links his post on [agentic engineering](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-02-04-agentic-engineering-vs-vibe-coding.md).
- First raised on [2025-12-27](https://x.com/karpathy/status/2004974725320347884): in a reply he said experienced developers have a real advantage, but only if they adapt fast, and that rejecting the new layer would be a mistake.

---

Date: 2026-01-26 · Kind: view · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2015883857489522876 · Themes: agentic-coding, ai-progress · Status: current

# LLM help is less a speedup than an expansion

Karpathy says it is hard to measure the speedup from LLM help. He feels faster at tasks he already planned. But the larger effect is that he does more in total. Two reasons: code that was never worth writing is now cheap to write, and code outside his skill is now within reach. So the gain is partly speed and partly a wider range of work. A related note: agents also lower the cost of stamina. They do not tire or lose heart. He calls stamina a core bottleneck of work, and LLMs have raised it a lot.

## In his words

> "certainly it's speedup, but it's possibly a lot more an expansion."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2026-01-26

## Apply

- Do not judge agent use by hours saved on old tasks. Also count the tasks you now do that you would have skipped.
- Make a list of small tools you never built because of cost. Give one to an agent this week.
- Give the agent hard, long problems and let it retry. It does not get discouraged.

## Context

- Part of the 2026-01-26 notes; see [Programming moved to English in December 2025](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-01-26-programming-in-english-december-shift.md).
- Later example of "expansion": [Code is now free, custom and disposable](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-12-19-code-is-free-and-ephemeral.md).

Date: 2026-01-26 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2015883857489522876 · Themes: agentic-coding, ai-progress · Status: current

# Programming moved to English in December 2025

Karpathy reports a fast change in his own work. In November 2025 about 80% of his coding was
manual with autocomplete. In December about 80% was agent coding with edits on top. He calls it
the biggest change in his workflow in about 20 years, and it took a few weeks. He thinks agents
(Claude and Codex in particular) crossed a threshold of coherence: generated chunks became larger
and more reliable. At Sequoia Ascent 2026 he described the new unit of work as a "macro action":
implement a feature, refactor a subsystem, research a library, set up a service, write tests and
fix failures, compare approaches. The programmer becomes an orchestrator of agents. He guesses that
a double-digit share of engineers already work this way, while public awareness is in the low
single digits. Writing code by prompt feels odd, a little like cheating.

## In his words

> "I really am mostly programming in English now"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2026-01-26

## Apply

- Write requests as whole outcomes with a way to check them, not as edits to specific lines.
- Include "write tests, run them, fix failures" in the task, so the agent closes the loop.
- Ask for a plan and a comparison of approaches before a big change, and review the plan.
- Learn the setup: configure the agent, write project instructions, and find what it does well
  and badly.
- Re-test your habits every few months. Work that needed hand-holding may no longer need it.

## Context

- Same post as [Give agents success criteria, not steps](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-01-26-success-criteria-not-steps.md)
  and [Coding agents make subtle conceptual mistakes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-01-26-coding-agents-make-subtle-conceptual-mistakes.md).
  On 2026-02-25 he repeated that agents mostly failed before December; see
  [Delegate long tasks](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-02-25-delegate-long-tasks-decompose-well.md).
- The Sequoia text (blog, 2026-04-30) is an LLM-made summary of the talk that he checked and
  posted.
- This replaces his earlier tool mix. It supersedes
  [Coding agents are weak on novel code](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-10-17-coding-agents-weak-on-novel-code.md)
  (October 2025: he found autocomplete the best fit for him) and
  [Stitch several coding tools together](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-08-24-stitch-coding-tools-by-task.md)
  (August 2025: tab completion gave about 75% of his AI help).

Date: 2026-01-26 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2015883857489522876 · Themes: agentic-coding, verification · Status: current

# Give agents success criteria, not steps

LLM agents are very good at looping until they meet a specific goal. Karpathy finds most of the
leverage there. So change from imperative instructions to declarative ones: say what "done"
looks like and how to check it, then let the agent iterate. He gives three patterns: have the
agent write tests first and then make them pass; put the agent in a loop with a browser tool so
it can see its result; and write a naive, obviously correct version first, then ask the agent to
optimize it while it keeps the output correct.

## In his words

> "Don't tell it what to do, give it success criteria and watch it go."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2026-01-26

## Apply

- Start each task with a check the agent can run: a failing test, a script that prints a
  number, or a page it can load and inspect.
- Ask for tests first: "Write tests for X that fail now. Then make them pass. Do not change the
  tests."
- For speed work, keep the slow correct version as the reference and compare outputs after
  every change.
- Give the agent the tool it needs to see the result (browser, logs, benchmark), so it can
  loop without you.

## Context

- In a reply the same day he called spec-driven development the limit of the move from imperative to declarative: being declarative entirely.
- From a long post of notes after weeks of coding mostly with Claude Code, written after models
  reached a new level of coherence in December 2025.
- The same post lists the agents' typical mistakes: silent wrong assumptions, overcomplicated
  code, and edits to unrelated code.

---

Date: 2026-01-26 · Kind: view · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2015883857489522876 · Themes: learning-and-education, agentic-coding · Status: current

# Writing code can atrophy while reading code stays strong

Karpathy notices that his ability to write code by hand is slowly fading because agents write most of it. He argues that generating code and judging code are different skills. Many small syntax details matter for writing, but you can review code well without remembering them. A related risk came from a reply he praised: "comprehension debt". When an agent produces something that seems to work, it is tempting to move on without understanding it. Our reading: review keeps the skill that matters, but only if you actually read and understand the result.

## In his words

> "Generation (writing code) and discrimination (reading code) are different capabilities in the brain."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2026-01-26

## Apply

- Keep one practice habit that needs you to write code by hand, such as a small weekly exercise.
- When an agent finishes, ask it to explain the change. Do not merge what you cannot explain.
- Track "comprehension debt": note the parts of the codebase that nobody has read, and schedule time to read them.

## Context

- From the 2026-01-26 notes. Related: [Coding agents make subtle conceptual mistakes, so watch them](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-01-26-coding-agents-make-subtle-conceptual-mistakes.md).
- In a reply that day he said the shift "feels like cheating" because code that was a point of pride is now free and instant.

Date: 2026-01-12 · Kind: practice · Source: https://github.com/karpathy/nanochat/blob/master/.claude/skills/read-arxiv-paper/SKILL.md · Themes: agentic-coding, context-and-prompting · Status: current

# Have the agent read a paper's TeX source and relate it to your repo

nanochat holds a small Claude Code skill, `read-arxiv-paper`. Given an arXiv link, it changes
the URL to the `/src/` form, downloads the archive into a cache folder (skipping files it has),
unpacks it, finds the main `.tex` file and reads all linked sources. It then writes a summary
into the project's own `knowledge/` folder, with a short tag in the file name that does not
overwrite older ones. The key instruction is about purpose. The agent must read the related
nanochat code and say how the paper could apply to the project. The skill is six numbered steps
in plain markdown.

## In his words

> "The goal is to fetch the TeX Source of the paper (not the PDF!)"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2026-01-12

## Apply

- For papers, give the agent the source (TeX, HTML or text) instead of a PDF.
- Write the skill with the report location and purpose: "summary for this repo, with links to
  our code".
- Store summaries in the project folder, not a hidden cache, so you can open them.
- Make the skill skip downloads that already exist.

## Context

- The date is a lower bound: the example arXiv ID 2601.07372 dates from January 2026, and the
  commit date was not in our source. The skill lives in `.claude/skills/` of the nanochat repo.
- Related: [Write the agent's operating rules as a program.md skill](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-06-program-md-is-the-research-org.md).

---

Date: 2026-01-07 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2009037707918626874 · Themes: research-and-training · Status: current

# Train a family of models controlled by one compute dial

Karpathy argues that you should not tune for one model. You tune a family of models controlled by one dial, the compute you spend, so results improve steadily as you turn it. This lets you do real scaling-law science and gives confidence that a big run will behave as extrapolated. In nanochat he fixed FLOP budgets, swept model sizes and found a tokens-to-parameters ratio of about 8, against about 20 in Chinchilla. A miniseries from d10 to d20 cost about 100 dollars. He compared it with GPT-2 and GPT-3 through the CORE score, since validation loss is not comparable across setups.

## In his words

> "controlled by a single dial (the compute you wish to spend)"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2026-01-07

## Apply

- Fix a FLOP budget, train several sizes, and find the size with the lowest loss at that budget.
- Repeat at three or more budgets. Fit a line for optimal size and tokens against compute.
- Use one objective score (such as CORE) when you compare with models that use other data.
- Run the full recipe in his repo with `scaling_laws.sh` and `miniseries.sh`.

## Context

- Source post links nanochat discussion 420. See [GPT-2 level training now costs under 100 dollars](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-01-31-gpt2-training-cost-falling.md).

---

Date: 2026-01-03 · Kind: practice · Source: https://github.com/karpathy/rustbpe · Themes: verification, agentic-coding · Status: current

# Port to an unfamiliar language by testing against your own reference

rustbpe is a Rust library that trains BPE tokenizers. Karpathy is not a Rust developer. He says
he wrote the Python reference himself, from scratch, and understands it fully. He then wrote
the Rust version against it with tests that check the outputs are equal, and got real
assistance from ChatGPT and Claude Code (Opus 4.5). He reports that every equality test passes, and he asks
readers to report style problems. The method gives a clear trust rule: you own the reference and
the tests, and the model owns the translation.

## Apply

- Keep a simple, correct reference that you understand. Do not let the agent rewrite it.
- Ask the agent to port it and to write tests that run both versions on the same inputs and
  compare outputs.
- State in the README which parts a model wrote and what checks back them.
- Accept review comments on structure and idiom from native speakers of the new language.

## Context

- Repository created 2026-01-03. Compare [success criteria, not steps](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-01-26-success-criteria-not-steps.md),
  which gives the same pattern of a naive version first and optimising later for speed work.

Date: 2025-12-28 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2005421816110862601 · Themes: agentic-coding, verification · Status: current

# Let the agent run experiments and keep a results log

Karpathy reports that Claude implemented ideas, tested them on toy examples, launched and watched training runs, kept a running markdown file of results, profiled code and triaged pull requests. He still had to catch subtle mistakes, ideas it missed, and bloated or tightly coupled designs. So the agent does the loop work, and the human keeps the design.

## Apply

- Ask a long-running session to keep a results file with a run table and short notes.
- Review its design choices yourself, not only the numbers.
- Give it a way to check each run, such as a metric and a threshold.

## Context

- Posted 2025-12-28 about his nanochat experiments.
- Related: [success criteria, not steps](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-01-26-success-criteria-not-steps.md).
