Date: 2025-12-28 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2005353145128583447 · Themes: agentic-coding, agent-native-software · Status: current

# Connect your tools so the agent needs no manual steps

In a reply about wiring everything into a coding agent through skills, Karpathy gave a short rule: aggressively JIT your work. The goal is that you add almost no latency and take almost no actions yourself. He calls it digital Factorio time, a reference to a game about automating factory chains. Each tool you connect removes one manual hand-off from the loop.

## Apply

- List the manual steps you repeat in a task (check a log, query a table, deploy). Make a skill or CLI for each.
- Give the agent scoped credentials for those tools so it can act without you.
- Measure a task by how many times it waits for you. Reduce that number.

## Context

- A reply from 2025-12-28. The source is a short reply, so the idea is small.
- Related: [learn the new programmable layer](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-12-26-learn-the-new-programmable-layer.md).

Date: 2025-12-28 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2005067301511630926 · Themes: agent-native-software, agentic-coding · Status: current

# Let an agent find your local devices and build a better control app

Inspired by a post where an agent controlled an oven, Karpathy tried Claude Code on his Lutron home system. The agent found the controllers on the local network, scanned ports, read metadata and firmware, and found the vendor's PDF online. It wrote a script to start pairing and told him which button to hold for 3 seconds. Then it got the certificates, listed all lights, shades, heating and sensors, and switched the kitchen lights to test. He is now vibe coding his own command centre and dropping the slow vendor app. Setup needs: the agent must be on the same Wi-Fi, and pairing needed a physical button press on the panel. He notes that many other devices may have no such step.

## Apply

- Pick one device whose vendor app is poor, and ask an agent to find it on your local network and read the vendor docs.
- Do the physical approval steps yourself (button, code). Our reading: keep the secrets it fetches out of git.
- Ask for a first test that is harmless, such as toggling a light, before you build anything on top.
- Our reading: treat local devices that need no pairing step as a security risk to check.

## Context

- Post of 2025-12-28 and replies the same day.
- Related: [Connect your tools so the agent needs no manual steps](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-12-28-aggressively-jit-your-work.md) and [Some apps should disappear](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-04-30-some-apps-should-disappear.md).

Date: 2025-12-26 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/2004607146781278521 · Themes: agentic-coding · Status: current

# Learn the new programmable layer of agent tools

In late December 2025 Karpathy said he had never felt so behind as a programmer. A new layer now sits on top of the old stack. It has agents and subagents, prompts and context, memory and permissions, tools, plugins, skills and hooks, MCP and LSP servers, slash commands, workflows and IDE integrations. To use it well you need a mental model of tools that are stochastic and fallible. If you do not claim the productivity boost, it feels like a skill issue. His advice is to take the work seriously and not fall behind.

## In his words

> "Roll up your sleeves to not fall behind."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-12-26

## Apply

- Pick one feature you do not use (hooks, subagents, skills, LSP) each week and wire it into a real task.
- Keep short notes on what each feature does well and where it fails.
- Treat agent output as fallible: plan for review and checks.
- Re-test what agents can do about once a month. A view from a month ago can already be out of date.

## Context

- Posted 2025-12-26, after the jump in agent quality that he describes in [success criteria, not steps](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-01-26-success-criteria-not-steps.md).
- Related: [connect your tools so you add no latency](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-12-28-aggressively-jit-your-work.md).

Date: 2025-12-19 · Kind: practice · Source: https://karpathy.bearblog.dev/year-in-review-2025/ · Themes: agentic-coding, agent-native-software · Status: current

# Run coding agents on the developer's own computer

Karpathy calls Claude Code the first convincing agent: it strings tool use and reasoning into
long problem solving. He adds that it runs on your computer, with your environment, data and
context. He thinks OpenAI chose wrongly when it focused early agent work on cloud containers
started from ChatGPT. Swarms in the cloud may be the endgame. But capabilities are jagged and
takeoff is slow, so a local agent suits the present better. What counts is not where the model
runs. It is the existing machine: installation, secrets, configuration, data and quick
interaction. He sees a new interaction style: an AI that lives on your computer, not a website.

## Apply

- Start agent work in a local checkout where your tools, credentials and config already work.
- Put project context in files the agent finds on your machine, such as AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md.
- Use cloud agents for jobs that are well specified and need no private setup.

## Context

- Written in December 2025, before he joined Anthropic. It is his view as an outside user.
- Related: [Success criteria, not steps](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-01-26-success-criteria-not-steps.md).

Date: 2025-12-19 · Kind: practice · Source: https://karpathy.bearblog.dev/year-in-review-2025/ · Themes: agentic-coding, agent-native-software · Status: current

# Code is now free, custom and disposable

In 2025, models crossed the threshold where English is enough to build many useful programs.
Professionals can now write software that would never have been worth writing. Karpathy had a
custom Rust tokenizer written this way, and he built a whole temporary app just to find one bug.
In February 2026 he gave a sharper example. Claude built him a dashboard for an 8-week fitness
experiment in about one hour, and had to reverse engineer a treadmill's cloud API to do it. His
conclusion: nobody should search a store for a "cardio tracker" when an agent can write 300 lines
on the spot. He thinks one hour is still too slow. With personal context and skill libraries in
place, it should take one minute. In replies he went further: code paths could be assembled for
one purpose and deleted after one run.

## In his words

> "code is suddenly free, ephemeral, malleable, discardable after single use"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-12-19

## Apply

- Before you install an app for a narrow personal task, ask an agent to write it.
- Build throwaway tools for one-time jobs: a viewer, a converter, a repro harness for a bug.
- Before you add a dependency, ask whether an agent can write the 200 lines you need.
- Keep personal context (goals, data, preferences) in files an agent can read, so the next tool
  takes minutes.
- Check details agents often get wrong, such as units and dates. Keep careful review for code that
  stays: see [agentic engineering](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-02-04-agentic-engineering-vs-vibe-coding.md).

## Context

- From his 2025 review, a year after he coined "vibe coding". The fitness dashboard posts are from
  2026-02-19.
- To a reply that a grandmother will not build an app, he answered that her agent should know
  about apps, she should not. He called the objection a "scarcity mindset" and expects a mixed,
  gradual change.
- The same posts say products must become sensors and actuators with agent-friendly interfaces:
  see [Apps should be APIs](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-20-apps-become-apis-agents-are-glue.md).
- Earlier chat-based form: [Ask the model to write a small app just for you](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-02-27-one-off-apps-on-demand.md).
  Sharing such tools: [Treat small apps as disposable](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-11-18-disposable-vibe-coded-apps.md).
  Throwaway software for review: [Work rises into oversight](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-10-02-oversight-and-discardable-software.md).
- Demand side: [Cheaper software raises the demand for software](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-20-cheaper-software-more-demand.md).

Date: 2025-12-19 · Kind: view · Source: https://karpathy.bearblog.dev/year-in-review-2025/ · Themes: research-and-training · Status: current

# RLVR became the major new training stage of 2025

Until 2025, labs trained a production model in three stages: pretraining, supervised
finetuning, and reinforcement learning from human feedback. In 2025, Reinforcement Learning
from Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) became the new major stage. The model trains against rewards
that code can check, such as maths and programming puzzles. It develops reasoning-like
behaviour by itself: it splits problems into steps and backtracks. Nobody could write those
traces by hand. Unlike the two older stages, RLVR rewards cannot be gamed easily, so it allows
long optimisation and gives much capability per dollar. It took compute that was planned for
pretraining. Model sizes stayed similar, but RL runs grew long. It also adds a new knob:
longer reasoning at test time. OpenAI o1 first showed it. The o3 release was the turning point.

## Apply

- Choose a reasoning model and a high thinking setting for tasks with a checkable answer.
- For a domain you care about, ask whether you can build a checker. A checker may let you
  improve a model on that domain with RL.
- Do not compare 2025 model gains with parameter count. Look at test-time compute too.

## Context

- First of six "paradigm changes" in his 2025 review. It links to
  [Software 2.0 automates what you can verify](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-11-17-software-2-automates-what-you-can-verify.md).

---

Date: 2025-12-10 · Kind: view · Source: https://karpathy.bearblog.dev/auto-grade-hn/ · Themes: ai-progress · Status: current

# Future LLMs will read everything we do today

While he graded old Hacker News threads, Karpathy noted a side effect. If analysing a past
discussion costs a few cents, then everything we write or do in public can be read in detail
later. Much of today's behaviour assumes security by obscurity: nobody will look closely. If
intelligence becomes too cheap to meter, a perfect reconstruction and synthesis of a person's
record becomes possible. The reader may be a future LLM, or a human using one. His advice is
short: be good.

## In his words

> "Be good, future LLMs are watching"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-12-10

## Apply

- Assume that public posts, commits, comments and reviews can be summarised and graded later.
  Write what you would stand behind.
- Do not rely on the belief that nobody will read it for anything you publish, including old archives.
- Keep private material out of public places, since cheap analysis covers it too.

## Context

- He quotes his own earlier tweets with the line above. The post uses it to explain why the
  hindsight project matters: [Grade old discussions with an LLM](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-12-10-llm-hindsight-grading-hn.md).
- Our reading: the claim is a forecast, not a measured result.

---

Date: 2025-12-10 · Kind: practice · Source: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46222634 · Themes: llm-psychology, verification · Status: current

# LLM judges grade too freely and recognise who wrote the text

Karpathy used an LLM to grade ten-year-old Hacker News comments with hindsight. Two flaws showed
up. The model gave good or bad grades to comments that made no strong prediction, if they were
good or bad in a broader sense. It also recognised usernames well, and its grades seemed biased by
who the author was. He tuned the prompt to fix the easy mistakes and thinks more iteration is
possible.

## Apply

- Remove names and other identity clues from the text before an LLM judge reads it.
- Tell the judge exactly what qualifies for a grade, such as "only score explicit predictions".
- Spot-check a sample of grades by hand, and keep the failures as test cases for the prompt.

## Context

- A reply on the Hacker News thread of his December 2025 hindsight-grading project.
- Related: [Software 2.0 automates what you can verify](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-11-17-software-2-automates-what-you-can-verify.md).

---

Date: 2025-12-10 · Kind: practice · Source: https://github.com/karpathy/hn-time-capsule · Themes: ai-progress, agentic-coding · Status: current

# Use an LLM to grade past predictions with hindsight

hn-time-capsule fetches the Hacker News front page from exactly ten years earlier, with each
article and its comment tree. For each thread, an LLM writes what actually happened, names the
most prescient and the most wrong commenters, and grades every commenter from A+ to F. The grades
are parsed and added up into a hall of fame. Karpathy calls the general idea the interesting part:
LLMs can go through old human writing and turn it into knowledge and insight. The pipeline has
five stages (fetch, prompt, analyze, parse, render) that run alone or together.

## In his words

> "LLMs automatically scouring human artifacts from the past and synthesizing them into knowledge and insights."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-12-10

## Apply

- Build a staged pipeline that saves each stage to files (prompt, response, parsed grades). You
  can re-run one stage and inspect each one.
- Test with a small `--limit` and a cheaper model before a full paid run.
- Ask the model to commit to labelled verdicts ("most prescient") so you can parse and rank.
- Point the same method at your own old notes, tickets or forecasts.

## Context

- Repository created 2025-12-10, 99% vibe coded with Opus 4.5 in a few hours. A related blog
  post is linked from the README.
- Related: [Treat small apps as disposable](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-11-18-disposable-vibe-coded-apps.md).

---

Date: 2025-12-09 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1998236299862659485 · Themes: research-and-training, verification · Status: current

# Do not split train and test with positive and negative seeds

Karpathy found a bug in nanochat. He had used the sign of the seed as a clever way to get different random streams for train and test. In Python, `random.seed(3)` and `random.seed(-3)` give the same generator, because the code takes the absolute value of an integer seed. The docs say only that the same seed gives the same sequence. They do not promise that different seeds give different sequences. He also argues that dropping the sign bit was a mistake, since the algorithm has many state bits that could use it. The bug was small and showed up only in one evaluation, but it made train equal to test.

## In his words

> "no guarantee is made that different seeds produce different sequences"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-12-09

## Apply

- Make train and test splits from a fixed list of ids or a hash, not from a seed trick.
- Add a test that proves your two random streams differ, and that the sets do not overlap.
- Do not rely on behaviour the docs do not state; read the contract.

## Context

- Post of 2025-12-09. A contributor on GitHub found the bug.
- Related: [Give agents success criteria, not steps](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-01-26-success-criteria-not-steps.md).

---

Date: 2025-12-07 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1997731268969304070 · Themes: llm-psychology, context-and-prompting · Status: current

# Ask the LLM to simulate experts, not to give its opinion

Karpathy says you should not ask a model for its own opinion on a topic. There is no "you" to ask. If you force one, the model simulates a personality implied by its finetuning data. A better prompt asks which people would be worth consulting on X, and what each of them would say. This gives you several views from the model's wide knowledge, and avoids one made-up personality.

## In his words

> "There is no 'you'."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-12-07

## Apply

- For a design review, ask: which roles should review this (security, performance, UX)? Then ask each role for its critique.
- Name the experts or the roles in the prompt instead of asking for 'your opinion'.
- Compare the views and decide yourself. See [llm-council](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-11-22-llm-council-anonymous-peer-review.md).

## Context

- Posted 2025-12-07.
- Related: [the space of intelligences](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-11-29-llms-shaped-by-commercial-evolution.md).
- He later said he does not mean old-style prompts such as "you are an expert programmer". He thinks distinct simulated views may give council-like gains, from ensembling and from the gap between generating and judging.

---

Date: 2025-11-29 · Kind: practice · Source: https://karpathy.bearblog.dev/the-space-of-minds/ · Themes: llm-psychology · Status: current

# LLMs are shaped by commercial evolution, not biological evolution

Animal intelligence is one point in a large space of possible minds. Karpathy lists what shaped
it: an embodied self, survival, power and status drives, heavy investment in social skills, and
curiosity and play. For LLMs the pressures differ. The base is a statistical imitation of human
text. Reinforcement learning then pushes the model to guess the task and collect rewards. At
scale, A/B tests for daily users select models that crave approval, which gives sycophancy.
Skills are spiky, because failing one task never meant death for the model. The substrate and
the algorithm also differ, but he says the objective matters most because it sets the long-term
direction. Good mental models of this new entity help us predict it.

## Apply

- When a model flatters you, read it as a trained urge to get an upvote. Ask for critique
  directly, and ask for what is wrong first.
- Do not credit a model with human motives such as fear, pride or loyalty.
- Expect it to guess what the task is. State the real goal and the grading criteria.
- Expect odd failures on simple tasks. Check them; do not assume general competence.

## Context

- Posted 2025-11-29, as a follow-up to [LLMs are ghosts, not animals](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-10-01-llms-are-ghosts-not-animals.md).
- He calls LLMs humanity's "first contact" with non-animal intelligence, but muddled, because
  they still digest human artifacts.

---

Date: 2025-11-25 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1993369287969718540 · Themes: agentic-coding, context-and-prompting · Status: current

# Ask an LLM whether a library function exists, and give it docs for new tools

A well-known programmer found that PyTorch had a built-in for a tensor rearrangement he had written by hand. Karpathy has had medium success asking LLMs whether such a thing exists. It works for well-known functions: two top models knew the function when he described the tensor change in words. For esoteric or new libraries (`uv` is his example) he has done better by packing the docs into one markdown file and adding it to the context. A built-in "Ask AI" over the docs, which uses retrieval, was not very bright. The limit: you must suspect the function exists, and then ask. He doubts that a model would offer it without being asked.

## Apply

- After you write a helper by hand, describe what it does in plain words and ask whether the standard library or a major package has it.
- For a new or niche library, export its docs to markdown and paste them with your question.
- Keep the docs file in your repo, so the agent can reuse it.

## Context

- Reply of 2025-11-25 to a thread with John Carmack.
- Related: [Write docs for LLMs](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-03-12-write-docs-for-llms.md) and [Check which tools the model has](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-02-27-check-which-tools-the-model-has.md).

Date: 2025-11-24 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1993010584175141038 · Themes: learning-and-education · Status: current

# Use AI to learn, but test without it

Karpathy argues that you cannot detect AI use in homework. Schools should move most testing to in-class, physically monitored work. Students need to be good with AI, and also able to work without it, as with calculators. They must understand enough to gut-check wrong answers. Verification skill is the key.

## In his words

> "move the majority of testing to in class settings"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-11-24

## Apply

- When you learn with an agent, test yourself without it: write from memory, then explain back.
- Check an AI answer against your own rough estimate before you accept it.
- Keep a short list of what you can do with no AI help, and keep it current.

## Context

- Posted 2025-11-24.
- Related: [learning takes effort](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2024-02-10-learning-is-not-supposed-to-be-fun.md).

Date: 2025-11-23 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1992711182537707990 · Themes: output-and-reading · Status: current

# Plan in text first, then ask an image model to illustrate, and re-roll

Karpathy tried Nano Banana Pro, an image model that also reasons. For a workout plan he first asked for a weekly plan in a separate text chat, giving his goals and preferences. Then he asked the model to illustrate the whole week, and each day, as posters to print. He also had it solve exam questions inside the exam page image, with doodles and diagrams, and fix a math problem "in my handwriting". It makes mistakes: one poster showed an odd push-up. You re-roll until it is right, and if it loops you start a new conversation. A second model can check the content. He sees this as a sign of a future where the model's interface is an intelligent canvas.

## Apply

- Settle the content in a text conversation. Only then ask for images.
- Ask for the whole set (a week), then for each item, so the style stays consistent.
- Check facts and spelling in the picture yourself, or paste it to another model; re-roll on mistakes.
- When the model gets stuck in a loop, start a new conversation with the finished text.

## Context

- Posts of 2025-11-23. The same day he wrote that this is the GUI for text chat: see [Text chat is the terminal era](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-03-31-text-chat-is-the-terminal-era.md).
- Related: [Use AI to learn, but test without it](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-11-24-learn-with-ai-but-test-without-it.md), which he posted the next day on exam answers.

Date: 2025-11-22 · Kind: practice · Source: https://github.com/karpathy/llm-council · Themes: verification, agentic-coding · Status: current

# Ask several models, then let them rank each other anonymously

LLM Council is a local web app. You ask one question and it goes to several models through
OpenRouter. Stage 1 collects the first opinions, shown in tabs. In stage 2, each model gets the
other answers with the model names replaced by "Response A", "Response B" and so on, so it
cannot favour a brand. It ranks them for accuracy and insight. In stage 3, a chairman model
turns everything into one answer. The repo's design notes (its CLAUDE.md) add practical rules:
a strict "FINAL RANKING" format so it can be parsed, keep going if one model fails, and show raw
outputs so the user can check the parsing. He says the project was 99% vibe coded, so these notes
were probably written by his coding agent, not by him.

## Apply

- For a hard question, send it to two or three different models and ask each to critique the
  others' answers with names hidden.
- From the repo's CLAUDE.md (probably agent-written): ask reviewers for a numbered ranking in a
  fixed format with a fallback parser, and treat one failed model call as a missing vote, not a
  failed request.
- Keep raw answers visible next to the summary, so you can audit the chairman.

## Context

- Created 2025-11-22 as a casual weekend project, 99% vibe coded, to compare models while reading
  books with LLMs. Model list in the README: GPT 5.1, Gemini 3 Pro, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Grok 4.
- Related: [Read books together with an LLM](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2024-12-11-read-books-with-an-llm.md).
- He already asked several vendors the same question in early 2025 and called them his "LLM council" ([video](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-02-27-fast-model-first-thinking-model-for-hard.md)).
- First raised on [2025-02-03](https://x.com/karpathy/status/1886220274821128668): he wished for a council where all models answer, then debate, and the top-ranked model writes the final answer. The repo came in November.
- On 2025-09-05 he described a quick eval: pool the answers of several models and ask each model to rank all of them. In his small tests the models showed little bias toward their own text. He explains this by the gap between producing good work and recognising it.
- In a reply he said every model ranks every answer, with names hidden, so the result is not simple flattery. On 2025-12-24 he guessed that one model with several different prompts might work as well, if the prompts are chosen with care.

Date: 2025-11-22 · Kind: view · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1992093128170655971 · Themes: llm-psychology, ai-progress · Status: current

# Slop is data that does not help a world model; it is regretted attention

Karpathy asked for a measurable definition of "slop". He feels he can judge a slop index, but he cannot yet define it. Replies offered "long low-perplexity text" (he noted that random tokens would then be the least slop) and a paper with three groups: information utility, quality and style. He felt these miss the core. His idea: slop is data without insight. It is filler that type-checks as information but is not. It is style without substance. When you attend to it or train on it, it does not help a model compress the world. A short form from a reply: slop is attention you later regret.

## In his words

> "Slop is "regretted" attention."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-11-22

## Context

- Post and replies of 2025-11-22. He suggested using small series of LLMs and thinking-token budgets as ways to measure it.
- Related: [The slopacolypse of 2026](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-01-26-slopacolypse-2026.md) and [Self-distillation: slop leaks](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-05-01-self-distillation-slop-leaks.md).

---

Date: 2025-11-18 · Kind: practice · Source: https://github.com/karpathy/reader3 · Themes: agent-native-software, agentic-coding · Status: current

# Treat small apps as disposable; ask your LLM to change them

Karpathy released several small tools with the same notice: reader3 (about 90% vibe coded),
llm-council (99%) and hn-time-capsule (99%, built in a few hours with Opus 4.5). Each says he will
not support or improve it. It is there for inspiration. His reasoning is that code is now cheap
and short-lived, so a reader should ask an LLM to change the tool in the way they want, instead
of waiting for a maintainer or a configuration option. He also states how much of the code a
model wrote, which tells the reader how much to trust it.

## In his words

> "Code is ephemeral now and libraries are over"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-11-18

## Apply

- For a one-off tool, build it with an agent in a day and keep it in its own small repository.
- Add a short README note: how much was model-written, and that you will not maintain it.
- When you want a change in someone else's small tool, clone it and prompt your agent. Do not
  open a feature request.
- Keep these tools small enough that an agent can read all of the code in one go.

## Context

- reader3 was created 2025-11-18, llm-council 2025-11-22, hn-time-capsule 2025-12-10. The quote
  is from the reader3 and llm-council READMEs. Opus 4.5 era.
- His view of "libraries are over" is stated for small apps. He still ships careful code in
  nanochat; see [Keep the codebase minimal and forkable](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-10-13-nanochat-one-dial-minimal-fork.md).
- Related: [Read books together with an LLM](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2024-12-11-read-books-with-an-llm.md).

Date: 2025-11-18 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1990854771058913347 · Themes: verification, llm-psychology · Status: current

# Public benchmarks are gameable, so keep your own evals

Reacting to a new frontier model in November 2025, Karpathy said public benchmarks are gameable
and advised people to talk to the model themselves. He expects people to build private ensembles
of evals for their own use. His 2025 review gives the reason. A benchmark is by design a verifiable
environment, so it is a target for RL with verifiable rewards and for synthetic data. Teams build
training environments next to a benchmark and grow "spikes" of skill that cover it; he calls
training on the test set a new art form. The result tops charts yet behaves oddly outside them. In
November 2026 he said benchmarks are in a very bad state and he basically does not trust them. He
now points to Epoch's Capabilities Index and its published benchmark reviews.

## In his words

> "Go talk to the model."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-11-18

## Apply

- Collect 10 to 20 real prompts from your work, with notes on what a good answer looks like.
- Run them on each new model release and compare with the last run.
- Add a case whenever a model fails you in real work, and test the edges of your task, not only
  its centre.
- Keep the private set out of prompts, training data and public repos.
- When you read a public score, check how the benchmark was built and reviewed.
- Keep a standing set of trick prompts that are easy for people and hard for LLMs, plus one open task such as an unsolved problem, and rerun it on each new model (his Grok 3 test, 2025-02).

## Context

- X post of 2025-11-18 (in February 2025 he described a personal set of gotcha prompts in a post on
  Grok 3); his 2025 review of 2025-12-19; a Hacker News reply of 2026-11-01.
- He also suggested using a different LLM every day to stay current, which he calls riding the LLM
  cycle.
- Related: [Jagged intelligence follows verifiability](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-20-jagged-intelligence-follows-verifiability.md),
  [RLHF is just barely RL](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2024-08-07-rlhf-is-just-barely-rl.md) and
  [A text-only eval](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-10-02-land-or-water-eval.md).
- First raised on [2025-03-02](https://x.com/karpathy/status/1896266683301659068): he spoke of an evaluation crisis. MMLU was saturated, SWE-Bench Verified too narrow, Chatbot Arena overfit by the labs, and vibe checks open to confirmation bias. An ensemble of private evals looked promising to him. See [Leaderboards get gamed](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-04-30-leaderboards-get-gamed-watch-real-usage.md).
- An example from November 2025: an early Gemini 3 build would not accept the real date and called his evidence fake, until he turned on its search tool. Check the tool settings before you judge a model.

Date: 2025-11-17 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1990577951671509438 · Themes: output-and-reading, learning-and-education · Status: current

# Read with an LLM in three passes

Karpathy describes a reading habit that he counts among his top uses of LLMs. Pass one: read the text yourself. Pass two: ask the model to explain or summarize it. Pass three: ask questions about it. He ends up understanding more than with a single pass. He also expects writers to write for an LLM, which then adapts the idea to each reader.

## In his words

> "I'm writing this for an LLM"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-11-17

## Apply

- Read a paper or doc once on your own before you ask for a summary.
- After the summary, ask the model to quiz you or to challenge a claim in the text.
- Write your own docs so an LLM can reread them: clear headings, plain text.

## Context

- Posted 2025-11-17. Our reading: the order differs from his 2025 book habit, where he asked for the summary before reading; here he reads first.
- Related: [docs for LLMs](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-03-12-write-docs-for-llms.md) and [read books together with an LLM](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2024-12-11-read-books-with-an-llm.md).
- He says about half the gain comes from having a reading group on demand: you must work with the text, not only watch it. He pastes text into whichever model he uses that day and needs no special tool.

Date: 2025-11-17 · Kind: practice · Source: https://karpathy.bearblog.dev/verifiability/ · Themes: verification, ai-progress · Status: current

# Software 2.0 automates what you can verify

Karpathy sees AI as a new computing paradigm. In the 1980s, the best predictor of whether
computers would take a task was specifiability: could you write rote rules for it? Hand-written
programs are "Software 1.0". Now we write programs by giving an objective and searching with
gradient descent. The new best predictor is verifiability. A task is easy to train if the AI
can practise it. The environment must be resettable (new attempts), efficient (many attempts)
and rewardable (an automatic score). Verifiable tasks, such as maths and code, improve fast and
sometimes pass top experts. Creative, strategic and context-heavy tasks lag. This uneven result
is the "jagged" frontier.

## In his words

> "Software 2.0 easily automates what you can verify."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-11-17

## Apply

- Before you give a task to an agent, ask: can it check its own result? If not, add a test, a
  script or a metric.
- Turn a fuzzy task into a checkable one: a rubric, a reference answer or a comparison with a
  known good output.
- Expect weak results where no automatic check exists, and put human review there.
- Check whether the task has an environment that you can reset, repeat cheaply and score automatically. If not, expect weak or uneven results.

## Context

- Builds on his Software 2.0 essay (2017). The Sequoia 2026 talk repeats the formula and adds a
  second axis: [Jagged intelligence follows verifiability and training focus](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-20-jagged-intelligence-follows-verifiability.md).
- Practical cousin: [Give agents success criteria, not steps](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-01-26-success-criteria-not-steps.md).

---

Date: 2025-11-12 · Kind: view · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1988705360723763242 · Themes: ai-progress, agent-native-software · Status: current

# One big neural net can replace a hand-written stack, if data and compute scale

After a test drive of a new Tesla, Karpathy describes what he sees as the full Software 1.0 to Software 2.0 rewrite. Long streams of sensor data (video, maps, motion, audio, about 30 seconds) go into one large network, and steering and acceleration come out. This scales with data from millions of cars and with chip compute. It does not depend on an engineer's clever special-case module, which has unclear memory and runtime behaviour at test time. He adds that the same general parts (world reconstruction, simulators that dream dynamics, RL) make a car one kind of robot. He still sees a long march of 9s: single drives no longer show faults, so problems must be mined from the fleet.

## Context

- Post of 2025-11-12 on his own experience of Tesla FSD v13, with a talk by a Tesla AI lead. Replies of 2025-11-12 define "self-driving" as a future where nearly all cars are autonomous.
- Related: [A demo is the first nine; each next nine costs the same work](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-06-17-demo-to-product-gap-march-of-nines.md) and [Software 2.0 automates what you can verify](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-11-17-software-2-automates-what-you-can-verify.md).

Date: 2025-11-10 · Kind: view · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1987926732255719862 · Themes: ai-progress, llm-psychology · Status: current

# A cheap AI shortcut can stop you before the deeper work

Karpathy groups CGI and today's AI as tools that trade time and cost for a small rise in slop. A maker feels the pull to accept the gain. A crude effect gets you 90% of the way and you stop. A video model may give something that looks fine for even less. A quick writing suggestion from a chatbot is decent, so you stop there. In his words below, the shortcut ends deeper work. The best filmmakers fear this and use the tools with discipline. He gives one test: use the tool where it lets you do what you could not do before, not where it is only cheaper and few people would notice. He also says AI could let many more people make small films and stories of their own, which he finds wholesome.

## In his words

> "It's a quick release valve that stops deeper work."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-11-10

## Apply

- Before you accept a first AI result, ask: would I have stopped here without the tool? If not, keep going.
- Use AI first where it gives you a new capability, then where it only saves time.
- Set a bar before you start (a quality check or a review step), so "good enough" is not decided by how cheap the result was.

## Context

- Replies in a thread on films and AI, 2025-11-10. He adds that the big films he praises still used plenty of CGI.
- Related: [The slopacolypse of 2026](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-01-26-slopacolypse-2026.md).

---

Date: 2025-10-24 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1981746327995465816 · Themes: research-and-training · Status: current

# Teach a small model a skill with a synthetic task that spreads the reasoning

Karpathy taught nanochat to count the letter "r" in "strawberry" and wrote a guide. He built a synthetic task that creates user questions and ideal assistant answers. He then finetunes on them, or trains further with reinforcement learning to make the skill robust. Three points matter. Keep the user prompts diverse. For a small model, handle tokenisation and whitespace with care, and spread the work over many tokens: put the word in quotes, spell it out, then count with an explicit counter. And let the model solve the task two ways: by hand and with a Python tool. All solutions are clean, which is a weakness; adding mistakes with recoveries, or RL, would help. A bigger model might pick up the skill without this effort.

## Apply

- Write a generator for the skill: many phrasings of the request and one ideal worked answer for each.
- Make the answer long enough that each step is easy: restate the input, break it into pieces, keep a running counter.
- Include a tool-call path (such as a code interpreter) next to the mental path, and check that they agree.
- After finetuning, test in the same format the data used; a long multi-turn chat may fail if you did not train for it.

## Context

- Post of 2025-10-24. The reply of the same day says the skill works best in a fresh chat.
- Related: [Give a model an identity with synthetic conversations](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-10-21-give-a-small-model-an-identity-with-synthetic-data.md).

---

Date: 2025-10-21 · Kind: view · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1980672126131794063 · Themes: ai-progress · Status: current

# AGI means a feature-complete remote worker; society-wide deployment is ASI

In replies of October 2025, Karpathy states the definition he has kept. AGI is an automated system that can do any economically valuable work a human can, with the "digital concession" that physical work is left out. It is a remote worker you hire instead of a person, reached by email, chat or video calls. He compares it to a build with all features and many 9s, like current self-driving. That such a system exists is different from its use across society, which takes longer (compute limits, sensors and actuators, law). Full deployment into the economy he would call ASI. He does not rate AGI by puzzle benchmarks. His 10-year estimate is a vibe; at OpenAI in 2015 he voted for 20 years.

## In his words

> "when you're fired because GPT-n is better, cheaper, takes no equity and works weekends"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-10-21

## Context

- A thread of replies on 2025-10-21 and 2025-11-03. The quote defines AGI, as opposed to a score.
- Related: [AI will blend into the same 2% growth curve](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-10-17-agi-blends-into-gdp-growth.md) and [This is the decade of agents, not the year of agents](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-10-17-decade-of-agents-not-year.md).
- First raised on [2025-04-19](https://x.com/karpathy/status/1913741942221144430): he said he sticks with the original OpenAI definition of AGI, at a time when his feed was full of LLMs solving prompt puzzles and of excited talk about AGI.

---

Date: 2025-10-21 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1980665134415802554 · Themes: research-and-training, llm-psychology · Status: current

# Give a model an identity with synthetic conversations, and make them diverse

By default a language model has no personality and no knowledge of its own abilities. Karpathy says it is not an animal-like entity, so it does not know what it is, who made it or what it can do. All of that must be added on purpose. His recipe for nanochat: describe in words what the conversations should look like, ask a bigger model to write about 1,000 multi-turn chats, then mix them into midtraining and finetuning. The hard part is diversity. Even at high temperature, a model writes near-identical samples. His script adds variety with lists of opening messages and topics that it samples explicitly, and with few-shot examples in the prompt. He also used it to make the model call him "King".

## In his words

> "LLMs have no clue of their identity or of their capabilities by default"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-10-21

## Apply

- Write down the facts the model must know about itself: name, maker, size, limits, languages.
- Generate conversations with a stronger model, from a prompt that contains those facts.
- Force variety: sample topics and first messages from explicit lists instead of relying on temperature.
- Mix the data into a late training stage and test with questions that were not in the data.

## Context

- Posts of 2025-10-21 on the nanochat project, with a written guide in the repo.
- Related: [Model outputs are silently collapsed, so synthetic data needs entropy](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-10-17-synthetic-data-and-model-collapse.md) and [LLMs are ghosts, not animals](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-10-01-llms-are-ghosts-not-animals.md).
- His view that models have no built-in sense of self: [Model self-knowledge comes from text about models](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-07-21-model-self-awareness-from-pretraining.md).

---

Date: 2025-10-20 · Kind: view · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1980397031542989305 · Themes: research-and-training · Status: current

# Pixels may be better LLM inputs than text tokens

Prompted by the DeepSeek-OCR paper, Karpathy asks whether text tokens are a poor input. Perhaps every input should be an image, even pure text, which you would render first. He lists four gains: more compression and so shorter contexts; a richer stream that carries bold text, colour and pictures; bidirectional attention by default; and no tokenizer at the input. He dislikes the tokenizer: it brings Unicode and byte-encoding baggage and jailbreak risks, and it gives two look-alike characters different tokens. Using raw bytes does not fix it, since byte encoding is still arbitrary. The output side stays text. In a reply he says nothing in principle stops text from using bidirectional attention; text is just trained left to right for efficiency.

## In his words

> "The tokenizer must go."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-10-20

## Context

- Post of 2025-10-20 and replies on 2025-10-21. He said he held back from building an image-only nanochat.
- Related: [Text chat is the terminal era](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-03-31-text-chat-is-the-terminal-era.md).
- First raised on [2025-07-11](https://x.com/karpathy/status/1943743424311832676): in a reply he wondered whether a VAE over image patches is the ultimate tokenizer, since Unicode plus UTF-8 takes too long to describe.

---

Date: 2025-10-20 · Kind: view · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1980347971935068380 · Themes: research-and-training · Status: current

# Text diffusion is a bidirectional transformer that re-masks a token canvas

Karpathy points to a short post that shows how simple discrete text diffusion can be. Image and video models mostly use diffusion, while text models mostly use autoregression. Without the formalism, diffusion is an ordinary transformer with bidirectional attention. It repeatedly re-samples and re-masks all tokens of a "canvas" on a noise schedule until the last step. In code terms, autoregression appends one token and looks only backwards. Diffusion sets any position in the canvas and looks both ways. Bidirectional attention is stronger, but it makes training costlier because you cannot parallelise over the sequence. He thinks the two may blend, and calls this part of the stack still fungible.

## Context

- Post of 2025-10-20. A later reply describes a small character-level text diffusion model as text "boiling" down to a simmer.
- Related: [Pixels may be better LLM inputs than text tokens](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-10-20-pixels-may-be-better-llm-inputs-than-text.md).
- First raised on [2025-02-27](https://x.com/karpathy/status/1894923254864978091): he called Mercury the first large diffusion LLM. Most LLMs are autoregressive and alike, so a diffusion model may have new strengths and weaknesses. He found it a puzzle that images and video use diffusion while text does not.

---

Date: 2025-10-17 · Kind: view · Source: https://www.dwarkesh.com/p/andrej-karpathy · Themes: ai-progress · Status: current

# AI will blend into the same 2% growth curve

Karpathy sees AI as an extension of computing and automation. He looked for AI in GDP data and
could not find a jump, just as computers and phones leave no visible step. Technology spreads
slowly and averages into one exponential growth rate. He expects the same for AI. So he
expects no sudden change, no single dramatic arrival. The model will do some tasks, fail at others and enter
society step by step. Recursive self-improvement is also old: search engines, IDEs and autocomplete
already help build the next tools. Dwarkesh argues for a jump, as with the Industrial Revolution;
Karpathy says that needs a discrete event he cannot find in the statistics.

## Context

- Dwarkesh Patel interview, 2025-10-17. He says he is open to being convinced.
- Related: [Decade of agents](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-10-17-decade-of-agents-not-year.md) and
  [Gradual loss of control and understanding](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-10-17-gradual-loss-of-control-and-understanding.md).

---

Date: 2025-10-17 · Kind: practice · Source: https://www.dwarkesh.com/p/andrej-karpathy · Themes: learning-and-education · Status: current

# To learn something, build it yourself without copy-paste

Asked how to learn from his nanochat repo, Karpathy says to put the repo on one monitor and
rebuild it on the other. You may look. You may not copy and paste. Building forces you to meet
what you do not know that you do not know. Tiny details are misarranged and you only think you
have the knowledge. He says not to write posts or make slides in place of this: build the code,
arrange it and get it to work. He adds that a final repo hides how it was grown in chunks, so a
build-up video would help.

## In his words

> "If I can’t build it, I don’t understand it."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-10-17

## Apply

- Rebuild a small project from a reference with a rule: read, then type it yourself.
- Use an agent as tutor (ask it to explain), not as the typist, while you learn.
- Write a short test or demo that proves your version works before you compare with the original.

## Context

- Dwarkesh Patel interview, 2025-10-17; he credits the line to Feynman.
- Related: [Build ramps to knowledge](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-10-17-ramps-to-knowledge.md).

---

Date: 2025-10-17 · Kind: practice · Source: https://www.dwarkesh.com/p/andrej-karpathy · Themes: learning-and-education, ai-progress · Status: current

# Build for the capability that exists; a real tutor is a high bar

While learning Korean, Karpathy had a one-on-one tutor. Within a short talk she saw what he knew
and did not, probed his mental model, and gave material that was neither too hard nor too easy.
He felt he was the only limit on learning. No LLM does this yet, so he judged it too early to build
an AI tutor, though the time will come. He says to calibrate to what exists. For his course he
uses AI as a helper in a loop he controls: it does boring work and speeds him up, but it cannot
create the content. He says that as a consultant, much of his value was telling firms not to use AI.

## Apply

- Before adding AI to a product, test it against the best human version of the task.
- Use AI for the dull parts of content or code and keep the design decisions human.
- Tell the AI to ask probing questions about your level before it explains.
- Say "do not use AI here" when it is the honest answer.

## Context

- Dwarkesh Patel interview, 2025-10-17, on Eureka Labs and the LLM101N course.
- Related: [Teach by building ramps](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-10-17-ramps-to-knowledge.md).

---

Date: 2025-10-17 · Kind: practice · Source: https://www.dwarkesh.com/p/andrej-karpathy · Themes: agentic-coding · Status: superseded (by 2026-01-26-programming-in-english-december-shift.md)

# Coding agents are weak on novel code

Building the nanochat repo, Karpathy found agents of little help. He sees three styles of coding:
write by hand, write with autocomplete, or hand the task to an agent. Agents do well on boilerplate
and on code common on the internet. They did badly on nanochat because it is unusual. The models
kept pushing the usual way, such as the standard PyTorch parallel wrapper he had replaced. They
added defensive code and used old APIs, so the repo got bloated. They did help with a
report script and with a Rust port of a tokenizer, where he had Python code he understood and tests.
He says models struggle with code that has never been written, which is what AI research needs,
so his timelines are longer.

## In his words

> "For now, autocomplete is my sweet spot."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-10-17

## Apply

- Use an agent for boilerplate, glue code and ports where you have a reference version and tests.
- For unusual design, tell the agent which standard choice you rejected and why, in the prompt.
- Use autocomplete when you know exactly where code goes: pointing is higher bandwidth than English.
- Review agent output for extra try/except blocks and old APIs.

## Context

- Dwarkesh Patel interview, 2025-10-17, model era of GPT-5 Pro and early Claude Code.
- Superseded. In January 2026 he wrote that he went from about 80% manual and autocomplete
  coding in November 2025 to about 80% agent coding in December, after models crossed a
  coherence threshold. See [Programming moved to English in December 2025](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-01-26-programming-in-english-december-shift.md).
  His warnings about bloat and wrong assumptions still hold:
  [Coding agents make subtle conceptual mistakes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-01-26-coding-agents-make-subtle-conceptual-mistakes.md).
- On 2025-10-13 he wrote that nanochat was almost all written by hand, and that the coding agents he tried were a net loss on it, maybe because the repo is far from their training data.

---

Date: 2025-10-17 · Kind: view · Source: https://www.dwarkesh.com/p/andrej-karpathy · Themes: ai-progress, agent-native-software · Status: current

# Coding came first because it is text with diff tools

Dwarkesh asks why a general AI mostly earns money from coding. Karpathy says code is the perfect
first use. It is text, models are trained on lots of text, and the world already has tools for code:
an IDE shows it, and a diff shows what an agent changed. Slides are harder. They are spatial and
visual, and no tool shows a diff for a slide. Someone has to build that. He adds that text is
not trivially easy: code is structured, while prose has more entropy. The lesson is about the
surrounding tools, not only the model.

## Apply

- Before you automate a task with an agent, ask how a person will see what changed.
- Prefer formats that diff well (markdown, code, plain data files) for agent output.
- If you need an agent to work on slides, diagrams or designs, plan a step that renders before
  and after for review.

## Context

- Dwarkesh Patel interview, 2025-10-17. Related: [Build partial-autonomy products](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-06-17-partial-autonomy-and-autonomy-slider.md).

---

Date: 2025-10-17 · Kind: view · Source: https://www.dwarkesh.com/p/andrej-karpathy · Themes: ai-progress · Status: current

# This is the decade of agents, not the year of agents

Karpathy uses Claude and Codex daily and finds them impressive. But he says they do not yet work
like an employee or intern you would hand work to. They are not smart enough, they cannot use a
computer well, and they have no continual learning: you cannot tell them something and expect
them to remember it. He expects about a decade to fix these gaps. He bases the number on roughly
15 years of watching predictions in AI. The problems look solvable but hard. He says he was
reacting to over-prediction in the industry, and that he is optimistic about the result.

## In his words

> "In my mind, this is more accurately described as the decade of agents."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-10-17

## Apply

- Plan around today's agent as a fast but forgetful junior. Give it written context every time.
- Keep notes files, specs and checks that carry memory for the agent across sessions.
- Treat timeline claims by vendors as marketing unless you can test them on your own tasks.

## Context

- Dwarkesh Patel interview, 2025-10-17.
- Related: [A demo is the first nine](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-06-17-demo-to-product-gap-march-of-nines.md) and
  [Coding agents are weak on novel code](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-10-17-coding-agents-weak-on-novel-code.md).
- Our reading: his later 2026 statements are more positive about agents after December 2025;
  see [Vibe coding raises the floor, agentic engineering raises the ceiling](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-02-04-agentic-engineering-vs-vibe-coding.md).
- First raised on [2025-01-23](https://x.com/karpathy/status/1882544526033924438), after OpenAI launched Operator, an agent that drives a browser. He compared such agents to humanoid robots: both do general work through a setting built for humans, and both leave people to supervise the automation. He expected the digital case to move first, because changing bits costs far less than moving atoms, and he pictured one person watching ten agents and stepping in to unblock them.
- In his own recap of the interview he said his timelines are five to ten times more pessimistic than the talk at a San Francisco party, but still optimistic compared with those who deny AI progress.

Date: 2025-10-17 · Kind: view · Source: https://www.dwarkesh.com/p/andrej-karpathy · Themes: ai-progress · Status: current

# The likely risk is a gradual loss of control and understanding

Karpathy treats superintelligence as automation continued: more digital work, then physical work, done
by autonomous entities. He expects it to look strange. What makes him nervous is slow loss of
understanding, as we layer AI through everything and fewer people know how it works. He also
expects loss of control. He imagines not one entity taking over but many competing ones that
gradually become more autonomous, with some going rogue and others fighting them off. Even if each
acts for a person, society may not get the outcomes it wants. This is why he works on education.

## Apply

- Keep a person who understands each system an agent builds. Make agents write docs and tests
  for that person.
- Review how much of your own stack you could still explain or fix without the AI.
- Record decisions and designs in plain files so understanding survives staff changes.

## Context

- Dwarkesh Patel interview, 2025-10-17. He admits he is far into territory he cannot picture.
- Related: [Outsource thinking, not understanding](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-31-understanding-is-the-bottleneck.md)
  and [AI will blend into the same 2% growth curve](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-10-17-agi-blends-into-gdp-growth.md).

---

Date: 2025-10-17 · Kind: practice · Source: https://www.dwarkesh.com/p/andrej-karpathy · Themes: learning-and-education · Status: current

# Learn on demand through projects, then explain it to others

Asked for study tips, Karpathy gives two. First, learn depth-first and on demand: pick a project
with a reward and learn what it needs. Mix this with breadth-first study, the "trust me, you will
need it" style of school. He likes the first more. Second, explain things to others. When you try
and fail, you find the gap in your understanding, and it forces you to fix it. He says people
should re-explain more often. He also gives advice to experts: the curse of knowledge makes your
explanation hard for beginners.

## Apply

- Choose a small project that uses the new topic, and learn from the errors it shows.
- After you learn something, write or say a plain explanation. Mark where you got stuck.
- Ask an agent to play a beginner and ask questions about your explanation.
- Alternate: one project, then one pass of the basics it exposed.

## Context

- Dwarkesh Patel interview, 2025-10-17. He also asks for beginners' "dumb" questions;
  see [Share your dumb LLM questions with experts](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-10-17-share-dumb-llm-questions-with-experts.md).

---

Date: 2025-10-17 · Kind: view · Source: https://www.dwarkesh.com/p/andrej-karpathy · Themes: research-and-training, agent-native-software · Status: current

# LLMs still lack culture and self-play

Karpathy names two powerful multi-agent ideas that nobody has made work. The first is culture: a
growing store of knowledge that LLMs write for their own use. The simple form is a large
scratchpad the model edits while it works. He asks why one LLM cannot write a book for other LLMs
to read. The second is self-play, as in AlphaGo: one model makes harder and harder problems for
another to solve. He says today's agents still feel like savant children. They have perfect memory
but cannot yet build culture. He sees organisations of agents as part of the same gap.

## Apply

- Give your agent a notes file that it updates as it learns the repo, and have it read that file
  at the start of each session.
- Let one agent write tasks or tests and another solve them, then compare results.
- Treat these as experiments. He says no one has shown convincing results.

## Context

- Dwarkesh Patel interview, 2025-10-17. Our reading: the notes-file practice in coding agents
  (project instruction files, memory files) is a simple form of the scratchpad he describes.
- Related: [Reinforcement learning sucks supervision through a straw](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-10-17-rl-supervision-through-a-straw.md).

---

Date: 2025-10-17 · Kind: practice · Source: https://www.dwarkesh.com/p/andrej-karpathy · Themes: learning-and-education · Status: current

# Teach by building ramps to knowledge

Karpathy treats education as a technical task: build ramps so that each idea depends only on
earlier ones. His method comes from physics. Find the first-order term, the simplest thing that
shows the effect, and add other terms later. His example is micrograd, about 100 lines of Python
that show how neural networks train; the rest of the field is efficiency. In the transformer
tutorial he starts with a lookup table of bigrams. He shows the problem before the solution and
lets the student try first, so the answer is valued. His goal is many "eurekas per second".

## Apply

- When you write a guide or explain code, start with the smallest runnable version, then add one
  term at a time.
- State the problem and let the reader guess before you give the fix.
- Ask an agent to produce a reading order where each step uses only earlier steps, and check it.
- Ask yourself: what is the first-order part, and what is only efficiency?

## Context

- Dwarkesh Patel interview, 2025-10-17, where he describes his Eureka Labs course plan.
- Related: [Build it yourself](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-10-17-build-it-yourself-no-copy-paste.md).
- First raised on [2025-06-25](https://x.com/karpathy/status/1937733819207151727): in a reply he described education as the technical problem of building ramps to knowledge.

---

Date: 2025-10-17 · Kind: view · Source: https://www.dwarkesh.com/p/andrej-karpathy · Themes: research-and-training · Status: current

# Reinforcement learning sucks supervision through a straw

Karpathy says reinforcement learning is much worse than most people think, and that what came
before, imitating humans, is worse still. In RL on a math problem, the model tries many
solutions. It then marks the ones with the right answer and boosts every token in them, even the
wrong turns. One final number is spread across a whole minute of work. A person would not learn
this way: they would review the attempt and decide which parts were good. LLMs have no such
step. Process supervision would help, but partial credit is hard to compute. He expects the field
needs three to five more big algorithm ideas.

## In his words

> "...you're sucking supervision through a straw."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-10-17

## Apply

- When you design an agent loop, give feedback at several points (tests per step), not only a
  final pass or fail.
- Make agents write a short review of what worked after a run, and keep that review in a notes
  file for the next run.
- Expect RL-trained models to be strong where an answer can be checked, and weaker elsewhere.

## Context

- Dwarkesh Patel interview, 2025-10-17.
- Related: [An LLM judge gets gamed](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2024-08-07-rlhf-is-just-barely-rl.md) and
  [Synthetic data collapses](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-10-17-synthetic-data-and-model-collapse.md).
- On 2025-10-19 he said he does not want to replace RL. The base model, instruction finetuning and RL are layers that all stay, and he wants more layers on top. In replies he found it odd that RL teaches a model to make errors only so that it can recover from them.

---

Date: 2025-10-17 · Kind: practice · Source: https://www.dwarkesh.com/p/andrej-karpathy · Themes: learning-and-education, output-and-reading · Status: current

# Share your beginner questions to an LLM with the author

Experts explain badly because of the curse of knowledge: they forget what is hard at the start.
Karpathy does something about this as a reader. Given a biology paper he did not follow, he put
the paper in ChatGPT's context, asked his many basic questions, and shared the thread with the
author, hoping it would help them explain better. He would like readers to send him their chats
about his own material for the same reason. Dwarkesh adds a related trick: authors are clearer
when they say the idea out loud, as at lunch, than when they write it. Karpathy asks why that is
not the abstract.

## Apply

- Read hard material with the source in context and ask the naive questions without shame.
- Send authors or colleagues the thread of questions that confused you.
- Before you publish, dictate the idea in three sentences and compare it with your draft's opening.
- Put that plain summary at the top of your docs.

## Context

- Dwarkesh Patel interview, 2025-10-17. Related:
  [Learn on demand, then explain](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-10-17-learn-on-demand-then-explain.md).

---

Date: 2025-10-17 · Kind: practice · Source: https://www.dwarkesh.com/p/andrej-karpathy · Themes: research-and-training, llm-psychology · Status: current

# Model outputs are silently collapsed, so synthetic data needs entropy

Karpathy asks why we cannot let a model think about a book and train on that. Any one sample
looks good. But ask ten times and the answers are almost the same, because the model covers only a
small part of the space of possible thoughts. Ask a chatbot for a joke and it knows about three.
Train on enough of this output and quality falls. People collapse too: children say surprising
things, adults repeat themselves. His fix for people is to seek entropy, for example by talking to
others. For models it is a research problem. He also says reading a book should be a set of
prompts for you to think with, which LLM pre-training does not do.

## In his words

> "They’re silently collapsed."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-10-17

## Apply

- Do not train or fine-tune on a pile of your own model's output without checking its variety.
- For brainstorming, make the model produce differently shaped answers (other personas, other
  constraints) and compare them. Do not ask ten times with one prompt.
- Bring human or external input into agent notes, so they do not become a loop of the same views.

## Context

- Dwarkesh Patel interview, 2025-10-17. The reading-as-prompts point links to his later
  interest in LLM-written knowledge bases (see [Outsource thinking, not understanding](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-31-understanding-is-the-bottleneck.md)).

---

Date: 2025-10-17 · Kind: practice · Source: https://www.dwarkesh.com/p/andrej-karpathy · Themes: context-and-prompting, llm-psychology · Status: current

# Weights are a hazy memory; the context window is working memory

Karpathy compares two kinds of knowledge in an LLM. What the model learned in training is
compressed hard: trillions of tokens in a few billion weights. So it is only a hazy recollection,
like something read a year ago. What sits in the context window is directly available, like
working memory. Ask about a book and you get roughly right answers. Paste the chapter and ask
again, and the answers improve a lot. The same view explains why models feel most intelligent
inside a conversation, where they spot and fix their own mistakes in context.

## Apply

- Paste the source (chapter, API doc, file, log) into the prompt before asking about it.
- For code questions, give the real files, not a description from memory.
- When an answer looks plausible but vague, suspect recall, and ask again with the text in context.
- Put stable facts the model must not get wrong in a file it reads at the start.

## Context

- Dwarkesh Patel interview, 2025-10-17. Related: [Cognitive core](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-06-27-the-llm-cognitive-core.md).
- Earlier talk, same idea in other words: [LLMs are people spirits](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-06-17-llms-are-people-spirits-with-deficits.md).

---

Date: 2025-10-14 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1978113809551065381 · Themes: security-and-dependencies, agentic-coding · Status: current

# Measure a project's weight with its lockfile, and rewrite heavy parts small

Critics said that counting only a project's own lines hides its dependencies. Karpathy answered that he counts and reports the lines in the lockfile (`uv.lock`). It includes every package, also the nested ones, so it is a simple 80:20 proxy for total weight. He would also like to measure "cognitive complexity". He dislikes shrinking line counts by packing code into unreadable lines. His example: to score a base model with a standard benchmark, he found that a job of about 300 lines needed a large pile of outside infrastructure. He wrote 263 clean lines instead and calls this "bacterial" code.

## Apply

- Put the lockfile line count and the source line count side by side in your README or report card.
- Before you add a dependency for a small task, check what it pulls in. If the task is small, write it yourself or ask an agent to.
- Judge size by how easy the code is to read, not by the smallest possible line count.

## Context

- Replies during the nanochat release, 2025-10-14 and 2025-10-18.
- Related: [Keep the codebase minimal and forkable, with one dial](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-10-13-nanochat-one-dial-minimal-fork.md) and [Rip out functionality with agents](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-02-11-rip-out-functionality-with-agents.md), which develops "bacterial code".
