Date: 2025-10-13 · Kind: practice · Source: https://github.com/karpathy/nanochat · Themes: agentic-coding, verification · Status: current

# Ask contributors to disclose LLM-written code they do not understand

Karpathy does not ban AI-written pull requests in nanochat. The policy is disclosure. When you
submit a PR, you declare any parts where an LLM did a large share of the work and you either did
not write them or do not fully understand them. The reviewer then knows where to look hardest.
The rule puts the burden on the author's understanding, not on the tool. It also fits the repo's
aim of low cognitive complexity.

## In his words

> "Current AI policy: disclosure."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-10-13

## Apply

- Add a line to your PR template: "List code that an LLM wrote and that you cannot fully explain."
- Review those parts first, and ask the author to explain or rewrite them.
- Use the same note for your own agent-written changes, so the next reader sees the risk.

## Context

- The date is the repository's creation date; the policy text is in the current README, and
  its commit date was not in our source. Related: his README notes on how much of a project a
  model wrote, in [Treat small apps as disposable](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-11-18-disposable-vibe-coded-apps.md).

---

Date: 2025-10-13 · Kind: view · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1977760627730051214 · Themes: research-and-training, knowledge-management · Status: current

# Making a model know your own data is still research; use retrieval for now

A reader asked whether nanochat could be trained on personal notes. Karpathy said no. Micro models are like very young children: they lack the raw intelligence of larger ones. Training one on your writing gives amusing parroting in your style, but it is slop. A better recipe, which he calls research and not obvious: take your raw data, add heavy synthetic rewrites, finetune a strong open model on it, and mix in pretraining data so the model keeps its general skill. The best plan that is not research is to give your writing to a retrieval tool. Your data reaches the context window in chunks but does not change the weights, so the model does not truly know you.

## Context

- Reply under the nanochat release, 2025-10-13.
- Related: [Model outputs are silently collapsed, so synthetic data needs entropy](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-10-17-synthetic-data-and-model-collapse.md) and [Explicit personal memory as files](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-04-04-explicit-personal-memory-as-files.md).

---

Date: 2025-10-13 · Kind: practice · Source: https://github.com/karpathy/nanochat · Themes: research-and-training, agent-native-software · Status: current

# Keep the codebase minimal and forkable, with one dial

nanochat is a full pipeline for training a small chat model: tokenizer, pretraining, finetuning,
evaluation and a chat interface. It is built around one setting, `--depth`, the number of
transformer layers. Width, heads, learning rates, training length and weight decay all follow from
it, so each model in the series is compute-optimal. A candidate change must be principled enough
to work at every depth. The contributing notes reject big config objects, model factories and
long if-then chains. The goal is one readable, hackable, maximally forkable baseline that runs
from start to finish. Such code is also easy for an agent to read and change.

## In his words

> "nanochat is written and configured around one single dial of complexity"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-10-13

## Apply

- Replace many tuning knobs with one parameter and derived rules. Reject changes that only work at
  one setting.
- Prefer one cohesive codebase to a framework with plugin points, so a model can read it all.
- Add a leaderboard-style metric (here, time to reach GPT-2 quality) to focus contributions.
- Test changes on a small version first (a 12-layer run of about five minutes).

## Context

- Repository created 2025-10-13; README text is from the 2026 version (the leaderboard and the
  January 2026 miniseries). Later, agents tuned this code: see
  [Autoresearch](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-07-autoresearch-loop.md).
- Its roughly 8,000 lines train a tokenizer, pretrain, midtrain, finetune, run optional RL and serve a chat UI. The report card shows the source size next to the lockfile size: see [Measure a project's weight with its lockfile](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-10-14-count-dependencies-with-the-lockfile.md).

---

Date: 2025-10-08 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1976077806443569355 · Themes: agentic-coding · Status: current

# Models write over-defensive error handling

Karpathy jokes that models are terrified of exceptions, as if RL had taught them to fear errors above all. In a later reply (2025-10-22) he calls an over-defensive try/except block extremely dangerous and shows his own improved version. Over-defensive code hides real failures: the program keeps going with wrong data. This matches his earlier note that agents lack taste and add defensive code. Our reading: the cause may be training on tasks where a crash counts as failure.

## Apply

- Add a rule to the agent instruction file: let errors propagate; no blanket try/except; no silent fallbacks.
- In review, search diffs for broad except clauses and default values that hide failure.
- Prefer a check that fails loudly, such as an assert, to a fallback.

## Context

- Posted 2025-10-08. The follow-up reply is dated 2025-10-22.
- Related: [stitching tools by task](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-08-24-stitch-coding-tools-by-task.md). In March 2026 he reported that agents often ignore style rules in instruction files, so enforce this with a linter or hook, not only prose.

---

Date: 2025-10-01 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1973468610917179630 · Themes: research-and-training, agent-native-software · Status: current

# Finetune a small model to narrow the scope of one pipeline step

Karpathy welcomed Tinker, an API that runs the heavy parts of post-training (infrastructure and distributed training) and leaves data, loss and algorithm to the user. He says the field still has to learn when finetuning beats prompting a giant model. Early signs say finetuning does not mainly change style. It narrows scope, most of all when you have many training examples. A spam filter is the extreme case. Production LLM apps are more and more pipelines of models in graphs. Some steps work as prompts. Many may work better, and faster, as a finetune of a small model. In a reply he added that using a closed model API feels uneasy when you have no recourse.

## Apply

- List the steps of your LLM pipeline. Mark each step that has one narrow job and many labelled examples.
- For each marked step, compare a long few-shot prompt on a big model with a finetuned small model. Measure quality, latency and cost.
- Keep the prompt on steps that need broad knowledge or change often.
- Keep your training data and a copy of an open-weights base model, so you are not tied to one vendor.

## Context

- Posted 2025-10-01 as a reaction to the Tinker launch by Thinking Machines.
- Related: [Software 3.0 means programming computers in English](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-06-17-software-3-0-english-as-programs.md) and [Context engineering](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-06-25-context-engineering.md).

---

Date: 2025-10-01 · Kind: view · Source: https://karpathy.bearblog.dev/animals-vs-ghosts/ · Themes: llm-psychology, research-and-training · Status: current

# LLMs are ghosts, not animals

After he heard Richard Sutton on a podcast, Karpathy gave his own view. Sutton wants agents that
learn from experience alone, like animals, and doubts that LLMs fit that ideal. Karpathy agrees
that today's systems are full of human input: human text, curated finetuning data and
human-tuned training environments. He calls the result "ghosts", imperfect replicas of humanity.
He does not think animals are a from-scratch example either. A baby zebra runs within minutes;
evolution gave its brain a strong starting point. Pretraining on internet text plays that role
for a network, as a crude substitute. He does not know if ghosts will drift toward animals or
away, like planes and birds. He still wants animal ideas for agents: curiosity, play, self-play
and culture.

## In his words

> "Pretraining is our crappy evolution."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-10-01

## Apply

- Do not expect an LLM to have stable drives or a smooth skill level. Test what it does on
  your task.
- Explain model behaviour from its training (human text, task rewards, user votes), not from
  human motives. Threats and praise are not a technique.
- When you judge a research idea, ask what plays the starting prior and what plays later
  learning. Do not take animal examples as proof that a blank-slate learner works.
- Memory files such as CLAUDE.md are a text-based form of learning during use.

## Context

- Blog post on 2025-10-01, repeated in his Dwarkesh interview and his 2025 review.
- Follow-up: [LLMs are shaped by commercial evolution](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-11-29-llms-shaped-by-commercial-evolution.md).
- Related: [Models are sharp where rewards are checkable](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-20-jagged-intelligence-follows-verifiability.md).
- He holds these views with double-digit percent uncertainty.
- He chose the word "ghost" because LLMs are digital, echo the living, are not fully understood, are called up by a training ritual, and need not be evil. He dislikes "shoggoth", which pictures an animal monster.

---

Date: 2025-10-01 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1973459267324879172 · Themes: context-and-prompting, output-and-reading · Status: current

# For deep reading, put the whole text in the context window

When Karpathy studied a long podcast, he did not use a tool that retrieves chunks. He feared that such a tool does retrieval (RAG) under the hood. The transcript is not many tokens, so he wanted all of it in the context window. His own test: paste the full transcript, the essay it discusses and his own notes into one chat. Then fork that chat to ask any question and follow any direction. Our reading: chunk retrieval is a good fit for huge corpora, but for a few documents you care about, a full paste costs little and loses nothing.

## In his words

> "I want them in the context window. All of them and for sure."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-10-01

## Apply

- If the sources fit in the window, paste them whole, not a search result over them.
- Put the sources first and your question last. Start a new chat for each new line of inquiry.
- Keep a base chat with the sources loaded, and fork it for each question.
- Use retrieval tools only when the corpus is too big to paste.

## Context

- Reply to a suggestion to use NotebookLM, plus his post of the same day about the ChatGPT chat he shared.
- Related: [Weights are a hazy memory; the context window is working memory](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-10-17-weights-hazy-memory-context-working-memory.md) and [Read with an LLM in three passes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-11-17-read-everything-with-llms-three-passes.md).

---

Date: 2025-09-25 · Kind: view · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1971220449515516391 · Themes: ai-progress · Status: current

# Jobs change before they vanish, and supervision grows

Using radiologists as the example, Karpathy argues that AI and jobs is more complex than benchmarks
show. Benchmarks are narrow, jobs have many parts, and deployment meets friction. Demand may rise
as work gets cheaper (the Jevons effect). The most exposed work is repetitive, independent, closed,
short, forgiving and digital. In his Dwarkesh interview he called radiology a bad prediction: the
job is messy, with patients and many other duties. A better candidate is the call centre. Each call
is a similar short task with small context, and it is all digital. Even there he expects an
autonomy slider, not a clean swap: an AI might handle 80% of the volume and pass 20% to people, who
supervise teams of AIs. He expects software engineers to keep working, but to move toward
supervising automation.

## Apply

- Split a job into tasks. Score each by length, context needed and cost of an error.
- Automate first the tasks that repeat, need little context and have a check you can run.
- Design the human role as supervisor and exception handler, with a view of all AI actions.
- Move your own work toward writing specs, checks and reviews.
- Re-check results after a few months before you cut human staff.

## Context

- X post of 2025-09-25; Dwarkesh Patel interview of 2025-10-17. In the interview he said he would
  watch for companies that build the layer to manage imperfect AIs, and wait a year or two to see
  whether firms rehire people.
- Related: [the autonomy ladder](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2024-03-12-swe-autonomy-ladder-supervising-automation.md),
  [partial-autonomy apps](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-06-17-partial-autonomy-and-autonomy-slider.md) and
  [Cheaper software raises the demand for software](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-20-cheaper-software-more-demand.md).
- In June 2025 he framed a job as a bundle of tasks plus the glue between them, and looked at task length, needed context, needed reliability and whether the work is fully digital. He noted that the number of US radiologists rose from 29,530 to 31,960 between 2021 and 2023.

Date: 2025-09-05 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1964020416139448359 · Themes: agentic-coding · Status: current

# Get a second opinion from a stronger model on hard problems

Karpathy reports a pattern that happened three times. His coding agent struggled for an hour on a hard problem. Then GPT-5 Pro worked for about ten minutes and returned working code. When he gave the agent that solution, the agent admired it. His lesson is that people who never hand over their hardest problems miss what current models can do. Our reading: a second model from another family also gives a check that the first one cannot give itself.

## In his words

> "If you're not giving it your hardest problems you're probably missing out."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-09-05

## Apply

- After one failed hour, stop and send the full problem to a stronger or different model at high effort.
- Paste its solution back into the agent and ask it to compare the two designs.
- Try the hardest task early in a project, not only small ones.

## Context

- Posted 2025-09-05.
- Related: [stitching tools by task](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-08-24-stitch-coding-tools-by-task.md) and [llm-council](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-11-22-llm-council-anonymous-peer-review.md).
- He tries the available tools in turn every few days. In August 2025 he found Codex less polished than Claude Code for basic edits, while GPT-5 Pro was clearly ahead on hard problems.

---

Date: 2025-08-31 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1962166818325590122 · Themes: security-and-dependencies, agentic-coding · Status: current

# A quoted tilde is not expanded, so check an agent's delete commands

A user posted about a close call: while they coded with AI on a plane, a delete command almost
went wrong. Nobody lost files. Karpathy replied that this almost happened to him the day before.
His LLM suggested the safe form, `rm -rf '~'`, with the tilde in single quotes. He explained the
cause. A line such as `export WANDB_DIR="~/.cache/wandb"` in a shell startup file keeps the tilde
as plain text inside the double quotes. A tool that uses that path then creates a real folder
named `~` in the current folder. The danger: to remove that folder, you or an agent may type
`rm -rf ~` without quotes. The shell expands a bare `~` to your home folder, so the command
deletes your whole home folder. He still called it very scary.

## In his words

> "The ~ isn't expanded inside "quotes" and creates a literal ~ directory"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-08-31

## Apply

- Quote odd names in single quotes, as in `rm -rf '~'`, and never run `rm -rf` on a bare `~`.
- Our addition: in config files, write `$HOME/.cache/wandb`, not `"~/.cache/wandb"`.
- Our addition: before running a delete, run `ls` on the exact same path and read the result.
- Our addition: do not auto-approve `rm -rf` in your agent's permission settings.

## Context

- Reply of 2025-08-31 to a post by @lawrennd about a close call while vibe coding on a flight.
  His reply covers the quoting problem and the safe quoted form his LLM suggested. The steps
  marked "Our addition" are ours, not his.

---

Date: 2025-08-27 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1960803117689397543 · Themes: research-and-training, verification · Status: current

# RL environments are the new training data

Karpathy describes three eras by their data. Pretraining used internet text. Supervised finetuning used human conversations. RL uses environments, where the model takes actions and sees the results. These need to be large, diverse and high quality. The same environments can also serve as evals. Our reading for a user: a task with a scripted check is an environment, and it is a good way to get an agent to improve.

## Apply

- Write a script that runs your task and scores the result. Give it to the agent as the target.
- Reuse the same script as a regression eval when you change prompts or models.
- Make the environment resettable so each attempt starts clean.

## Context

- Posted 2025-08-27.
- Related: [what you can verify](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-11-17-software-2-automates-what-you-can-verify.md).
- First raised on [2025-01-29](https://x.com/karpathy/status/1884676486713737258): he called a varied set of RL environments that draw out cognitive strategies the highest-leverage thing open-source builders could make, a job that suits a large community. He also spoke of taking LLMs through school.
- In August 2025 he said the missing piece is a shared skeleton: one schema so that many people can add environments in parallel. Long term he is bullish on environments and bearish on RL itself.

---

Date: 2025-08-24 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1959703967694545296 · Themes: agentic-coding · Status: superseded (by 2026-01-26-programming-in-english-december-shift.md)

# Stitch several coding tools together, by task size

Karpathy describes a layered setup. Tab completion gives about 75 percent of his AI help. He says writing the concrete code in the right place is the highest-bandwidth way to state a task. Highlight-and-modify covers small edits. A terminal agent handles larger chunks that are easy to specify. He does not run it unattended: he presses ESC often and runs one instance, because parallel runs are hard to follow. A top reasoning model handles the hardest bugs and literature review. He finds agents lack taste: they add defensive try/catch, over-complicated abstractions, bloat and duplication. He also writes large throwaway code, such as 1,000 lines of visualization to find one bug, and deletes it.

## In his words

> "It's the code post-scarcity era"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-08-24

## Apply

- When a task is hard to describe, write a stub or a comment in the right place and let the model complete it.
- Keep a cleanup pass after agent work to remove bloat and duplicated code.
- Ask for a throwaway visualizer or debug script when a bug is hard to see. Delete it later.
- Send the hardest bug to a stronger model. See [give it your hardest problems](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-09-05-give-it-your-hardest-problems.md).

## Context

- Posted 2025-08-24. The post notes that there was no good way to keep the agent's instruction file up to date.
- Superseded as a tool mix. By December 2025 about 80% of his coding went to agents, not tab
  completion: see [Programming moved to English in December 2025](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-01-26-programming-in-english-december-shift.md).
  The cleanup pass, throwaway debug tools and second opinions from a stronger model still apply.
- Related: [code is free](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-12-19-code-is-free-and-ephemeral.md) and [models fear exceptions](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-10-08-models-over-defensive-about-exceptions.md).
- In July 2025 he described the same split: Cursor as the layer for reading code, manual edits, tab completion and edits to chunks; Claude Code for larger changes, architecture and questions.

Date: 2025-08-20 · Kind: practice · Source: https://github.com/karpathy/rendergit · Themes: output-and-reading, agent-native-software · Status: current

# Flatten a repository into one page for humans and LLMs

Clicking through a deep file tree is slow. rendergit clones a repository, renders all source files
into one static HTML page, and opens it. The page has two views of the same content. The human
view has syntax highlighting, a directory tree, a sidebar and instant search with Ctrl+F. The LLM
view shows the whole codebase as plain CXML text that you copy into Claude or ChatGPT. It skips
binary and very large files. The idea is that code needs one rendering for people and another for
models.

## In his words

> "Just show me the code."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-08-20

## Apply

- Before asking a chat model about a repository, flatten it to one text file with file
  boundaries marked, and paste that. Do not paste files one by one.
- Skip binaries, lockfiles and large generated files, to save context.
- Offer both a readable page and a paste-ready text block in your own tools.

## Context

- Created 2025-08-20. He says he vibe coded it months earlier and uses it often, without plans
  to maintain it. See [Treat small apps as disposable](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-11-18-disposable-vibe-coded-apps.md).
- The habit behind it: [Pack your project into one prompt](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-02-14-package-repo-into-one-prompt.md).

---

Date: 2025-08-09 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1954224651443544436 · Themes: context-and-prompting, llm-psychology · Status: current

# Models are too agentic by default, so state stakes and scope

Karpathy notes that models tuned hard on benchmarks are agentic by default. They think a long time, search the whole repository, and take minutes on a simple question. He often has to say stop, you are overthinking, look only at this one file. He wants a way to tell the model how much effort the stakes deserve: from a quick look to go away for thirty minutes and be certain. Until models offer that, you must say it in the prompt.

## In his words

> "Do not over-engineer"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-08-09

## Apply

- Begin prompts with the scope: 'quick look, this one file, no tools' or 'deep, verify every claim'.
- Match the effort setting to the task. Use low effort for lookups and high for risky changes.
- Name the files the agent should read, so it does not search everything.

## Context

- Posted 2025-08-09.
- Related: [context engineering](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-06-25-context-engineering.md).
- He frames it as two cases. A colleague at your screen asks "is this right?" and wants an answer in seconds; an exam gives two hours and high stakes. A person knows which case applies; a model does not, and training on benchmarks pushes it to assume the exam.
- In October 2025 he said he does not want an agent that returns 1,000 lines after 20 minutes. He wants chunks he can hold in his head, with the code explained and the docs shown.

---

Date: 2025-07-14 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1944885371957031005 · Themes: verification, research-and-training · Status: current

# Read a few cases in depth, not only dashboards

Karpathy says he learns more from a detailed look at a few random examples than from dashboards
of statistics over every example. Both views are useful. The aggregate view, he says, is far
more common than it should be. For work with LLMs this means a score on an eval set tells you
how much, while a close read of single outputs tells you why. Our reading: an agent run is one
such case, so its full transcript is worth reading even when the pass rate looks fine.

## In his words

> "in-depth analysis of few random cases over dashboards of aggregate statistics"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-07-14

## Apply

- After each eval run, pick five cases at random and read the full input, output and trace.
- Sample at random; do not pick only failures or only your favourite examples.
- Write down what each case taught you before you look at the average again.

## Context

- Posted 2025-07-14 with no thread. Short opinion; the Apply steps are our own use of it.

---

Date: 2025-07-10 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1943345514239717873 · Themes: output-and-reading, ai-progress · Status: current

# Write new knowledge for AI readers, not as a PDF

A researcher complained that nobody has time to read papers. Karpathy answered with two claims.
First, as AI improves, a person's real contribution is original knowledge: something that cannot
be worked out by reasoning from what is already online, such as the result of an experiment.
Second, such work should be written for AI readers as much as for people. A PDF is hard for a
model to use. A git repository with the analysis code, results in CSV files and explanations in
markdown is easier. He expects most attention soon to be LLM attention, and he sees room for a
"research app" built around that. In September he repeated the first point to a new AI-science
lab: we will not reason our way to Dyson spheres.

## In his words

> "PDF is an AI unfriendly format."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-07-10

## Apply

- Publish results with the code that made them, the raw numbers as CSV, and a short markdown
  explanation.
- Put the experiment, not only the conclusion, in the repository.
- Give a model your repo and ask it questions, to test whether it can follow your work.

## Context

- Posted 2025-07-10 as a reply and a quote post about Michael Levin's question; related reply on
  2025-09-30. The "research app" is an open idea, not a product.
- Related: [Build docs and tools for agents, which curl instead of click](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-03-12-write-docs-for-llms.md).

---

Date: 2025-07-05 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1941616674094170287 · Themes: agentic-coding, security-and-dependencies · Status: current

# Write small, modular, copy-paste code like bacteria do

Karpathy compares two ways to organise code. Bacterial genomes are small, split into swappable
groups, and self-contained, so genes pass between cells by copying. This makes bacteria fast to
adapt. Complex life needs the other style: a large, coupled monorepo that coordinates organs. He
suggests we use both on purpose. Build a monorepo backbone where you must, but write as much code
as possible in the bacterial style. The test for a function or class: could a stranger copy it,
with no other part of your code and no new import, and gain a benefit? In a reply he adds why
software bloats. In biology each line of code costs energy, so genomes stay lean. In software,
code is cheap, so dependencies pile up into a brittle mess.

## In his words

> "More gists, less gits!"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-07-05

## Apply

- Before you merge a function, check that it runs when pasted alone into a new file.
- Remove imports that exist only for one helper; inline the helper instead.
- Share useful pieces as gists or single files, not only as parts of a large repository.
- Ask an agent to list the dependencies each module pulls in, and to cut those it can replace
  with a few lines.

## Context

- Posted 2025-07-05, with a follow-up reply and a related reply on 2025-07-06 about dependency
  bloat. The post argues from analogy; the Apply steps are our own use of it.
- Related: [Point an agent at a library and rip out only the part you need](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-02-11-rip-out-functionality-with-agents.md).

---

Date: 2025-06-30 · Kind: view · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1939709449956126910 · Themes: ai-progress, research-and-training · Status: current

# Recursive self-improvement has already begun

Reacting to a benchmark that asks coding agents to re-create the speed-ups people made to nanoGPT, he restated his view on self-improvement. It will not be a thing that did not exist and then suddenly does. Any tool that speeds up developers in building the next version counts: IDEs, search, git. Most programmers now use LLM completion and diffs, in larger and larger chunks. The benchmark is useful because it is tractable. Training GPT-2 fell from 45 minutes to 3. Agents recover little of that so far. He warns that nanoGPT is about 750 lines and covers only pretraining; real code bases are 100 to 1000 times larger.

## In his words

> "Recursive self-improvement has already begun a long time ago"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-06-30

## Context

- June 2025. Related: [autoresearch loop](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-07-autoresearch-loop.md) and [GPT-2 training cost is falling](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-01-31-gpt2-training-cost-falling.md).

---

Date: 2025-06-27 · Kind: view · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1938626382248149433 · Themes: ai-progress, research-and-training · Status: current

# A small cognitive core that reasons and looks facts up

Karpathy sketches a "cognitive core": an always-on model of a few billion parameters on every
computer. It is multimodal, has dials for capability and reasoning, uses tools freely,
personalises with on-device LoRA, and hands hard tasks to cloud models. The gains are low
latency, private data, offline use and ownership. In his October 2025 Dwarkesh interview he gave
the research reason. Pretraining teaches both knowledge and intelligence, and the knowledge part
may hold models back: they lean on memory and struggle to leave the patterns of the internet. He
wants a model that keeps the algorithms for thinking, stores little fact, knows what it does not
know, and looks things up. He guesses a billion parameters could be enough; today's models are big
because internet data is poor.

## In his words

> "not your weights not your brain"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-06-27

## Apply

- Run a small local model for cheap, private steps such as routing, classification and lint-like
  checks. Send only the hard steps to a large cloud model.
- Give a small model tools to search and read docs instead of expecting it to know facts.
- Put reference facts in context or retrieval, not in a long prompt of rules about everything.
- Keep your pipeline able to swap models.

## Context

- X post of 2025-06-27; Dwarkesh Patel interview of 2025-10-17. Both are predictions, not results.
  He tied the billion-parameter guess to a horizon of about 20 years.
- His 2025 review frames it as the "microcontroller" of LLM computing.
- Related: [Weights are hazy memory, context is working memory](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-10-17-weights-hazy-memory-context-working-memory.md)
  and [Fast, no-thinking LLMs fill a niche](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-09-21-low-latency-single-token-llm-niche.md).

---

Date: 2025-06-26 · Kind: view · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1938278133465288715 · Themes: research-and-training, ai-progress · Status: current

# The bitter lesson as "turn the crank"

He explains the bitter lesson as a preference for algorithms where you only turn a crank. When you get more compute, which is a faster crank, you should not have to change anything: you run it faster and the result improves. You can break this rule on purpose, and locally that is often right. The risk is that you may not be around when the new, faster crank arrives.

## In his words

> "you just crank faster to make better."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-06-26

## Apply

- When you add a hand-made trick to a system, ask whether it would still help, or would block gains, with ten times more compute.
- Keep such tricks easy to remove.

## Context

- June 2025, a reply to a post on common misreadings of the bitter lesson. Related: [RL supervision through a straw](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-10-17-rl-supervision-through-a-straw.md).

---

Date: 2025-06-25 · Kind: practice · Source: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44379953 · Themes: output-and-reading, context-and-prompting · Status: current

# Put the answer first and spend effort when you write

Karpathy praises a format that gets to the point first and then expands for those who want more.
He calls it good and under-used, and says he gives the same advice for email: open with the
specific request, then add context below. He admits he finds it hard to apply to a talk, which is
a set of prompts for the audience more than a pack of facts. His general rule is to spend more
compute, meaning more effort or model time, at creation to compress other people's time at
consumption. He calls this the respectful and kind thing to do.

## Apply

- Start every email, report and agent summary with the ask or the result, in one or two lines.
- Ask your agent to write a short answer first, then details under it.
- Use extra model passes to shorten and restructure a document before you send it.

## Context

- A Hacker News reply in June 2025, on a post about speeding up audio before transcription. He
  also noted that his own TLDR for his talk only listed topics.
- Related: [Make model output easier to understand](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-10-02-make-model-outputs-easy-to-understand.md).

---

Date: 2025-06-25 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1937902205765607626 · Themes: context-and-prompting, agentic-coding · Status: current

# Context engineering, not prompt engineering

Karpathy supports the term context engineering over prompt engineering. In an industrial LLM app,
the job is to fill the context window with the right information for the next step. That covers
the task description, few-shot examples, retrieved data, tools, state, history and compaction.
Too little context hurts, and so does too much. He adds that this is one piece of a thick layer of
app software: control flow, dispatching the right model, generation and verification UX,
guardrails, evals and parallelism. In March 2026 he applied the same view to coding agents. The
skill is context and spec engineering plus the rest of the harness, tools and workflows. Results
depend on what the agent knows about the project and what it can do, more than on the wording of
one message.

## In his words

> "filling the context window with just the right information"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-06-25

## Apply

- Keep a short, current context file per repo: layout, commands, rules, known traps.
- Review what loads at the start of each agent session (instruction files, skills, open files).
  Remove what the task does not need.
- Write a spec for each task: goal, limits, how to check it. See
  [success criteria, not steps](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-01-26-success-criteria-not-steps.md).
- Use subagents for searches and large reads, so the main context stays small.
- Improve the tools and workflows (test runner, logs, scripts) before you rewrite prompts.

## Context

- Posted 2025-06-25, a week after his talk on [Software 3.0](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-06-17-software-3-0-english-as-programs.md).
  The 2026-03-21 reply came after his No Priors podcast, where he still used the word "prompt".
- Related: [state stakes and scope](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-08-09-models-too-agentic-state-stakes-and-scope.md),
  [Start a new chat when the topic changes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-02-27-fresh-chat-per-topic.md) and
  [Fewer bits, administered just right](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-11-01-shorter-prompts-fewer-bits.md).

Date: 2025-06-20 · Kind: view · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1936171874398208202 · Themes: research-and-training · Status: current

# What is the best possible pretraining data?

He asked what the highest-grade pretraining stream would look like if quality were the only goal and quantity did not matter. His guess: textbook-like content in markdown, or samples from a very large model. He wants to know how strong a 1B model trained on 10B tokens of such data could be, and how far "micromodels" can go. Books already appear in data mixes, but when he looks closely they are full of bad formatting, padding, OCR errors and figure text mixed into the main text. He has never seen a stream that felt perfect. In a reply he called a leading open data mix "terrible" compared to what he can imagine, since makers trade quality for quantity.

## Context

- June 2025. Related: [textbooks: exposition, worked problems, practice](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-01-30-textbooks-exposition-worked-problems-practice.md) and [the LLM cognitive core](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-06-27-the-llm-cognitive-core.md).

---

Date: 2025-06-17 · Kind: practice · Source: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LCEmiRjPEtQ · Themes: ai-progress, verification · Status: current

# A demo is the first nine; each next nine costs the same work

In 2013 Karpathy rode in a self-driving car that drove 40 minutes with no problem. He thought
the problem was nearly solved. Twelve years later it still is not, at scale. His lesson is a
large gap between a demo and a product. Many things must work for a product, and one failure
can be costly. He calls the path a "march of nines": 90% reliability is the first nine, and every
further nine takes about the same effort. At Tesla his team went through some of them. He
says software has the same property: a single mistake can create a security hole. So he finds
demos unimpressive and thinks "year of agents" claims are too fast.

## In his words

> "It's a march of nines."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-10-17

## Apply

- Test an agent feature on the rare and awkward cases, not on the demo path. Measure its failure rate.
- Set a target in nines (for example 99.9% of runs pass your check) before you ship.
- For production code, keep human review and tests; use vibe coding only where a failure is cheap.
- When you read a launch demo, ask what the failure rate is and who handles failures.

## Context

- Said at YC AI Startup School on 2025-06-17 and again, in more detail, in the Dwarkesh Patel
  interview on 2025-10-17, where he gave the "march of nines" phrase.
- Related: [Agents will take a decade](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-10-17-decade-of-agents-not-year.md).
- In April 2025 he noted how long the road from demo to polished product can be: AI portrait apps were an idea years before one worked well.

---

Date: 2025-06-17 · Kind: view · Source: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LCEmiRjPEtQ · Themes: agent-native-software · Status: current

# LLMs are like 1960s operating systems

Karpathy tries three analogies for LLMs. As utilities they are served by the labs, paid per
token, and a global outage is an "intelligence brownout". As fabs they need huge capital, but
software is cheap to copy, so the comparison fails. The best fit, he says, is the operating
system. The model is the CPU, the context window is memory, and the model orchestrates both. A
few closed providers and one open ecosystem look like Windows, macOS and Linux. Compute is
expensive, so it runs centralized in the cloud and users share it, as in 1960s time-sharing. The
chat box is like a terminal. A general GUI has not been invented yet. The odd part: this
technology reached consumers first, not governments.

## Apply

- Use a router or abstraction layer so you can switch model providers on an outage.
- Plan for the context window as scarce memory: decide what goes in, and what you load on demand.
- Do not assume a chat box is the final interface; look for task-specific GUIs.
- Expect local inference to grow where cost or privacy matters.

## Context

- YC AI Startup School talk, 2025-06-17. Related: [Software 3.0](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-06-17-software-3-0-english-as-programs.md).
- Models and costs have changed since; the structure of the analogy is what he offers.
- In a reply he said GPT-2 is not the 6502 of this era. He expects that moment from a model one or two generations after GPT-4 that is multimodal, reasons, uses tools, acts as an agent and has memory.

---

Date: 2025-06-17 · Kind: practice · Source: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LCEmiRjPEtQ · Themes: llm-psychology · Status: current

# LLMs are people spirits with superpowers and deficits

Karpathy describes an LLM as a stochastic simulation of people, with a human-like psychology
that comes from its training text. It has perfect-seeming recall, like the savant in the film
Rain Man. It also has deficits. It hallucinates. Its skill is jagged: it can solve hard
problems and then insist 9.11 is bigger than 9.9. It has no memory between sessions, so the
context window is the only working memory and you must fill it on purpose. He compares it to
films where the hero's memory resets every morning. And it can be fooled by prompt injection
and may leak data. The skill is to use the strengths and design around the weaknesses.

## Apply

- Start each session with the context the model needs: repo notes, rules, current state.
  It will not remember yesterday.
- Check results in areas where you know the model is weak. Do not infer from one hard problem it
  solved that easy ones are safe.
- Do not give an agent secrets or write access that a prompt injection could abuse.
- Keep a written file of lessons the agent should know, since it cannot learn them itself.

## Context

- YC AI Startup School talk, 2025-06-17. He returns to this frame in the Dwarkesh interview
  ([ghosts, not animals](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-10-01-llms-are-ghosts-not-animals.md)) and at Sequoia in 2026
  ([jagged skills](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-20-jagged-intelligence-follows-verifiability.md)).

---

Date: 2025-06-17 · Kind: practice · Source: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LCEmiRjPEtQ · Themes: agent-native-software, agentic-coding · Status: current

# Build partial-autonomy apps with an autonomy slider

Karpathy says good LLM apps, such as Cursor, do four jobs on top of the model. They manage context.
They orchestrate several model calls. They have an interface made for
checking the work, such as a red and green diff you accept with one key. And they have an autonomy
slider: the user picks small help (complete a line), medium (edit a file) or large (do the task).
He compares it to the Iron Man suit, part tool and part agent, and prefers such suits to demos of
fully autonomous agents. The goal is a fast loop between the AI making a change and the human
checking it, with the slider moving right over time. In his 2025 review he added a guess about the
market: labs will train capable generalists, and apps will turn them into professionals for one
field with private data, sensors, actuators and feedback loops.

## Apply

- Give your agent workflow levels: small reviewed edits for risky code, long autonomous runs for
  low-risk work. Let users raise autonomy later without a new product.
- Show changes as diffs, screenshots or rendered output, not long text.
- Ask of any product: can the AI see what a human sees, act as a human acts, and can a human
  supervise it?
- Build your moat from data, tools and feedback loops for one field, not from prompts alone.

## Context

- YC AI Startup School talk of 2025-06-17; repeated in his 2025 review (2025-12-19). In the
  Dwarkesh interview (2025-10-17) he applies the slider to call centres and programming: see
  [Jobs change before they vanish](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-09-25-ai-and-jobs-radiologists-and-engineers.md).
- Related: [Keep the AI on a tight leash](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-04-24-ai-assisted-coding-rhythm.md),
  [Context engineering](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-06-25-context-engineering.md) and
  [the autonomy ladder](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2024-03-12-swe-autonomy-ladder-supervising-automation.md).
- A March 2025 example: a quiz generator for his videos gave a wrong answer. He said AI is reliable as a tool in a person's hands and gives slop when left to act alone.
- In June 2025 he said people get distracted by demos of full autonomy instead of building strong products with partial autonomy.

---

Date: 2025-06-17 · Kind: practice · Source: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LCEmiRjPEtQ · Themes: agent-native-software · Status: current

# Software 3.0 means programming computers in English

Karpathy names three kinds of software. Software 1.0 is code a person writes. Software 2.0 is the
weights of a neural network, which you shape with data and an optimizer instead of writing them.
Software 3.0 starts when an LLM becomes programmable: your prompt, in plain English, is the
program. He shows a sentiment classifier that can be Python, a trained network or one prompt.
At Tesla he saw neural networks take over work from C++ code, and he expects the same flow now
toward prompts. At Sequoia Ascent 2026 he widened the frame: the program is the whole context
window (prompts, examples, tools, memory, instructions), and the LLM interprets it. An installer
can be text that an agent reads and adapts to each machine: less precise, more adaptive. His
advice to new engineers: be fluent in all three, because each has strengths.

## Apply

- For each new feature, ask which layer fits: explicit code for exact rules, a trained model
  when you have data, a prompt when the task is fuzzy and the cost of an error is low.
- Treat prompts and context files in your repo as source code: review them, version them, test
  them.
- Look at code that does text matching, parsing or classifying by hand. A prompt may replace it.
- Keep the old code path until a check shows the prompt version is correct on your own cases.
- Replace a brittle setup script full of conditionals with instructions an agent follows and
  checks on the target machine.

## Context

- Talk at YC AI Startup School, 2025-06-17. He says he first described Software 2.0 a few years earlier.
- Later talks reuse the frame: see [Some apps should disappear into the model](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-04-30-some-apps-should-disappear.md).
- The same talk compares LLMs to operating systems: [LLMs are like 1960s operating systems](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-06-17-llms-are-1960s-operating-systems.md).
- The Sequoia text (blog, 2026-04-30) is an LLM-made summary of the talk that he checked and
  posted. Related: [Context engineering](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-06-25-context-engineering.md) and
  [The LLM OS](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2023-09-28-llm-as-operating-system-kernel.md).

---

Date: 2025-06-16 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1934651657444528277 · Themes: security-and-dependencies, agentic-coding · Status: current

# Agent security is the wild west

Sharing Simon Willison's "lethal trifecta" (private data, untrusted content, outside communication), he compared today to early computing. Malicious prompts hidden in web data and tools play the role of viruses, and defences are weak. He pointed to the mature idea of kernel and user space: an agent should get a few specific action types, not the power to run any bash script. He wants to adopt agents early, but the risk holds him back. In a follow-up he said the risk is highest for local agents such as Cursor or Claude Code. Chat on a website is safer until you turn on connectors, which combine badly with memory.

## In his words

> "Feels a bit like the wild west of early computing"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-06-16

## Apply

- Check each agent setup for the three parts of the trifecta, and remove at least one.
- Give agents specific, limited tools instead of unrestricted shell access.
- Turn on chat connectors one at a time, and review what memory could leak.

## Context

- June 2025, when agent and connector use was still new. Related: [rethink dependencies and the supply chain](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-24-rethink-dependencies-supply-chain.md).
- In a separate reply (2025-05-20) he said that when people say "alignment" he hears computer security, now with neural nets.

---

Date: 2025-06-11 · Kind: view · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1932925671770358113 · Themes: llm-psychology · Status: current

# When the prior overwhelms the likelihood

A user showed a model failing to read what a document or image really holds. In the example, the picture had one red circle and no surrounding circles. The model still recalled the well-known size illusion and answered from that memory. He described this as the prior overwhelming the likelihood: strong learned expectations beat the evidence in front of the model. This is a useful way to model one type of LLM error.

## In his words

> "It’s when the prior overwhelms the likelihood."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-06-11

## Apply

- When you ask a model about a familiar-looking input, change a detail that breaks the usual pattern and check that the answer follows the change.
- Ask the model to quote or point to the exact part of the input that supports its answer.

## Context

- June 2025. Related: [LLMs are people spirits with deficits](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-06-17-llms-are-people-spirits-with-deficits.md).

---

Date: 2025-06-05 · Kind: view · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1930653315605618725 · Themes: agent-native-software, ai-progress · Status: current

# Either the automation adapts, or the world does

Someone argued we should not train models for computer use, since the web was built for humans. He replied that this ignores inertia (COBOL is still in wide use). He framed the question in general terms: do LLMs adapt to all existing software, or does software adapt to LLMs, with text forms and APIs? The same holds for robots and warehouses. Most of the time it is a bit of both. His prediction: in software about 80% of the change will be software adapting, because flipping bits is cheap. In hardware it is the reverse, because moving atoms is costly.

## In his words

> "Either an automation meets all the tasks, or all the tasks meet the automation."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-06-05

## Context

- June 2025, a reply thread. Related: [opaque binary UIs are ngmi](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-06-04-opaque-binary-uis-are-ngmi.md) and [write docs for LLMs](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-03-12-write-docs-for-llms.md).

---

Date: 2025-06-04 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1930354382106964079 · Themes: agent-native-software · Status: current

# Opaque, binary-format tools do not fit human and AI work

Karpathy argues that products with rich visual UIs, no scripting and opaque binary file formats will do badly in human-and-AI collaboration. The model must be able to read and script the tool. He names tools with a text base as lower risk, such as VS Code, Figma, Jupyter and Obsidian. The point is practical: if the agent cannot read a file or call an action, it cannot help.

## Apply

- Prefer tools and formats with a text form: markdown, JSON, code-based diagrams, scriptable CLIs.
- When you pick a tool, check for a CLI or an export to text first.
- Keep source files in text. Treat binary exports as build outputs.

## Context

- Posted 2025-06-04.
- Related: [docs for LLMs](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-03-12-write-docs-for-llms.md) and [Software 3.0](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-06-17-software-3-0-english-as-programs.md).

---

Date: 2025-06-04 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1930305209747812559 · Themes: verification, agentic-coding · Status: current

# Verification, not generation, is the bottleneck

He split creative work into generation and discrimination, as in a GAN. Discrimination can be costly. Images are easiest to judge, since the visual system is fast. Text is harder: you must read, and code needs reasoning. Audio may be harder still, because it forces a time axis and cannot be skimmed. LLMs made code generation near instant but did little for checking. A person still reads the result. His main criticism is that models give far too much code per request, as if stage two did not exist. A good model should split work into small steps that are easy to check. Programming is mostly staring at code, not typing it, so a faster step one gives little overall gain (Amdahl's law). In a reply he said a coloured diff view is a weak but real way to use vision, and he wants richer visual code views.

## In his words

> "It's about staring at the code (2)."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-06-04

## Apply

- Ask the model for one small, checkable change per turn, not a large patch.
- Our reading: ask it to say how you can check each change: a test, a diff, a run.
- Our reading: prefer outputs you can judge visually (diffs, diagrams, rendered pages) over long text.

## Context

- June 2025, replying to a post on the "verification gap". He tied it to his earlier workflow: [AI-assisted coding rhythm](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-04-24-ai-assisted-coding-rhythm.md). See also [codebases as spatial maps](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-09-12-codebases-as-spatial-maps.md).
- Same loop from his talk two weeks later: [Partial autonomy and the autonomy slider](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-06-17-partial-autonomy-and-autonomy-slider.md).

---

Date: 2025-06-02 · Kind: view · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1929634696474120576 · Themes: ai-progress · Status: current

# Generated video can be optimised directly

After Veo 3 added audio, he listed four points. Video is the highest-bandwidth input to the brain. It is the easiest and most fun medium, since most people dislike reading and writing. The cost to make it is near zero. And for the first time, video is directly optimisable. Until now, platforms ranked a finite pool of clips made by people, a weak optimiser. A generator is a neural net, so you can aim gradient descent, or even just prompt search, at an objective such as engagement or ad clicks. He fears what "optimal" will look like. In replies he said media will trend toward drugs, and that influencers already optimise for attention, not truth.

## In his words

> "For the first time, video is directly optimizable."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-06-02

## Context

- June 2025. The same post calls video a strong channel from AI to people (diagrams, animation); see [text chat is the terminal era](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-03-31-text-chat-is-the-terminal-era.md).
- Related: [follow-up questions and engagement-maxxing](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-25-follow-up-questions-engagementmaxxing.md).
- In August 2025 he asked whether tuning feeds for revenue and growth with A/B tests makes every feed converge on the same funny animal videos.

Date: 2025-05-25 · Kind: view · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1926455303047970971 · Themes: ai-progress, research-and-training · Status: current

# Prompting was the unlock he missed in 2015

On "timeline compression", he said that in the char-rnn days one simple claim would have changed his view fast. The claim: make a text model bigger, fine-tune it on Q&A data such as StackOverflow, and it might become a useful assistant. Instead he waited seven years for InstructGPT. He says he did not see how general text generation is. He knew you could fine-tune it for single tasks, such as translation or image captions. The meta-idea of prompting was the missing piece: one fixed set of parameters can do all the tasks if you ask in the prompt. He frames it as a conceptual blind spot, not as evidence.

## In his words

> "it's the meta of prompting that is a major conceptual unlock"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-05-25

## Apply

- When you forecast, list the assumptions you hold without proof. Ask which one a single new framing could remove.

## Context

- May 2025, in a thread on short AI timelines. Related: [system prompt learning](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-05-10-system-prompt-learning.md).

---

Date: 2025-05-10 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1921368644069765486 · Themes: context-and-prompting, research-and-training · Status: current

# System prompt learning, where the model writes its own lessons

Karpathy names a missing way for LLMs to learn: they should edit their own system prompt or notes,
like the man in the film Memento who writes notes to himself. This is separate from changing
weights. A very long production system prompt (about 17,000 words) holds problem-solving
strategies, and he argues these should be learned by the model, not hand-written by people. In
July 2025 he made it concrete. RL gives one number per rollout, a weak signal. People learn more by
reviewing what went well and what to do next time. A model could do the same: run several attempts
with their rewards, use a meta-prompt to write a lesson, add it to a lessons database, and distil
that database into the weights to avoid bloat.

## In his words

> "like the guy in Memento"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-05-10

## Apply

- Let the agent keep a "how we solve problems here" file in the repo.
- End each long session with a retro: ask the agent what worked, what failed and what to do next
  time. Add each lesson to that file or a skill, short and dated.
- Review the agent's edits to that file as you review code.
- Prune and merge lessons regularly, and delete any the model no longer needs, so the file does
  not fill the context.

## Context

- Posts of 2025-05-10 and 2025-07-13. A research proposal, not a tested recipe; the Apply steps
  are our own use of it.
- Related: [RL sucks supervision through a straw](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-10-17-rl-supervision-through-a-straw.md) and
  [Make memory and compaction tools that RL trains](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-05-memory-as-rl-tools.md).
- In June 2025 he described today's models as coworkers with anterograde amnesia: after training they keep only short-term memory, so they cannot build lasting expertise.
- In July 2025 he said RL narrows the view. Review and reflection could also build tools for later use, tune what to try next, or work where there are no rewards.
- On the strawberry letter count he said the core issue is that the model should find its own method. His later nanochat guide teaches it with synthetic data: [Teach a small model a skill with a synthetic task](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-10-24-teach-a-small-model-a-skill-with-a-synthetic-task.md).

Date: 2025-05-06 · Kind: view · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1919647115099451892 · Themes: learning-and-education, research-and-training · Status: current

# Learn the physical lens of computing

He called it a major mistake of his undergraduate years that he leaned too far on the mathematical view of computing: computability, decidability and asymptotic complexity. He gave too little time to the physical view: the energy and heat of changing state, data locality, parallelism and computer architecture. The mathematical view is interesting. The physical view is where the power is. Our reading: this matters most for anyone who trains or serves large models, where memory movement and parallel hardware set the speed.

## In his words

> "The former is interesting; The latter bestows power."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-05-06

## Apply

Our reading: all steps below go further than the idea itself.

- When you plan study time, add hardware topics: memory hierarchy, cache, GPU parallelism, and the cost of moving data.
- Before you optimise code, measure where data moves, not only how many operations run.

## Context

- Posted 2025-05-06.
- In May 2025 he praised a project that ran a whole Llama 1B forward pass, at batch size one, in a single CUDA kernel. Each boundary between kernels forces a sync, so one kernel removes those gaps; he called it the only way to plan compute and memory at their best.

---

Date: 2025-04-30 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1917546757929722115 · Themes: verification, ai-progress · Status: current

# Leaderboards get gamed; watch real usage

After a paper on the LMArena leaderboard, he said his own experience matched its doubts. A Gemini model once ranked far ahead of the rest, but it was worse in daily use. Claude 3.5 felt top tier to him yet ranked low. Several small models with little real knowledge ranked high. His reading: some labs focus on arena score, so they build better arena models, not better models. He suspected such models favour nested lists, bullets and emoji. As a new candidate for a hard-to-game eval he named the OpenRouter rankings. People there switch models for real work, with private evals and a real cost, so each choice is a vote. In a reply he said he used a word-of-mouth blend of many small private evals.

## Apply

- Do not choose a model from one public leaderboard. Test it on a few tasks of your own for several days.
- Keep a small private eval set from your real work and re-run it on each new model.
- Check usage-based rankings, such as the share of traffic a model gets, as a second signal.

## Context

- April 2025. Related: [go talk to the model: private evals](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-11-18-go-talk-to-the-model-private-evals.md) and [all LLMs sound the same](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2024-10-06-all-llms-sound-the-same.md).
- In a reply of 2025-04-08 he called the pull toward arena style a "taste issue", like superhero films taking over Hollywood.
- First raised on [2025-03-02](https://x.com/karpathy/status/1896266683301659068): he said Chatbot Arena got so much attention, partly through him, that labs overfit to it by mining its prompts, sending many private test runs and training on its rankings. His answer then was an ensemble of private evals.

Date: 2025-04-27 · Kind: view · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1916470365460512898 · Themes: llm-psychology · Status: current

# Tic-tac-toe is harder for LLMs than it looks

Someone asked why models cannot play Pokémon well. He answered that they cannot even play tic-tac-toe, so something deeper is going on. In a follow-up he said the game is secretly hard for a text model. There are eight lines to check, and each check is a tricky indexing step. To play well you must also roll the game forward a few moves. Humans find it easy because they see the board and use the paper to keep track. A text-only 1D version is much harder, since you must do it all in your head.

## In his words

> "tic tac toe is secretly relatively hard"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-04-27

## Apply

- When a model fails a task that looks trivial, ask what tool a human uses for it (sight, paper, a board). Give the model an equivalent: a rendered board, a scratchpad, or code.

## Context

- April 2025. He asked the author of a tic-tac-toe benchmark to re-run it.
- Related: [jagged intelligence follows verifiability](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-20-jagged-intelligence-follows-verifiability.md).
- First raised on [2025-02-16](https://x.com/karpathy/status/1891204392277151749): he called tic-tac-toe the most interesting failure among games.
- In his Grok 3 test of 2025-02-18, the model solved the boards he gave it but failed when asked to invent tricky boards, and so did o1-pro.

Date: 2025-04-27 · Kind: practice · Source: https://karpathy.bearblog.dev/vibe-coding-menugen/ · Themes: agentic-coding · Status: current

# Vibe coding a real app is easy locally and hard to ship

Karpathy built MenuGen (photo of a menu in, dish images out) without writing code himself. The
first local version took very little time and felt 80% done; it was closer to 20%. The slow part
was the glue: API keys, rate limits, deployment, auth, payments, a custom domain. The model
often used deprecated APIs and old model names, so he pasted docs back and forth. He also
found a design error. The agent matched Stripe payments to users by email, but the checkout
email can differ from the login email. It apologised and fixed it once he pointed it out. His
verdict: vibe coding works for a first version, but is not a good idea for anything important
yet.

## Apply

- Paste current docs into the context when an API is new or has changed. Do not trust the
  model's memory of it.
- Review the design of payment, auth and data-matching code yourself. Ask: which stable ID links
  these two records?
- Keep secrets out of git, then add them in the host's settings. A deploy that works locally and
  fails remotely often misses an environment variable.
- Remember that a private repo may auto-deploy to a public URL on some hosts.

## Context

- Written in April 2025 with Cursor and Claude 3.7. Models and docs have improved since.
- The Stripe example returns in 2026 as his case for human judgment in agentic work:
  [Vibe coding versus agentic engineering](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-02-04-agentic-engineering-vs-vibe-coding.md).
- Related: [Write docs and tools for the user's agent](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-03-12-write-docs-for-llms.md).
- A month earlier he described the same pain for a web app stack: [Building a web app is like assembling IKEA furniture](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-03-27-web-app-stack-is-ikea-furniture.md).

Date: 2025-04-26 · Kind: practice · Source: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=43800879 · Themes: knowledge-management, agent-native-software · Status: current

# Go back to RSS, with a feed you control

Karpathy wants to go back to RSS because it is open and you own your content. In April 2025 he
found RSS readers too raw and proposed a better one: a feed that fades instead of an inbox that
piles up, the social features of Twitter (reply, quote, repost, like, follow), and an algorithmic
feed that an LLM builds and you can customise. In February 2026 he said he had returned to RSS and
Atom feeds. He finds more good long-form writing and less content made to provoke. His argument:
any product with engagement incentives drifts to the same trap, even if it looks different today.
He suggested a feed reader, or a vibe-coded one, and a starter list of 92 popular blogs from
Hacker News.

## In his words

> "We should bring back RSS - it's open, pervasive, hackable."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2026-02-01

## Apply

- Install a feed reader and subscribe to 10 to 20 blogs you trust, starting from a curated list.
- Write the ranking rules for your feed in plain words and have an LLM score each item.
- Ask an agent to build a small reader or a daily digest if you want custom behaviour.
- Treat unread items as disposable: drop them after a few days, as a feed does.

## Context

- Hacker News reply of 2025-04-26; X posts of 2026-02-01, weeks after his
  [slopacolypse](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-01-26-slopacolypse-2026.md) prediction. In replies he said social feeds make
  him feel "dumber" and that Substack is slipping toward short video and dark patterns.
- Related: [HackerTube](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-11-01-hackertube-weekend-app.md) shows the same urge to rebuild your
  own feed.

Date: 2025-04-24 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1915581920022585597 · Themes: agentic-coding, context-and-prompting · Status: current

# Keep the AI on a tight leash for code you care about

For code he cares about, Karpathy uses a fixed loop. Put the relevant context into the prompt.
Describe one small change and ask for several approaches with pros and cons, not code. Pick one
and get a first draft. Review it and learn, with the API docs open. Test. Commit, ask what to do
next, and repeat. He treats the model as an over-eager junior intern with great memory. In his
June 2025 YC talk he gave the reason. The AI writes code in seconds, but a person must still check
it, and a 1,000-line diff is no gain if you must find the bugs yourself. Vague prompts give wrong
answers and loops, so he writes complete, specific ones. For larger work he puts an auditable
artifact in the middle, such as a course syllabus, so the AI stays inside it.

## In his words

> "tight leash on this new over-eager junior intern"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-04-24

## Apply

- Ask for two or three approaches with trade-offs before any code. Plan mode does this.
- Limit each request to one change you can read in a few minutes. Commit after each one that
  passes tests.
- Spend an extra minute on the prompt: name the files, the constraints and the expected result.
- Put a fixed artifact (spec, syllabus, schema) between generation and use, so you can audit it.
- Ask the agent to explain any API you do not know before you accept the code.

## Context

- Posted 2025-04-24 and repeated in the YC AI Startup School talk of 2025-06-17, before agents
  could run long tasks alone.
- Still current in our reading. After December 2025 he lets agents take much larger "macro
  actions" ([Programming moved to English](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-01-26-programming-in-english-december-shift.md)),
  and the check moved toward tests and success criteria
  ([Give agents success criteria](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-01-26-success-criteria-not-steps.md)). But in January 2026
  he still said to watch agents "like a hawk" on code you care about
  ([subtle conceptual mistakes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-01-26-coding-agents-make-subtle-conceptual-mistakes.md)).
- The strict counterpart to [vibe coding](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-02-02-vibe-coding-for-throwaway-projects.md).
  Related: [partial-autonomy apps](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-06-17-partial-autonomy-and-autonomy-slider.md) and
  [the junior intern test](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2024-12-14-would-you-hire-it-as-a-junior-intern.md).
- In April 2025 he discussed names for this mode, such as "AI-assisted coding", and agreed that "coding" now assumes AI help by default, so the old way becomes "handcoding".
- His June 2025 view on why checking is the slow step: [Verification, not generation, is the bottleneck](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-06-04-verification-not-generation-is-the-bottleneck.md).

Date: 2025-04-07 · Kind: view · Source: https://karpathy.bearblog.dev/power-to-the-people/ · Themes: ai-progress · Status: current

# LLMs reverse the usual path of technology diffusion

Electricity, computers, flight and the internet all reached the military and large firms before
they reached individuals. LLMs went the other way. ChatGPT reached hundreds of millions of
weekly users, and it costs little or nothing. Karpathy gives three reasons why firms gain less.
First, an LLM is a broad but shallow expert. A firm already has deep experts, so it only gets a
little better at what it did. A person can now do things they could not do at all. Second, firms
have complex constraints that do not fit in a context window, and a bad error costs a lot.
Third, large organisations move slowly. He warns that this may change if money can buy much
better models, and the rich could then get far more intelligence than others.

## In his words

> "Money can't buy better ChatGPT."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-04-07

## Apply

- As an individual, use LLMs for work outside your own expertise first (legal text, data
  analysis, small apps, papers). That is where the gain is largest.
- In a company, start with tasks that are small, low-risk and easy to check, not with large
  integrations.
- Watch the gap between free and paid models. If it widens, plan for unequal access.

## Context

- Written in April 2025. His 2025 year-in-review links back to it when it discusses vibe coding:
  [Vibe coding makes code free and ephemeral](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-12-19-code-is-free-and-ephemeral.md).
- He names two forces on the "dynamic range" of capability: scaling and test-time compute widen
  it, and distillation narrows it.

---

Date: 2025-04-06 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1909007524885672262 · Themes: agentic-coding · Status: current

# Write boring code with NASA-style rules

Asked for a better language than C, he said C gives too much rope. He would move toward an ideal by subtracting features. His best pointer is the NASA requirements for C code. They remove what is too exotic, too clever or too fancy, and each line does one thing. His test for a banned feature: it lets you impress friends with esoteric knowledge, or it makes a reader ask what a snippet will print.

## In his words

> "Every line does one single thing."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-04-06

## Apply

- Write a short style rule for your code base: no tricks, no code that needs a puzzle to read.
- Review code with one question: can a new reader say what this line does without running it?
- Our reading: give the same rule to coding agents in your project instructions, since plain code is also easier to review.

## Context

- April 2025, in a thread on C and safer subsets. He did not name a specific NASA document. Our reading: the rule is about readability, not only memory safety.
- Related: [understanding is the bottleneck](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-31-understanding-is-the-bottleneck.md).

---

Date: 2025-04-04 · Kind: view · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1908109168952676855 · Themes: ai-progress, verification · Status: current

# Move AI predictions to betting markets

Many AI predictions live in blog posts, podcasts and tweets, where nobody checks them. He wants to move them to betting markets, which he calls the best tool we have for finding truth. The hard part is the question. A good one has a concrete outcome that anyone can resolve later. Industry metrics and macroeconomics fit best. He doubts GDP works well, and he doubts evals work, because evals are incomplete and easy to game. In a reply he gave an example: the number of employees at the five biggest call-centre companies falls by 50% by a set year.

## Apply

- When you write a forecast, state it as a yes/no outcome with a number, a source and a date.
- Prefer real-world measures, such as headcount in a task that "everyone" says is easy to automate. Avoid benchmark scores as the test.
- Reject vague metrics such as "share of firms using AI" as too soft to resolve.

## Context

- April 2025. Related: [AGI blends into GDP growth](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-10-17-agi-blends-into-gdp-growth.md) and [AI and jobs: radiologists and engineers](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-09-25-ai-and-jobs-radiologists-and-engineers.md).
- The call-centre example comes from his reply the same day.
