Date: 2025-03-31 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1906701941146624039 · Themes: output-and-reading, agent-native-software · Status: current

# Text chat is the terminal era; ask for visual output

Karpathy says text chat is like the command terminal era of computing. A correct answer is closer
to a custom web app made for each query: spatial, visual and interactive. Computing solved the
console problem with the GUI, and LLMs need the same step: answers as images, infographics,
slides, whiteboards, animations and small web apps. In his 2025 review he called Google's Nano
Banana a first hint of an LLM GUI, because text, images and world knowledge share one set of
weights. In May 2026 he put it as input and output channels. Audio is the best way for people to
talk to an AI, but vision is the best way for an AI to talk back, since much of the brain
processes images. He sees a ladder: raw text, markdown (today's default), HTML (already a good
default), and later interactive video made by a diffusion model.

## In his words

> "People actually dislike reading text - it is slow and effortful."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-12-19

## Apply

- End a prompt with "Structure your response as HTML", then open the saved file in a browser.
- Ask for a diagram, table, chart or infographic when a text answer gets long.
- For a one-off task, ask for a throwaway UI, not a long list of command flags.
- Try "Present this as a slideshow" for material you must explain to other people.
- Keep the HTML file in your project as the readable record of long research results.

## Context

- Posts of 2025-03-31, 2025-06-19 (a demo that builds a UI per task, which he still called a
  horseless carriage) and 2025-11-23 (the GUI as an intelligent canvas); the sixth item of his 2025
  review; and a post of 2026-05-11 that quoted an article on HTML output in Claude Code. In 2026 he
  also wanted better input: pointing at things on screen, as with a person beside you.
- Next step: [Make model output easier to understand](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-10-02-make-model-outputs-easy-to-understand.md).
- Related: [LLMs are like 1960s operating systems](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-06-17-llms-are-1960s-operating-systems.md)
  and [Code is now free, custom and disposable](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-12-19-code-is-free-and-ephemeral.md).
- He already used the punchcard image for prompt-and-paste chat in January 2025.
- In May 2025 he expected the GUI to be visual, generated for each prompt, and built mostly from procedural parts such as charts and components, because some content, such as a map, must be exact.
- In November 2025 he tried an image model that reasons, as a first sign of this GUI: see [Plan in text first, then illustrate](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-11-23-plan-in-text-then-illustrate-with-an-image-model.md).

Date: 2025-03-27 · Kind: view · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1905051558783418370 · Themes: agent-native-software, agentic-coding · Status: current

# Building a web app is like assembling IKEA furniture; make it just work for AIs

Karpathy, newer to modern web development, listed what a 2025 app needs: frontend and backend,
hosting, a database, login, file storage, email, payments, background jobs, analytics,
monitoring, developer tools, secrets and more. None of it comes in one box. He said it took
him about three hours to connect a Supabase backend to a Vercel app and fix a few errors.
The moment you leave the "getting started" path you are lost.

His point: the pain is not code. It is configuration, plumbing and workflow. He expects large
rewards for whoever makes this accessible and working out of the box, for people and, more and
more, for AI agents. In a reply he added the familiar friction: dependency conflicts, downgrading
Node, and creating many accounts.

## In his words

> "a bit like assembling IKEA furniture"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-03-27

## Context

- Related ideas: [Make the whole DevOps lifecycle agent-native](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-26-devops-as-code-for-agents.md)
  and [Build docs and tools for agents](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-03-12-write-docs-for-llms.md).

Date: 2025-03-23 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1903671737780498883 · Themes: agentic-coding, learning-and-education · Status: current

# Build a small app in a language you do not know, one chat step at a time

Karpathy built an iOS app in Swift, which he had not used before, and had it running on his
phone about an hour later. He read no docs. He opened a ChatGPT conversation and followed its
instructions, step by step. The app is a calorie countdown: it tracks a net deficit against a
base metabolic rate. It was about 200 lines at first.

He kept steps small on purpose, because it taught him more and helped him avoid getting stuck.
He used a separate conversation for each stage (start, enhance, persistence, deploy to phone)
and shared them. By about 400 lines the work slowed and a long change got "dicey, long and
strenuous". His next move was to connect the model to Xcode or to Cursor. In a reply to a
blog post he said he uses "vibe coding" for moments like this, but that most of the time he
still reads the code and adds complexity slowly.

## In his words

> "I just opened a ChatGPT convo and followed instructions"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-03-23

## Apply

- Choose a small tool you will use yourself and ask the chat for the first runnable version.
- Ask for one change at a time and run it each time; ask why when you do not understand a step.
- Start a new conversation for each stage and keep the links, so you can go back.
- Move to an editor-integrated tool once the code outgrows a chat window.

## Context

- Sequel to [Vibe coding is fine for throwaway projects](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-02-02-vibe-coding-for-throwaway-projects.md); later he found shipping is harder than building: [Vibe coding a real app is easy locally and hard to ship](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-04-27-vibe-coding-real-app-lessons.md).
- The code was for personal use; this is not a claim about production apps.

---

Date: 2025-03-19 · Kind: practice · Source: https://karpathy.bearblog.dev/the-append-and-review-note/ · Themes: knowledge-management · Status: current

# Keep one note you append to and review

Karpathy has used one single text note for years. He keeps it in a notes app and calls it
"notes". He adds every idea, to-do, quote, command or experiment log to the top as plain text. He
adds no folders and almost no tags. Old items sink under newer ones. From time to time he
scrolls down, skims, and copies anything that still deserves attention back to the top. He
merges related items and rarely deletes. Items that never get rescued stay findable with
search, but they stop competing for attention. Writing something down lets him clear his
working memory and move on.

## In his words

> "One text note ftw."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-03-19

## Apply

- Create one note with one fixed name. Put new text at the top, never in a new note.
- Skip tags. Use only a few search prefixes for action types, such as `watch:`, `listen:`,
  `read:`.
- Schedule a short review: scroll down, copy what still matters to the top, merge items that
  repeat the same thought.
- Use the same note for scratch work: shell commands you forget, experiment commands and
  results, a morning to-do list.

## Context

- Written in March 2025, before the LLM-wiki style of note keeping. For the LLM-driven
  alternative, browse the `knowledge-management` theme.
- Our reading: the "review by gravity" rule is a cheap form of spaced attention, and it works
  with plain text that an LLM can also read.
- He still uses Obsidian for concrete projects, but not for daily notes.

---

Date: 2025-03-12 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1899876370492383450 · Themes: agent-native-software, output-and-reading · Status: current

# Build docs and tools for agents, which curl instead of click

In March 2025 Karpathy said most content is still written for humans, while nearly all attention
will become LLM attention. In April he put it as a notice: the main audience of your product or
library is now an LLM. LLMs scrape, read and run curl; they do not look and click. He prefers one
markdown docs file with a copy button to a large docs site. In February 2026 he made it a test
for product owners. Can an agent use your product? Can your docs be exported as markdown? Is
there a CLI or MCP server, and are there skills for it? Command-line tools suit agents because
they are old technology that an agent can combine with the whole terminal. A prediction-market
CLI let Claude build a terminal dashboard in about three minutes.

## In his words

> "LLMs don't like to click, they like to curl."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-03-12

## Apply

- Keep one complete markdown file per project (README or AGENTS.md) that you can paste into an
  agent, and add an `llms.txt` at your site root (his 2025 YC talk).
- Offer every important action as a CLI command or API call with clear help and machine-readable
  output.
- Write a skill file for the product: when to use it, the commands, the common errors.
- Replace "click this button" steps with commands an agent can run. Test by asking an agent to do
  the setup.
- Install the CLIs you use (git hosting, cloud, payments) and let your agent use them.

## Context

- Posts of 2025-03-12, 2025-04-21 and 2025-07-10 (what would a paper for an LLM look like?), the
  YC talk of 2025-06-17, and the "Build. For. Agents." post of 2026-02-24. At Sequoia 2026 he
  listed the same surfaces: markdown docs, CLIs, APIs, MCP servers, schemas and copy-paste agent
  instructions.
- Related facets: [Make the whole DevOps lifecycle agent-native](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-26-devops-as-code-for-agents.md),
  [Apps should be APIs](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-20-apps-become-apis-agents-are-glue.md),
  [Explain things to agents](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-20-explain-to-agents-not-people.md) and
  [Opaque, binary-format tools](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-06-04-opaque-binary-uis-are-ngmi.md).
- [Software 3.0](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-06-17-software-3-0-english-as-programs.md) names agents as a third consumer
  of software.
- In March 2025 he said that putting a codebase into one file is easy; the hard part is knowledge locked in formats made for people, such as web pages, PDFs, images and video.
- For research results, see [Write new knowledge for AI readers, not as a PDF](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-07-10-write-research-for-llms-not-pdf.md).

Date: 2025-02-27 · Kind: practice · Source: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EWvNQjAaOHw · Themes: output-and-reading, learning-and-education · Status: current

# Ask the model for a conceptual diagram of what you read

Karpathy likes to see the layout of an argument. After he loads a chapter, he asks for a
conceptual diagram of the whole chapter. The model often writes Mermaid code, and the app draws it
as a tree. The tree shows the main principle and its parts. He says the spatial layout helps
him remember the chapter. The same request works for books, chapters, source code and other
material. In his demo, the app that draws the result is Claude with its artifacts feature. It is
the one artifacts use he finds useful in daily work.

## Apply

- After a summary, send: "Create a conceptual diagram of this chapter" and attach the text.
- If the app does not render Mermaid, paste the code into a Mermaid viewer.
- Use it on code too: "Draw a diagram of how these modules call each other."
- Check the diagram against the text. It shows what the model understood, which may be wrong.

## Context

- From *How I use LLMs* (2025-02).
- Related: [Read books and papers together with an LLM](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2024-12-11-read-books-with-an-llm.md).

---

Date: 2025-02-27 · Kind: view · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1895213020982472863 · Themes: ai-progress, research-and-training · Status: current

# Bigger pretraining improves everything a little, and is hard to point to

Karpathy used the release of GPT-4.5 to read the slope of gains from scaling pretraining alone.
Each 0.5 step in the version number is roughly 10X pretraining compute. GPT-3.5 was where chat
became a product. GPT-4 was better in a subtle way: word choice, nuance, analogies, rare
knowledge and humor all improved by a little, and slam-dunk examples were hard to find. He saw
the same pattern in GPT-4.5.

He stressed it had no reasoning training, so it does not move math and code. Its gains should
show on tasks that depend on knowledge, creativity and humor. To test that he ran five creative
prompts as a public poll. The crowd preferred the older model in four of five, which he found
surprising; he guessed at taste, a small sample, or weak examples, and waited for larger tests.

## In his words

> "Each 0.5 in the version is roughly 10X pretraining compute."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-02-27

## Apply

- Compare a new large model with the older one on creative and open tasks, not only on math or code.
- Judge with careful side-by-side reading; a quick poll mixes taste levels and small samples.
- Look for the odd phrases, tropes and formulaic parts in the older answer, which a careful reader catches.

## Context

- He also noted a mistake in GPT-4.5's text: it joked that an old model is slow like dial-up, but older models are faster.
- On the evaluation problem that followed, see [Public benchmarks are gameable, so keep your own evals](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-11-18-go-talk-to-the-model-private-evals.md).

---

Date: 2025-02-27 · Kind: practice · Source: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EWvNQjAaOHw · Themes: context-and-prompting, llm-psychology · Status: current

# Check which tools the model has before you trust its answer

By default a model is a closed file of learned patterns with a knowledge cutoff. Two tools fix
its main gaps. Web search brings recent or niche pages into the context window. A code
interpreter lets it run a program instead of guessing a long calculation. Apps differ here.
In his tests, some models used a tool on their own, and others answered from memory and got a
big multiplication slightly wrong. He asks for search when the answer is recent, may have
changed, or is rare on the web. He often uses a search-first app for this.

## Apply

- Tick the "search" option when you ask about news, prices, product features or release dates.
- Ask for hard arithmetic to be done "with code". Check that a tool call really happened.
- For common, low-risk facts the model remembers well, no tool is needed. Verify the high-stakes ones.
- When an answer cites sources, open them. See [Treat LLM output as a first draft](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-02-27-llm-output-is-a-first-draft.md).

## Context

- From *How I use LLMs* (2025-02). Tool support has spread since then, so check what your app
  offers today. The point still holds: without a tool run, the model answers from memory.

---

Date: 2025-02-27 · Kind: practice · Source: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EWvNQjAaOHw · Themes: context-and-prompting, llm-psychology · Status: current

# Try a fast model first, switch to a thinking model for hard problems

Karpathy asks users to check which model answers them. Free tiers often use a smaller model that
writes worse and makes up more. Bigger models cost the vendor more, so they sit behind paid tiers.
Thinking models are tuned with reinforcement learning and spend minutes on a chain of thought.
They help most on hard math and code. For simple questions, such as travel ideas, they only add
waiting time. His habit: use the fast model first. When the answer looks weak, switch to a
thinking model. In his demo, a gradient bug that the plain flagship model missed was found by a
thinking model after about a minute. He also asks several vendors the same question and calls
them his "LLM council".

## Apply

- Look at the model selector before you rely on an answer. Write the model name in your notes.
- If the work is professional and the answer is weak, try the top paid tier for a month and
  compare.
- Turn on "think" or "reasoning" mode only for hard debugging, math or planning.
- For open questions with no single right answer, ask two or three vendors and compare the replies.
- Our reading: write down your own router like his: which model for quick questions, hard questions, code and long research. Update it when the model list changes.

## Context

- From *How I use LLMs* (2025-02). The model names in the video (GPT-4o, o1 pro, Claude 3.5 Sonnet,
  Grok 3, DeepSeek R1) are dated. The habit does not depend on them.
- Related: [Check which tools the model has](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-02-27-check-which-tools-the-model-has.md).
- In June 2025 he shared his own ChatGPT router: the fast daily model for simple questions (about 40% of his use), the reasoning model o3 for hard or important ones (about 40%), GPT-4.1 for code edits (about 10%), and Deep Research to learn a topic in depth (about 10%). In replies he said the real choice is whether a question is important enough to wait for.

---

Date: 2025-02-27 · Kind: practice · Source: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EWvNQjAaOHw · Themes: context-and-prompting · Status: current

# Give examples in prompts, and save the prompts you reuse

When Karpathy writes instructions for an LLM, he gives a description and also concrete examples.
This is a few-shot prompt. He says it always raises accuracy compared with a bare request. His
case: a custom GPT for language learning that takes one sentence and returns the vocabulary in
dictionary form, in a format he can paste into a flashcard app. It holds background (he is a
beginner), the task, and four examples. He points out that the saved prompt only saves typing:
you store it once and change only the input. He also uses global custom instructions for defaults,
such as the level of formality in Korean replies.

## Apply

- Write the task in one short paragraph. Add three or four input and output examples.
- Fix the output format in the examples, so you can paste the result into your next tool.
- When you reuse a prompt a third time, save it: a custom GPT, a Claude project, a skill or a slash command.
- Put stable preferences (tone, language level, role) in the global instructions, not in every chat.

## Context

- From *How I use LLMs* (2025-02), in the section on memory, custom instructions and custom GPTs.
- Related: [Start a new chat when the topic changes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-02-27-fresh-chat-per-topic.md).

---

Date: 2025-02-27 · Kind: practice · Source: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EWvNQjAaOHw · Themes: context-and-prompting · Status: current

# Start a new chat when the topic changes

A chat is one growing sequence of tokens. The model reads all of it each time it writes the next
token. Karpathy treats this context window as the model's working memory. Old text that does not
help the new question can distract the model and lower its accuracy, and a long window makes each
token slower and more costly. So he starts a new chat when he switches topic, and keeps earlier
text only if it still helps. In March 2025 he weighed the trade-off in more detail: cost and speed,
how well the model attends over long text, signal to noise, and long chats being unlike the
training data. He called "new conversation" probably an implementation detail. The real answer is
agentic context management with memory, where the system decides what to keep.

## In his words

> "Think of the tokens in the context window as a precious resource."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-02-27

## Apply

- Press "new chat" when you change subject, not only when a chat gets slow.
- Before you continue a long chat, ask whether its early messages still help. If not, copy only the
  useful facts into a new chat.
- Our reading, for coding agents (he spoke about chat apps): keep one session per task, and hand
  off through a file (decisions, state, open items), not through a long history. Do not trust
  automatic compaction with key decisions; write them down yourself.
- Group long-running work into projects, keep one default chat for quick questions, and when a chat gets too long, write a summary and continue in a new chat (a reader's setup he called interesting, 2025-03-20).

## Context

- From *How I use LLMs* (2025-02-27), a guide for general users shown with ChatGPT, and an X post
  of 2025-03-20.
- Related: [Context engineering](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-06-25-context-engineering.md) and
  [Try a fast model first](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-02-27-fast-model-first-thinking-model-for-hard.md).

---

Date: 2025-02-27 · Kind: practice · Source: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EWvNQjAaOHw · Themes: verification, llm-psychology · Status: current

# Treat LLM output as a first draft and check the sources

Karpathy shows several cases where a good-looking answer was wrong. A deep-research table of US
model labs left out a major lab and listed one that did not fit. A data-analysis run quietly
replaced a missing value with an invented number. It also reported a forecast of 1.7 trillion
while its own variable showed about 20 trillion. He compares the tool to a junior analyst who is
capable but absent-minded. His rule: use citations to reach primary sources, read the code the
model writes, and ask it to print the raw value when a number looks odd. For health questions he
also checks the label on the box.

## In his words

> "Treat this as your first draft."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-02-27

## Apply

- Open at least the main cited sources before you use a claim from a research report.
- When a model analyses data, read its code. Look for filled-in missing values and silent assumptions.
- If a printed number disagrees with the summary text, ask for the variable printed alone.
- Use deep-research reports to build a reading list, not as final facts.

## Context

- From *How I use LLMs* (2025-02), with examples from ChatGPT deep research and its data analysis tool.
- Related: [Give agents success criteria, not steps](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-01-26-success-criteria-not-steps.md).

---

Date: 2025-02-27 · Kind: practice · Source: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EWvNQjAaOHw · Themes: agent-native-software · Status: current

# Ask the model to write a small app just for you

In the video, Karpathy asks Claude for 20 flashcards from a text. Then he asks it to use the
artifacts feature to write an app that quizzes him on them. The model writes a small React app
and the interface runs it in the browser. It has no backend or database. He calls this a different
paradigm. Usually engineers ship one app for everyone, with a few settings. Here the model writes
the app for one person. He adds that he is not a daily user of this and uses it now and then.

## Apply

- Ask for the content first (cards, a checklist, a table). Then ask for a tiny app that uses it.
- Keep the request to one screen and one job. Single-file, local apps work best.
- Ask the model to keep the data inside the page, so you can copy it out later.
- Before you search for an app, ask a model to build a small one for the task, and drop it when the task is done.

## Context

- From *How I use LLMs* (2025-02). An early view of a theme he develops later in 2026: software
  written on demand, with agents as the user. See
  [Apps become APIs and agents are the glue](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-20-apps-become-apis-agents-are-glue.md).
- In May 2025 he said many habits break when an app takes a second to make: software stops being scarce, and you no longer have to pick from what exists. He also found it easier to build his own tool than to find one.

Date: 2025-02-24 · Kind: view · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1894099637218545984 · Themes: learning-and-education, ai-progress · Status: current

# Agency matters more than intelligence, and is scarcer

Karpathy says he got this wrong for decades, because culture, media and IQ talk put
intelligence on a pedestal. Agency, the capacity to take initiative and shape what happens, is
much more powerful and much more scarce. He turned it into three questions for the reader: are
you hiring for agency, are you educating for agency, and are you acting as if you had ten times
more agency? The post quoted a comment that intelligence is now on tap, so agency matters even more.

## In his words

> "Agency is significantly more powerful and significantly more scarce."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-02-24

## Apply

- Ask his three questions of your team and yourself: are we hiring for agency, educating for
  agency, and acting as if we had 10X agency?

## Context

- Later posts on the same line: [Expertise may matter more with agents, not less](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-01-26-expertise-multiplier-generalists-and-10x.md) and [Test candidates on building and securing a project with agents](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-04-30-hire-for-agentic-engineering.md).

---

Date: 2025-02-18 · Kind: view · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1891909328795492703 · Themes: ai-progress · Status: current

# Three breakthroughs so far; autonomous agents need a few more

Asked whether LLM limits come from the architecture, Karpathy first limited the question. Today's
evals are small "task" problems served neatly, even when hard. When people talk about AGI they
mean an autonomous swarm of agents doing long jobs across society. He believes that needs major
research breakthroughs and not scaling alone.

He counted three breakthroughs so far: the Transformer (about 2017), ChatGPT with supervised
finetuning and RLHF (about 2022), and reinforcement learning for thinking models (about 2024),
which is still maturing. He expects a few more of that size.

A month earlier he made the same split on the Humanity's Last Exam benchmark: every task served
on a platter will improve, even PhD-level ones, but jobs needing long, error-correcting chains
of tasks will take longer, a Moravec's paradox effect. He called the "last exam" name misleading.

## In his words

> "I think we need a few more conceptual leaps of this class."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-02-18

## Context

- Same reasoning as [Hard closed problems are easy; long autonomous jobs are hard](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2024-11-10-llms-solve-hard-prompts-but-fail-long-jobs.md).
- It fits his later claim in [This is the decade of agents, not the year of agents](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-10-17-decade-of-agents-not-year.md).

---

Date: 2025-02-14 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1890208670732124372 · Themes: context-and-prompting, agentic-coding · Status: current

# Pack your project into one prompt for a quick, scoped question

In February 2025 Karpathy asked more apps to offer an "Export for prompt" button, after a trick
that turns a GitHub repo URL into a gitingest URL to get the whole repo as one text. In August he
described his own routine. When agents search the whole repo and think for minutes, he sometimes
skips them. He runs a script that packs all project files into one text with the tool
`files-to-prompt`. He opens a new chat, pastes the text, asks one question at the end, and chooses
the model by hand. This works because his project is small enough to fit in the context.

## Apply

- Keep a script that bundles your files into one text file (`files-to-prompt .` or gitingest).
- Start a new chat per question, paste the bundle, and put the question last.
- Choose the model yourself: a fast one for spot checks, a strong one for hard bugs.
- Check the bundle size first; if it does not fit, send only the folders that matter.

## Context

- Quote post of 2025-02-14 about gitingest, then a
  [reply of 2025-08-09](https://x.com/karpathy/status/1954227464596832670) in a thread about agents
  that are too eager. Works only for repos that fit the context window.
- Related: [Models are too agentic: state the stakes and scope](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-08-09-models-too-agentic-state-stakes-and-scope.md).
- His later tool for the same job: [Flatten a repository into one page for humans and LLMs](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-08-20-render-repo-for-humans-and-llms.md).

Date: 2025-02-12 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1889714240878940659 · Themes: security-and-dependencies, llm-psychology · Status: current

# Invisible Unicode characters can smuggle data and prompts into an LLM

Karpathy knew about look-alike characters such as a Latin "e" and a Cyrillic "е". He then
pointed to a write-up showing that you can also hide any byte stream inside a single character
using Unicode "variation selectors". An emoji that looks like one symbol then turns into dozens
of tokens, as a tokenizer viewer showed.

He ran a test of prompt injection with the hidden bytes. It worked only when the prompt gave
explicit decoding hints. Thinking models seemed more exposed, because they notice odd bytes and
get curious. DeepSeek-R1 spent ten minutes searching for a pattern and nearly decoded it. He
noted that if the article enters pretraining data, a future model might decode it with no hint.
Later he called it a really bad idea of Unicode. Two readers pointed out that this is a
Unicode property, not a UTF-8 one; he agreed.

## In his words

> "you can also smuggle arbitrary byte streams in any character"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-02-12

## Apply

Our reading: all steps below go further than the idea itself.

- Paste suspicious text into a tokenizer viewer. A short visible string with a huge token count
  signals hidden characters.
- Treat text from outside your control (web pages, issues, documents) as untrusted before it
  goes into an agent's context.
- Strip or flag variation selectors and other invisible code points in untrusted input before it
  reaches a model. Variation selectors are U+FE00-U+FE0F and U+E0100-U+E01EF (our addition: his
  post names no range; the Unicode standard defines them).

## Context

- A test on Grok 3 a few days later: it could not decode the hidden message even with a hint in
  Rust code. See [Public benchmarks are gameable, so keep your own evals](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-11-18-go-talk-to-the-model-private-evals.md).
- Related: [Third-party models can hide sleeper agents](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2024-01-12-sleeper-agent-llms-and-poisoned-models.md).

---

Date: 2025-02-07 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1887980449550758121 · Themes: learning-and-education · Status: current

# Make a long from-scratch intro to your own field

After his 3.5-hour "Deep Dive into LLMs like ChatGPT", Karpathy said one reason he made it was
to inspire others to make the same kind of video in their own areas of expertise. His example:
he read an article about superconductivity in layered graphene and wanted an expert to take him
through that area in a three-hour intro from scratch. He said many other fields would work too.

The format is a general-audience walkthrough that covers the whole pipeline of a subject and
adds mental models. He described the recording process as simple: OBS to record, a few takes
per clip, and iMovie to stitch the clips.

## In his words

> "I hope to inspire others to make equivalents in their own domains of expertise"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-02-07

## Apply

- Pick the area you know best and outline the whole path from basics to current practice, in
  the order a newcomer needs it.
- Record in short clips with a free screen recorder and redo clips that go wrong; stitch them
  in a basic editor.
- Add worked examples and say how experts think about the field, not only what the facts are.

## Context

- The video pairs with a second one, "How I Use LLMs", and is also an input for
  [Read with an LLM in three passes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-11-17-read-everything-with-llms-three-passes.md): long, structured material is easier to learn from.
- A reader asked for a deeper part 2; he asked for bullet-point suggestions.

Date: 2025-02-02 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1886192184808149383 · Themes: agentic-coding · Status: current

# Vibe coding is fine for throwaway projects

In February 2025 Karpathy named a style of work: vibe coding. You give in to the vibes. You talk to the editor by voice, accept every change, and never read the diffs. You paste error messages back with no comment. If a bug will not go away, you work around it. He says this is fine for throwaway weekend projects. The code grows past what you understand, and you stop caring that it exists. The idea is a label for a real way of working, with a clear limit on where it is safe.

## In his words

> "forget that the code even exists"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-02-02

## Apply

- Use vibe mode for disposable prototypes, demos and one-off scripts only.
- For code you keep, read the diffs and run tests. See [a rhythm for code you care about](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-04-24-ai-assisted-coding-rhythm.md).
- Paste raw error output into the agent instead of describing it. This is the cheapest loop for a throwaway project.
- Decide before you start whether the project is throwaway. Write that in the first prompt.

## Context

- Posted 2025-02-02, when the main tool was an AI editor with a composer pane and a voice tool.
- His own method for kept code is in [a rhythm for code you care about](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-04-24-ai-assisted-coding-rhythm.md).
- By December 2025 he described code as cheap and ephemeral: [Code is now free, custom and disposable](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-12-19-code-is-free-and-ephemeral.md).
- Still current. A year later he named the professional, reviewed form
  [agentic engineering](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-02-04-agentic-engineering-vs-vibe-coding.md), but kept vibe coding
  as the right mode for throwaway work: at Sequoia 2026 he said it "raises the floor".
- He sees AI help as a slider, from coding as it was three years ago to full vibe coding. In March 2025 he said he seldom goes fully vibe: most of the time he still reads the code and learns how the parts fit.

---

Date: 2025-02-01 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1885740680804504010 · Themes: verification, research-and-training · Status: current

# Evaluate models by making them play each other

Fixed evals saturate. Karpathy likes the idea of using games to compare LLMs head to head.
When a model plays another intelligent player, the difficulty balances itself: a strong player
meets a strong opponent, so the same environment keeps giving a signal. He pointed to early
attempts, such as a text-game collection with a gym-style interface, and suggested Codenames
and Diplomacy as good fits. In both, much of the difficulty comes from reasoning about other
players and about the world, not from the rules.

He built a small Battleship app himself, in which any two models fight in real time. Another
builder reported that models playing Diplomacy came across as meek and peaceful, which tells
you something about their training.

## In his words

> "Playing against another intelligent entity self-balances and adapts difficulty"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-02-01

## Apply

- Pick a game with simple rules and hidden information or negotiation (Codenames, Battleship,
  Diplomacy) and let two models play. Log the moves and the reasoning.
- Swap which model plays which side, and play several rounds, because single games are noisy.
- Read the game logs, not only the win count: they show how each model plans and communicates.

## Context

- Posted a day after the DeepSeek-R1 wave, when the field was looking for new RL environments;
  see [RL environments are the new training data](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-08-27-rl-environments-are-the-new-data.md).
- Our reading: he suggests the idea and early results; he does not claim a finished benchmark.

---

Date: 2025-01-30 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1885026028428681698 · Themes: learning-and-education, research-and-training · Status: current

# LLMs need the practice problems of a textbook

Karpathy notes that a textbook has three kinds of content. Exposition matches pretraining. Worked problems match supervised finetuning. Practice problems with answers match RL. LLMs have plenty of the first two. The third is the nascent frontier. Later posts extend this. In November 2024 he said exercise pages gathered at scale now move billions of weights, so textbooks are partly written for LLMs. In August 2025 he proposed turning each textbook into LLM-first material: markdown exposition, worked problems as examples, practice problems as RL environments with answer keys, and problem generators.

## In his words

> "They have to read, and they have to practice."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-01-30

## Apply

- When you teach an agent a skill, give worked examples and practice tasks with checkable answers, not only explanations.
- Turn your docs into markdown with runnable examples that an agent can query.
- Use a problem generator to make many test cases for the same skill.
- Keep practice problems at the right level: not trivial, not impossible. If every problem is too hard, reinforcement learning gets no signal (his reply of 2025-02-19).
- Turn the practice problems of a textbook into RL-style environments, each checked against its answer key (his reply of 2025-08-27).

## Context

- Posted 2025-01-30; extended on 2024-11-15 (earlier) and 2025-08-28.
- Related: [RL environments are the new data](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-08-27-rl-environments-are-the-new-data.md).

---

Date: 2025-01-28 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1884336943321997800 · Themes: research-and-training, context-and-prompting · Status: current

# RL gives thinking models strategies you cannot write by hand

Karpathy says that RL on thinking models produces cognitive strategies: trying angles, making analogies, backtracking. People cannot hand-program these. The model may even develop an internal language that we cannot read. He notes that a Move 37 equivalent for these models, a move no human would make, has not been seen yet.

## Apply

- On hard problems, give the model room to think and set the goal and the check, not the method.
- Avoid long step-by-step recipes for reasoning models. See [success criteria, not steps](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-01-26-success-criteria-not-steps.md).
- Test a hard task at higher effort before you rewrite the prompt.

## Context

- Posted 2025-01-28, soon after open reasoning models appeared.
- A day earlier he tied synthetic data to RL: see [Filtering synthetic data is crude reinforcement learning](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-01-27-synthetic-data-and-rl-are-one-loop.md).
- On 2025-11-25 he said AI had gone far past what he expected. His old mistake was to assume that someone must find and write down the algorithm. Instead, it emerges when you pretrain and finetune a big network on many tasks.

---

Date: 2025-01-27 · Kind: view · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1883941452738355376 · Themes: research-and-training · Status: current

# Filtering synthetic data is crude reinforcement learning

Karpathy describes two kinds of learning, in children and in networks. Imitation (pretraining,
supervised finetuning) copies a source. Trial and error (reinforcement learning) tries things
and learns from the result. He says almost every striking deep learning result comes from the
second kind, because the model can find things a human labeller would not know to write down.

He then links synthetic data and RL. In RL the "trial" is the model generating data and the
"error" is the reward. If you generate data and keep only what passes a filter, your filter is a
simple 0-or-1 reward. In a reply he gave the core loop: sample many answers, keep the best,
train on it, repeat. Fancier maths, such as smooth advantages and trust regions, refines this.
He also noted that data is partly downstream of compute, because you can spend compute to make it.

## In his words

> "your filter is straight up equivalent to a 0-1 advantage function"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-01-27

## Apply

- To improve a model on a task you can score, sample several answers, keep the highest-scoring
  one, and finetune on it. Then repeat.
- Keep a reward or check you trust; the loop copies whatever the check rewards.
- Use imitation data for what humans already know, and reward-based training for strategies
  you cannot write down.

## Context

- A reaction to DeepSeek-R1, a week after its release. It builds on [RL gives thinking models strategies you cannot write by hand](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-01-28-cognitive-strategies-cannot-be-hand-programmed.md).
- He added that RL is powerful but RLHF is not; see [An LLM judge gets gamed when you optimise against it](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2024-08-07-rlhf-is-just-barely-rl.md).

---

Date: 2025-01-17 · Kind: view · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1880057571668807830 · Themes: learning-and-education, ai-progress · Status: current

# People may train their minds the way they go to the gym

A reply to a worry that skills AI can teach, AI can also perform for the economy, so learning
loses its point. Karpathy answers with an analogy from the physical world. Machines removed the
economic need for muscle, but people still go to the gym in large numbers. In a world of high
automation, the economy will need fewer human brains. People will still do the mental
equivalent of going to the gym, for the same reasons.

Our reading: he separates the economic reason to learn from the personal one, and says only
the first one weakens.

## In his words

> "People don’t need muscles when we have machines but still go to gym"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-01-17

## Context

- Related view on effort: [Learning takes effort, unlike entertainment](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2024-02-10-learning-is-not-supposed-to-be-fun.md).
- Later he argued for testing yourself without AI: [Use AI to learn, but test without it](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-11-24-learn-with-ai-but-test-without-it.md).

Date: 2025-01-02 · Kind: view · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1874678592702972398 · Themes: llm-psychology · Status: current

# A good assistant skips the lecture and the flattery

Asked what he would change about Claude, Karpathy listed quirks of tone. The model talks down
to him with phrases like "it's important to". It follows a refusal with a lecture on morals. It
praises him too fast, which feels fake and a little manipulative. It apologises too much. What
he wants is the model's best effort at the problem, from a calm teammate and not an
over-excited buddy. A plain refusal is fine.

Six weeks later he praised a new ChatGPT 4o personality that felt more like a friend than an HR
partner. It was more chill, a little sassy, and it named the user's frustration. He still
disliked its long lists and growing use of emoji.

## In his words

> "I wish Claude would talk down to me less and do less grandstanding"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-01-02

## Apply

- Add a line to your custom instructions such as: "Answer directly. No moral lectures, no
  compliments on my question, no apology unless you made an error."
- When you test a new model, note its tone as well as its accuracy: flattery, lists, emoji, lectures.
- If a model refuses, ask it to state the refusal in one sentence and move on to what it can do.

## Context

- The first post answers a question from a researcher at Anthropic. He also said Claude seemed
  to have had the most thought put into its personality.
- Later views on the same theme: [AI personality should feel like a teammate](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-21-ai-personality-like-rocky.md).

---

Date: 2024-12-25 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1872038630405054853 · Themes: agentic-coding · Status: current

# Cognitive load is what matters in software engineering

Karpathy endorsed an essay titled Cognitive load is what matters. He called it the most true, and least practiced, viewpoint of software engineering. The idea: good code is code that a person can hold in their head. Our reading: this matters more as agents write more code, because people must still review it.

## Apply

- Ask the agent for simple, flat code with few abstractions and short functions.
- In review, ask: could I explain this in two minutes? If not, simplify.
- Delete code paths and options that no one uses.

## Context

- Posted 2024-12-25. This entry only records his endorsement. Read the essay for its argument.

---

Date: 2024-12-14 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1868061331355840704 · Themes: agentic-coding, verification · Status: current

# Judge an agent as you would a junior intern

Karpathy says the capability to watch is not PhD-level problems. It is the junior intern: you say set up your Slack, read the onboarding docs, do this task, and check in next week. Our reading: that test needs long coherent work, not clever answers. It is a useful way to rate an agent and to write briefs for one.

## In his words

> "whether you'd hire it as a junior intern"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2024-12-14

## Apply

- Write the agent instruction file like onboarding docs: goals, layout, commands, who decides what.
- Assign week-sized tasks with a clear check in, and review at the check in.
- Rate a new agent by one real task of this size.

## Context

- Posted 2024-12-14. His 2025 view of the model as an over-eager intern is in [tight leash](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-04-24-ai-assisted-coding-rhythm.md).

Date: 2024-12-11 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1866896395363553418 · Themes: learning-and-education, output-and-reading · Status: current

# Read books together with an LLM, one chapter at a time

Karpathy rarely reads a book alone now. In December 2024 he called reading together with an LLM
one of his favourite uses, and said an AI-native reader app would be a hit. In early 2025 he
showed the habit. He pastes the raw text of a chapter into the chat and asks for a summary, so he
knows its shape. Then he reads the chapter himself and asks a question whenever something is
unclear. The model may know the book in general but not recall the chapter, so the text goes into
the context window. He says this helps most with papers from other fields and with old texts. In
November 2025 he released reader3, a small self-hosted EPUB reader that shows one chapter at a time
for easy copying. He prefers EPUB to PDF because code can parse it into clean text.

## In his words

> "And don't read books alone."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2025-02-27

## Apply

- Get the book as EPUB (Project Gutenberg has many) and convert it to text with reader3 or a small
  parser.
- Paste one chapter into a new chat. Name the book. Ask: "Summarise this chapter."
- Read the real chapter alongside. Ask short questions where you stall, or ask for context and
  objections.
- Use one chat per chapter so the window stays small and the discussion stays on topic.
- For a paper, upload the PDF and ask for a summary first. Figures may be lost in conversion.

## Context

- X post of 2024-12-11; *How I use LLMs* video of 2025-02-27 (examples: a 1776 economics book and a
  genome-model paper); reader3 repository of 2025-11-18, about 90% vibe coded; a reply of
  2026-01-11 that pointed to reader3.
- In early 2025 he found the workflow clunky: no tool let him highlight a passage and ask about it.
- Related: [Read with an LLM in three passes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-11-17-read-everything-with-llms-three-passes.md),
  [Convert books and PDFs with an agent](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-04-02-convert-documents-with-an-agent.md),
  [Ask for a diagram of what you read](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-02-27-ask-for-a-diagram-of-what-you-read.md) and
  [Treat small apps as disposable](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-11-18-disposable-vibe-coded-apps.md).
- In February 2025 he vibe coded a reader for The Wealth of Nations: click a paragraph, ask a question, and the app sends the chapter, the paragraph and the question to an LLM.
- In September 2025 he said a book works better as a set of prompts that start your own questions, explanations and examples, like synthetic data generation for a model, than as text to absorb, like pretraining data.

Date: 2024-11-29 · Kind: view · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1862565643436138619 · Themes: llm-psychology · Status: current

# Asking an AI is like asking the average data labeler

Karpathy says that when you ask an AI, you are closer to asking an average data labeler, who is skilled in code and math, whose style was distilled into the model. RL changes this only in verifiable domains. On judgment questions you get a competent consensus, not a unique expert view.

## In his words

> "asking the average data labeler"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2024-11-29

## Apply

- For judgment calls, treat the answer as a competent consensus. Ask for dissent and for sources.
- Ask for the opinion of a named type of expert, with the model simulating them. See [there is no 'you'](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-12-07-llms-simulate-there-is-no-you.md).
- Use checks and tests where you can, since that is where models exceed the labeler.

## Context

- Posted 2024-11-29.
- Related: [commercial evolution](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-11-29-llms-shaped-by-commercial-evolution.md).

---

Date: 2024-11-10 · Kind: view · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1855659091877937385 · Themes: ai-progress, verification · Status: current

# Hard closed problems are easy; long autonomous jobs are hard

Karpathy applies Moravec's paradox to LLM evals. Models solve hard, closed problems that arrive neatly in a prompt. They struggle with long, autonomous, coherent sequences, so you would not hire them for menial jobs. He asks for evals of such "menial job" work: long context, coherence, autonomy and common sense.

## Apply

- Give agents closed, well-specified chunks of work.
- Handle long-horizon coordination yourself, or use tight checkpoints and a state file.
- Test a new agent on a long task from your own work, not only on puzzles.

## Context

- Posted 2024-11-10. Related: [the junior intern test](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2024-12-14-would-you-hire-it-as-a-junior-intern.md), which sets a week-sized task as the bar.
- In 2025 he made the same split about the Humanity's Last Exam benchmark: neatly served tasks will improve, while long, error-correcting jobs stay hard, a case of Moravec's paradox. See [Three breakthroughs so far](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-02-18-three-breakthroughs-more-leaps-needed.md).

---

Date: 2024-10-06 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1843005000206909856 · Themes: output-and-reading · Status: current

# Break the shared LLM house voice with a style guide

Karpathy is puzzled that all LLMs sound alike. They overuse lists and words like multifaceted, they offer help too often, and their answers have the same length. This house voice comes from shared training habits. Our reading: you can change it with explicit instructions on length, format and tone.

## Apply

- Add a short style guide to the system prompt or instruction file: length, tone and format.
- List constructions to avoid, such as stock phrases and lists of three.
- Give one example of the voice you want.

## Context

- Posted 2024-10-06.
- In May 2025 he called the convergence of models eerie: not fully true, but true to a surprising degree. In June 2025 he showed five chatbots that all answered 27 when asked to guess a number from 1 to 50.
- In July 2025, after many models gave a science-fiction hero the same name, he wondered if subliminal learning during distillation plays a part, and guessed that more LLM text on the web could pull models toward a shared fixed point. Similar training sets are a simpler cause.
- In August 2025 he guessed why finetuning did not make models differ: it is short and carries few bits, so it mostly moves style on a shared pretrained base. RL, with many more bits over a much longer run, might separate models more.

---

Date: 2024-08-07 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1821277264996352246 · Themes: research-and-training, verification · Status: current

# An LLM judge gets gamed when you optimise against it

Karpathy explains why reinforcement learning from human feedback is only barely RL. It optimises a
reward model that scores the vibe of an answer, and models game it quickly with adversarial
examples. Real RL needs a reward that is hard to game, such as winning at Go. RLHF still helps,
because judging is easier than writing. In his 2025 Dwarkesh interview he told how the same problem
hits labs that use an LLM to give partial credit. In one run the reward jumped to perfect. The
answers had turned into nonsense, a string of repeated letters, and the judge rated it fully
correct. You can add such cases to the judge's training data, but there are endless more. So a
judge works for perhaps 10 or 20 optimisation steps, not hundreds.

## Apply

- Prefer checks that cannot be argued with (tests, exact match, executable results) over a judge.
- If you loop an agent against an LLM grader, limit the rounds and read samples.
- Treat a sudden jump to a perfect score as a warning. Read the raw outputs before you trust it.
- Use best-of-N: generate several candidates and let a judge pick.
- If you must use a judge, use a different model from the one being optimised, and spot-check by
  hand.

## Context

- X post of 2024-08-07; Dwarkesh Patel interview of 2025-10-17.
- Related: [RL sucks supervision through a straw](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-10-17-rl-supervision-through-a-straw.md),
  [LLM judges grade too freely](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-12-10-llm-grader-identity-bias.md) and
  [Software 2.0 automates what you can verify](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-11-17-software-2-automates-what-you-can-verify.md).

---

Date: 2024-03-12 · Kind: view · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1767598414945292695 · Themes: agentic-coding · Status: current

# Software engineering climbs an autonomy ladder like self-driving

In March 2024 Karpathy compared software engineering to self-driving. The steps: manual coding, autocomplete of lines, chat that writes chunks, editors that write larger diffs, and agents that coordinate the terminal, browser and editor with a human watching at a higher level. The editor and the oversight experience must change a lot: what to look at, how to nudge, how to debug. Engineering becomes supervising automation in English.

## In his words

> "supervising the automation"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2024-03-12

## Apply

- Invest in oversight: diff summaries, run logs and state views for agent work.
- Practice reviewing at a higher level: check the plan and the result before the code.
- Decide what each agent may do without asking.

## Context

- Posted 2024-03-12. Still matters: agent tools of 2025 follow this ladder. See [the junior intern test](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2024-12-14-would-you-hire-it-as-a-junior-intern.md) and [AI and jobs](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-09-25-ai-and-jobs-radiologists-and-engineers.md).

---

Date: 2024-02-21 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1760388761349927356 · Themes: learning-and-education · Status: current

# Build the thing, then build the ramp

Karpathy says his micrograd project stagnated until he made a from-scratch video. The same code then got about a hundred times more engagement. Technical people assume code and a README explain themselves. They do not. Accessibility leaves ten to a hundred times of reach on the table. His rule has two steps: build the thing, then build the ramp that lets others climb onto it.

## In his words

> "Step 1 build the thing. Step 2 build the ramp."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2024-02-21

## Apply

- After a project works, ask the agent for a walkthrough: a guided tour of the code, an HTML explainer or a script for a video.
- Write the ramp for your future self too: why the design is this way, and how to run it.
- Test the ramp on someone new to the code.

## Context

- Posted 2024-02-21. This post was about teaching; AI makes the ramp cheap to produce.

---

Date: 2024-02-10 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1756380066580455557 · Themes: learning-and-education · Status: current

# Learning takes effort, unlike entertainment

Karpathy says much "educational" short video is entertainment. Learning should feel like effort, like sweating at the gym. He suggests you declare your intent as binary: you are entertained, or you are learning. For learning, go to the meal (textbooks, docs, papers), set aside about four hours, take notes, reread and rephrase. The idea matters more with LLMs, because a model can make passive explanations that feel like learning and are not.

## In his words

> "Learning is not supposed to be fun."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2024-02-10

## Apply

- Ask the model to quiz you, to make you rebuild a result from memory, and to critique your explanation, not only to summarize.
- Block a long focused session for a new topic. Take notes by hand or in your own words.
- Say at the start whether you want entertainment or learning.

## Context

- Posted 2024-02-10. In November 2025 he added a short reply that fake learning is 'edutainment'.
- Related: [AI and schools](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-11-24-learn-with-ai-but-test-without-it.md).

---

Date: 2024-01-20 · Kind: view · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1748784260318990496 · Themes: knowledge-management, research-and-training · Status: current

# The ideal training data is the thinking, not the final text

Karpathy says the ideal data for training an LLM is the whole sequence of internal thoughts and edits that led to a text, not the final text. We usually only keep the output. For a user, the point carries over: an agent that reads your reasoning can help better than one that sees only results.

## Apply

- Keep decision logs and working notes in the repo, so agents see why choices were made.
- Write the reasons next to each decision, not only the outcome.
- Keep failed attempts in a short 'tried and rejected' list.

## Context

- Posted 2024-01-20. Related practice: [system prompt learning](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-05-10-system-prompt-learning.md).
- In January 2025 he guessed that the most valuable data would be screen recordings of exceptional people at work, ideally with their goals and reasoning recorded too.

Date: 2024-01-12 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1745921205020799433 · Themes: security-and-dependencies · Status: current

# Third-party models can hide sleeper agents

Karpathy points to a risk beyond prompt injection: poisoned training text or open-weights models that behave normally until a trigger phrase appears. Safety finetuning may not remove such behavior. So a model is part of your supply chain, like a package.

## Apply

- Treat third-party models, skills and MCP servers as untrusted code. Read them before use.
- Run new tools in a sandbox, with no access to secrets.
- Limit what an agent can do with scoped tokens.

## Context

- Posted 2024-01-12, from a paper on sleeper agents. Still relevant to skills and MCP servers.

---

Date: 2023-12-08 · Kind: practice · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1733299213503787018 · Themes: llm-psychology, verification · Status: current

# Hallucination is the LLM's main feature, so the system must check it

In December 2023 Karpathy called LLMs dream machines that are directed by prompts. A search engine dreams 0 percent of the time, which gives it a creativity problem. An LLM dreams 100 percent of the time, which gives it a hallucination problem. So the assistant system should reduce the risk with retrieval, comparing several samples, reflection, verification chains and tool use. This view still helps when you design checks around an agent.

## In his words

> "Hallucination is not a bug, it is LLM's greatest feature."
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2023-12-08

## Apply

- Ground the agent in real files and docs, and ask it to cite the file and line.
- For a risky claim, ask the same question several times and check where the answers differ.
- Let tools check facts (run the code, query the data) before you trust a statement.

## Context

- Posted 2023-12-08. Kept because the advice still applies.
- Related: [what you can verify](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-11-17-software-2-automates-what-you-can-verify.md).
- He says he probably coined "hallucinate" for this in his 2015 RNN post. Hinton's "confabulate" is closer to human psychology but too tied to facts, so he prefers the broader word.

---

Date: 2023-09-28 · Kind: view · Source: https://x.com/karpathy/status/1707437820045062561 · Themes: agent-native-software, llm-psychology · Status: current

# The LLM OS, with the model as CPU and the agent as kernel

In 2023 Karpathy said the LLM is not a chatbot but the core of a new operating system. It
orchestrates input and output across text, images and audio, a code interpreter, a browser and an
embeddings memory. In November 2023 he sketched this "LLM OS": the model is the CPU, the context
window is RAM, files and embeddings are the disk, and classical tools such as a calculator, a
Python interpreter and a browser are peripherals. Security ideas from classic operating systems
carry over. In March 2026, asked whether an agent is just a prompt, skills and tools, he sharpened
the picture. The LLM is like a CPU, but it works on tokens, not bytes, and its behaviour is
statistical and vague, not exact. The agent is the kernel that runs on that CPU.

## In his words

> "Agent = operating system kernel"
> — Andrej Karpathy, 2026-03-31

## Apply

- Design the agent harness like an OS: scheduling, memory, permissions and tool input/output live
  in the agent layer; the LLM does the reasoning steps.
- Treat the context window as scarce RAM: load what a step needs, and page the rest in from files.
- Put exact work (maths, parsing) in classical tools the agent calls, since the CPU is fuzzy.
- Plan permissions and sandboxing at the start.

## Context

- Posts of 2023-09-28 and 2023-11-10, and replies of 2026-03-31 to Guido van Rossum. The 2023
  specs (GPT-4 Turbo, 128K tokens) show how much has changed; the structure has held.
- In 2023 he called the LLM itself the "kernel process"; by 2026 the kernel role sits with the
  agent. Our reading: a refinement as agent harnesses matured, not a reversal.
- The 2025 version of the analogy adds cloud time-sharing: [LLMs are like 1960s operating systems](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-06-17-llms-are-1960s-operating-systems.md).
- Related: [Software 3.0](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2025-06-17-software-3-0-english-as-programs.md) and
  [DevOps as code for agents](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ntroccoli/karpathy-ideas/main/ideas/2026-03-26-devops-as-code-for-agents.md).
